channel.title: SugarMount – Small Android apps that each do one thing
channel.description: Small Android apps that each do one thing simply, from shrinking photos and opening Korean HWP documents to checking Korean spelling and playing puzzle games.

item.title: AXFamily: shared family calendar and AI assistant – SugarMount
item.description:
AXFamily

AXFamily is an Android shared family calendar that gathers your family's events and to-dos in one place and shows who is taking care of each one.

Coming soon

AXFamily privacy policy

Use it to

  • Stop sorting out school notices and class schedules over chat every time
  • Share childcare with grandparents and decide who takes care of what
  • Plan a trip with kids around nap and meal times

What it does

  • Decide who does what

    Tap "I'll do it" on a to-do so your family sees who's on it, or "Can't do it" when you can't. Check off things to bring one by one, and turn on notifications for reminders before events.

  • A heads-up every Sunday evening

    With notifications on, every Sunday evening you see to-dos nobody took, overlapping events, deadlines and birthdays within 7 days. The list is free and doesn't count toward AI uses.

  • Dates and things to bring from a notice photo

    Upload a photo of a school notice and AI finds its dates and things to bring. It is added only after you check it and tap Save.

  • Ask the AI assistant

    Open "Ask the family" and ask "What am I in charge of this week?" It answers from your family's events and to-dos, shows which record it used, and says so if there's none. Ask it to add an event and it drafts one; it's saved only when you tap Save.

  • Trip and weekend helper

    Pick where, when and who's going for a day-by-day plan, with packing, a budget and who does what. It fits around your kids' nap, meal and bed times, and marks opening hours, prices and travel times "Check details". The plan is added only after every adult on the trip says yes.

  • Family memories

    Within a week after a trip or event, it suggests an album of its events and photos. Ask "When was our beach trip last year?" to find it. Only records of adults who agreed to AI are used.

  • Your items stay yours

    New events and records start private. Share them with the whole family or chosen people, or pick "Time only" to show when you're busy, not what it is. No one else, even the family admin, sees your private items, not even through the AI.

At a glance

StatusComing soon
FamilyAdults join from an invite message. Kids are added as profiles, no sign-in or phone needed.
AccountGoogle account or email, age 19 or older
PlansEvents, to-dos, reminders, the Sunday heads-up and sharing settings are free (5 AI uses a month, 1,000 photos, one banner ad). Family Plus subscription: no ads, 150 AI uses a month, 10,000 photos
AIGoogle's Gemini model. Each adult turns it on with their own consent.
InternetNeeded (records are shared with your family).
LanguagesKorean and English
Android12L or later
Package namecom.sugarmount.axfamily
Developersimpest (SugarMount)

Data and permissions

  • Family records are never shared with advertisers. Personalized ads are shown only if you agree.
  • Photos are uploaded as small copies without location data. Originals stay on your phone.
  • For children under 14, names and notes aren't sent to the AI. Events and trips a child joins use an age group (like "elementary") instead of a name.
  • Health records are not sent to the AI unless you turn them on, and then only your own.
  • Delete your account and records in the app's Settings or from the account deletion request page. Cancel subscriptions in Google Play.

See AXFamily privacy policy for details.

What it can't do

  • AXFamily is in internal testing and not yet public on Google Play.
  • AI can be wrong. AI text is labeled "AI-generated"; always check opening hours, prices and travel times yourself.
  • AI uses are shared by the family and refill on the 1st of each month. Daily limits apply (20 per person, 30 per family).
  • AXFamily isn't made by a school. Upload the notices you receive yourself.

Frequently asked questions

Do kids need an account?

No. Kids are added as profiles without signing in, and they don't need a phone. Accounts are for adults aged 19 or older.

Can I use it without AI?

Yes. Events, to-dos and reminders all work without AI. AI turns on only for adults who each agree to it.

Can my partner see my private events?

No. Items you keep private can't be seen by anyone else, even the family admin, and don't show up when someone else asks the AI.

How do I delete my account?

Delete it in the app's Settings or request it from the account deletion request page. Cancel subscriptions separately in Google Play.

Related apps

  • SugarSpeller
  • SugarClip
  • HWP Viewer SugarDoc

Last updated October 31, 2026

Contact

If something isn't working or you have a question, email us.

Email: sugarmount21@gmail.com · Package name: com.sugarmount.axfamily

item.title: TrimBox: 3D trunk packing for camping gear – SugarMount
item.description:
TrimBox

TrimBox is an Android app that auto-packs your camping gear into a 3D Kia Sorento trunk and checks whether the tailgate still closes.

Coming soon

TrimBox privacy policy

Use it to

  • Find out before a camping trip whether everything fits in one go
  • Decide what to load first: tent, cooler, chairs or table
  • Check whether new gear fits alongside what you already pack, before buying it

What it does

  • One tap: Will it fit?

    Tells you how many items in your current layout are blocked and how many would fit after repacking, and applies the better layout with one tap. Blocked items turn red with the reason: wheel arch, ceiling, tailgate, seatback or another item.

  • Tailgate check and second-row slide

    If the top of a load hits the sloped tailgate, it shows how far it sticks out. If not everything fits, it suggests how many centimeters to slide the second-row seats forward.

  • Auto-pack

    Big items go low and deep, long items are laid flat, small items fill the gaps. Items of 20 kg or more stay on the floor and things you reach for often, like a cooler, go near the tailgate. It never returns a layout with floating or overlapping items.

  • Loading order guide

    Numbers every item in the order to load it and steps through them one at a time.

  • 184 camping items

    184 camping items such as tents, tarps, tables, chairs, coolers, sleeping bags, mats and storage boxes, plus 8 suitcases and 5 moving boxes. Search, set a quantity, or add one of 3 suggested sets (Minimal for 2, Family of 4, Solo backpacking). Enter the size of anything missing.

  • Move things yourself, and save

    Rotate and zoom the trunk, drag items, rotate or delete them, undo and redo. Layouts save automatically, and you can save several by name.

At a glance

StatusComing soon
Supported carKia Sorento 4th gen (MQ4), 5-seat and 7-seat with the third row folded. Other cars as a simple box from trunk sizes you enter
StorageLayouts stay on your phone.
InternetNot needed (no internet permission).
LanguagesKorean and English (follows your phone's language by default; change it from the app menu)
AccountNot needed.
Package namecom.sugarmount.trimbox
Developersimpest (SugarMount)

Data and permissions

  • The app has no internet permission and no ads, analytics or crash reporting SDK.
  • Layouts and their names are stored only on your phone.
  • Sharing or saving an image, exporting or importing a layout file and sending feedback email happen only when you tap them, through Android's share sheet, photo storage, file picker or your mail app. The error log stays on your phone and goes into a feedback email only if you choose to include it.

See TrimBox privacy policy for details.

What it can't do

  • This is a beta. The Kia Sorento MQ4 is the only car with a real trunk shape for now.
  • Some dimensions (height, tailgate slope, wheel-arch length) are estimates from owner measurements and published data and may differ from your car by a few centimeters. Leave some room for tight fits.
  • Every item is treated as a box of its width, depth and height. Under-floor storage, an upright third row and the luggage cover are not modeled.
  • Weights are estimates from product data or typical values for the item type.
  • A layout holds up to 64 items.
  • TrimBox is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by Kia Corporation. SORENTO is a trademark of Kia Corporation.

Frequently asked questions

Does it work with other cars?

The only car with a real trunk shape for now is the Kia Sorento MQ4 (5-seat, or 7-seat with the third row folded). For other cars, enter trunk width, depth and height (wheel arches optional) to get a simple box shape.

How close is the verdict to my real car?

Dimensions come from 8 owner tape-measure reports and published data, but some are estimates and may be off by a few centimeters. Leave room for tight fits, and tell us at sugarmount21@gmail.com if a dimension looks wrong.

Does it need the internet?

No. The app has no internet permission and does every calculation on your phone.

Related apps

  • SugarCard
  • SugarAlbum
  • Compress Image

Last updated October 31, 2026

Contact

If something isn't working or you have a question, email us.

Email: sugarmount21@gmail.com · Package name: com.sugarmount.trimbox

item.title: Our .gz Android assets hit FileNotFoundException – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException

Our pre-gzipped level packs were each 18 bytes larger than the APK's own compressed copies, and the build dropped the trailing .gz, so the files could not be opened on the device.

The five pre-gzipped level packs totaled 705,234 bytes. The same packs shipped as plain text take 705,144 bytes compressed inside the release APK. The "4.4×" that justified gzip at design time compared raw files with gz files; the draft never compared gz with what the APK does on its own. The choice surfaced at 22:28 on October 3, 2026 (KST), when the 1,000-level update of Arrow Knots died with FileNotFoundException right after launch on our S21. Every JVM test that read the same packs had passed.

Sources: the game repository's git history (f5b50c0, e3c7781, 4d46413), the monkey log and APK listing in that day's agent session record, and compressed sizes read with Python's zipfile from the release and debug APKs built on October 28, 2026. Checked October 30, 2026.

705,234 bytes as gz files, 705,144 inside the APK

We opened the release APK built on October 28, 2026, read the raw and compressed size of each of the five level packs, and set them next to the .gz files the repository held until commit 4d46413. The pack contents haven't changed since 4d46413, and each old .gz, decompressed, has the same SHA-1 as its plain pack, so these are the same bytes.

PackRawOld .gz fileCompressed in release APKDifference
p1 (1-200)122,96625,89625,87818
p2 (201-500)524,852111,113111,09518
p3 (501-700)679,344147,461147,44318
p4 (701-1000)1,397,319310,108310,09018
endless (1001-1100)492,814110,656110,63818
Total3,217,295705,234705,14490

Every pack differs by exactly 18 bytes. A gzip file wraps deflate data in a 10-byte header and an 8-byte trailer (CRC32 and original length), so the compressed bodies are the same size and the gap is the gzip wrapper. Don't pre-gzip text assets.

In the debug APK the same packs take 1,195,288 bytes, about 1.7 times the release figure. We haven't checked why. Measure asset sizes in a release APK.

The design's 4.4× compared the wrong pair

The case for gzip was one line in a design draft an agent wrote that afternoon: "300 levels = 535 KB raw / 121 KB gz (4.4×)", with an estimate of 0.7 to 0.85 MB gzipped for 1,000 levels. Raw sizes never ship, since the APK compresses the plain packs too. The pair to compare was the gz files against the plain packs as the APK compresses them.

The format went into the update spec committed at 17:18 (f5b50c0). Its commit message says 24 agents cross-checked it. It put the packs in assets as .pack.gz and had the app read them with GZIPInputStream. At 18:32 commit e3c7781 generated the five packs in that format. That commit was part of a 41-agent workflow (implementation, review and merges) that finished at 22:27 with "none failed". Why that "done" meant JVM tests and a debug build is covered in "Use hundreds of agents" in practice.

The APK listing had only arrows-p1.pack

The fresh-install monkey test caught it first; it ran because the operator's first request said to install on the S21 and run E2E. The script clears app data and sends 800 random events with seeds 7, 21 and 99. Seeds 7 and 21 each logged two fatal exceptions, and every one that made it into the log had the same message:

E AndroidRuntime: java.lang.RuntimeException: Unable to start activity
  ComponentInfo{…/sugar.arrows.MainActivity}:
  java.io.FileNotFoundException: arrows-p1.pack.gz

Thirty seconds later the agent listed the assets inside the debug APK. The source folder had arrows-p1.pack.gz at 25,896 bytes; the APK had assets/arrows-p1.pack at 122,966 bytes. All five packs looked like that: no .gz in the name, stored at their decompressed size. The commit message attributes this to aapt.

The tests opened the same files through a different function

The app and the tests share PackStore, the class that reads packs, but each passes in its own way to open a file. MainActivity uses PackStore(open = assets::open). ProgressTest uses PackStore(open = { FileInputStream(File(ASSETS, it)) }), where ASSETS is src/main/assets. The tests read the repository files as they are, so they see the .gz name and the gzip bytes. The generator module's test helper Shipped even carried the comment "read the way the app and tools read them". The app reads through AssetManager.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Plain packs, and what renaming the extension would have kept

At 22:31, 4d46413 decompressed the packs into plain .pack files and removed GZIPInputStream from Levels.kt. The generator's writeGz became writePack, which writes text. The same commit deleted arrows-v2.pack (534,864 bytes), an old pack the app no longer read; two tests still did, and were moved to the new packs. Before the commit, 256 tests passed (engine 83, generator 40, app 133). At 22:34 the reinstalled app on the S21 had 0 fatal exceptions on all three monkey seeds and got through the tutorial to level 1.

Two other fixes were possible. Renaming the extension to something else would keep the build away from the name, so gzip could stay. But the table shows there is no size to gain, and all that would remain is GZIPInputStream plus the mtime-0 header the generator wrote to keep builds byte-identical. Keeping .gz in the source and having only the app open .pack would work on a device, but the tests would go on reading a different name and format than the app, which is how this crash got through. Neither alternative was tried in the repository; this comparison is our judgment while writing the note.

What the 19-line name test doesn't look at

The body of AssetNamesTest, added in 4d46413, is two statements. It was run before the fix and failed at 22:29 with no asset name ends in gz FAILED.

val gz = File("src/main/assets").listFiles().orEmpty().map { it.name }.filter { it.endsWith(".gz") }
assertTrue(gz.isEmpty(), "aapt renames these on install: $gz")

listFiles() doesn't descend into subfolders, so a file like assets/levels/x.gz slips past. Other source sets such as src/debug/assets, and the assets of the other app module in the same repository, aren't checked either. The "on install" in the message is also wrong: the APK listing showed .pack before anything was installed, so the rename happens at build time. We haven't confirmed which step of AGP 9.4.1 does it. The size result comes from 1,100 levels of text packs only; files that deflate can't shrink are outside it.

Checking asset names and sizes in your own APK

  1. Put the release APK listing next to the source folder: unzip -l app-release.apk | grep assets/ and ls src/main/assets. If names or counts differ, find the code that opens those files.
  2. Add a JVM test that fails on any asset name ending in .gz, and watch it fail before you fix anything. If you have subfolders, use walkTopDown().
  3. Decide whether to pre-compress from the compressed sizes inside the release APK. In Python, add up compress_size over zipfile.ZipFile(apk).infolist() and compare with your gz files.
  4. Open the first screen on a real device from a fresh install with app data cleared. The script is in the fresh-install monkey test note.

Still to do: .pack.gz left in the spec

As of HEAD on October 29, 2026 (2310d1f), the update spec docs/09-parts-1000-spec.md still names .pack.gz five times, on four lines, and still says the packs are read with GZIPInputStream. The helper that reads the plain packs is still called Shipped.gzLines. When the spec gets fixed, we'll also decide how far AssetNamesTest should look.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Why does opening a .gz file from Android assets throw FileNotFoundException?

Because this project's build (AGP 9.4.1) dropped the trailing .gz and stored the file decompressed: the APK listing showed a decompressed x.pack instead of x.pack.gz. Open the name without .gz and drop GZIPInputStream.

Does pre-gzipping assets make the APK smaller?

Not for our 1,100 levels of text packs. The release APK's deflate came to 705,144 bytes; the pre-gzipped files were 705,234 bytes, larger by the 18-byte gzip header and trailer per pack.

Can a JVM unit test catch this kind of packaging problem?

It can enforce the naming rule. Whether AssetManager actually opens the file is only confirmed by running the app on a device or emulator.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • A market:// link opens a store chooser on SKT-sold Samsung phones: set the Play package first
  • A splash that never moved on: addOnCompleteListener(this) and onStop
  • "6.7" < "6.11" is false: comparing Remote Config versions as strings froze content updates
  • R8 kept 5 AdMob test IDs in our release build: one listOf().any line and a dex count

item.title: market:// store chooser on SKT-sold Samsung phones – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · How-to

A market:// link opens a store chooser on SKT-sold Samsung phones: set the Play package first

On two Samsung phones sold by SKT in Korea (Galaxy S21 and S20), three store apps answer a market:// link. Pointing the intent at the Play Store app first skips the chooser and opens the Play listing.

On a Galaxy S21, tapping a store link in our app's drawer brought up a sheet asking whether to open ONE store (a Korean app store), Galaxy Store (Samsung's store) or Play, instead of the Play listing. It was October 9, 2026, and we were tapping through commit efc0acf, which added a menu of our puzzle games to the drawer of SugarSpeller, on the S21. All 300 unit tests had already passed. Fifty-nine minutes later, commit 8bbe179 changed the store link to target Play first.

Sources: the SugarSpeller repository's git history (f6ef50e, efc0acf, 8bbe179, b6cda27), CHANGELOG entry 1.6.026, the monitoring log (WATCH.md, Oct 23), and adb queries we ran again on a Galaxy S21 and S20 on 2026-10-30.

Three store apps answer one market:// link

On October 30 we asked two SKT-sold phones which apps handle market://details?id=…. A Galaxy S21 on Android 15 and a Galaxy S20 on Android 13 both listed three: Play, Galaxy Store and ONE store, each with isDefault=true, meaning its filter accepts implicit intents (it declares CATEGORY_DEFAULT). When such an intent has more than one candidate and no default app is set, Android asks the user to choose.

The drawer links to Block Turn, Arrow Knots and SugarCard, and all three are on Play only. The game links carry the referrer utm_source=sugarspeller&utm_medium=crosspromo&utm_campaign=drawer, which only Play reads and reports in the Play Console acquisition report. A user who picks another store lands on a page with no app, and even an install that follows doesn't count as cross-promotion.

The old code read a failure as "no Play"

The first version opened market:// and fell back to the https address on ActivityNotFoundException. The comment on that branch said the device had no Play Store app. The assumption was that only Play opens market:// links. That code first went in with the SugarCard menu in commit f6ef50e on September 20, and on October 9 efc0acf moved it unchanged into a launcher shared by the games and SugarCard. Claude co-authored both commits.

On SKT-sold Samsung phones that assumption means the fallback never runs. With three candidates there is no exception; the chooser appears, and the code treats the store as opened. The same check showed that the SugarCard menu had carried the same problem since the September 20 code.

Why 300 unit tests and two reviews missed it

The store test in efc0acf compared the started intent's URI and never looked at its package. Robolectric has no other store apps installed, and by default startActivity doesn't fail there. In the same piece of work, three analysis agents and two adversarial reviews found and closed three test gaps (a missing <queries> entry, hiding the rows on Android 6.0, and the Classic drawer wiring). None of them questioned the market:// assumption.

The chooser showed up when we tapped the menu on the S21 itself. The repository's working notes say runtime checks are done on a release APK, and the check after the fix ran on one (the routine is written up in the release gate note).

Try Play, then plain market, then https

8bbe179 keeps three candidates in a list and opens them in order, moving on only when one throws.

val attempts = listOf(
    view("market://details?$query").setPackage(PLAY_STORE),
    view("market://details?$query"),                           // no Play: any store
    view("https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?$query"), // no store app: browser
)

An intent pinned to the Play package throws on a device without Play, which gives the list the failure signal the old code never had. The existing test gained an assertion that the started intent's package is Play, and a new test checks that with only another store present (checkActivities(true)) the plain market:// address opens with no package. Unit tests went to 301/301. Delete the setPackage call and the package comes back null, so the assertion fails (the same check we describe in deleting the guard).

On the S21 release APK that day, the installed Arrow Knots launched straight away, Block Turn, not installed, opened in Play with no chooser, and SugarCard went to Play as well. The GA4 log showed game_open{game=arrows,installed=1}, {game=blocks,installed=0} and sugarcard_open{installed=0}. The fix went into the 1.6.026 release branch, so the game menu pointed at Play from the first build users got, published the same morning.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Keeping the chooser, or opening https first

We dropped the idea of leaving the chooser alone because the apps are on Play only. Pinning Play with nothing after it would open nothing on a phone without Play, so plain market and https stay as fallbacks.

On the S21 on October 30, Play and Chrome both handle the Play https listing, and play.google.com is a system-verified link for Play, so opening https first would probably have opened Play too (we didn't tap it to check). But a browser accepts https on nearly every phone, so there is no exception, and which app opens depends on the device's settings. That doesn't fit a list that moves on when a candidate fails, so https stays last.

Don't pin Play if your app is on other stores too

If you send Korean users to an app that is only on Play, set the Play package on the market:// intent. If the app is also on ONE store or Galaxy Store, don't: the pin pulls those stores' users over to Play. On a phone without Play, the second candidate opens another store, which doesn't list our apps. We checked that path only in a Robolectric test; we have no such phone. We also checked only two Samsung phones sold by SKT, not KT or LG U+ models, unlocked models or other makers.

Two adb queries and one package assertion

  1. Connect the phone and run adb shell cmd package query-activities --brief -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "market://details?id=com.example.app". If the first line says 2 or more activities found, the phone can show a chooser; each candidate also shows its isDefault value.
  2. Run it again with the Play Store app's package, -p com.android.vending, at the end. You should get one.
  3. Change the store link to try Play, then plain market, then https, catching only ActivityNotFoundException to move to the next one.
  4. Assert the started intent's package in a unit test, and check once that the test fails when you remove setPackage.
  5. Put the release APK on a phone sold in Korea and tap the link yourself.

Still open: UTM installs and 16 drawer E2E tests

From October 9 to 22 the game rows were tapped 33 times in GA4 (Block Turn 5, Arrow Knots 16, and 12 from 1.6.026 with no game value). Whether those taps became installs is only in the Play Console acquisition report, and we haven't judged it yet. On the S21, 16 E2E tests that open the drawer fail, and they fail the same way on the baseline build before the change (360bed3), so the game-row E2E tests never ran on the device and we tapped the rows by hand instead. Finding the cause of those failures comes next.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Why does a Galaxy phone ask which store to use when I open a Play link?

More than one store app on the phone handles market:// addresses. On SKT-sold Galaxy S21 and S20 phones on 2026-10-30, Play, Galaxy Store and ONE store all did, and when the link names no target app, Android asks the user to pick.

How do I open the Play Store listing directly from my app?

Set the Play Store app as the package of the market://details intent with setPackage. On a device without Play that intent throws ActivityNotFoundException, so keep plain market:// and the https address as fallbacks, in that order.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • Daily users rose after the redesign while organic D1 retention fell from 15.2% to 11.2%

item.title: Splash hang from addOnCompleteListener at onStop – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

A splash that never moved on: addOnCompleteListener(this) and onStop

A listener added with addOnCompleteListener(this) is removed at onStop. If the screen went off during the fetch, the code that opens the next screen never ran.

Launch our Korean spelling app SugarSpeller with the phone's screen off, get past the lock screen, and it stayed on a black splash screen. On October 11, 2026, during a device check before a production release on a Galaxy S21 running the R8 release APK, we first saw it stuck on vc95, then reproduced it on vc96 by launching with the screen off. The cause, fetchAndActivate().addOnCompleteListener(this), had been in the repository since its first commit on December 16, 2020. Commit ab95e9a fixed it at 15:43 on October 11.

Sources: the app repository's git history (d5ac5e2, ab95e9a), CHANGELOG 1.6.029, the device-check notes in the release document, the agent session log from that day, the monitoring log (WATCH.md), and the Google Play services Task reference. Rechecked on 2026-10-30.

A listener removed at onStop is not called when the user comes back

The splash activity, ActivityEmpty, starts one Remote Config (RC) fetch in onCreate. When the fetch completes, it checks versions and calls checkMyPermission(), which moves on to the next screen. That completion listener was the only path to the next screen.

// ActivityEmpty just before ab95e9a, abridged (same line since d5ac5e2, 2020-12-16)
// [START fetch_config_with_callback]
remoteConfig.fetchAndActivate().addOnCompleteListener(this) { task ->
    ...
    checkMyPermission()   // (annotation) every branch moves on from here
}

The Task reference says of the overload that takes an Activity: "The listener will be automatically removed during onStop." If the screen turns off or the user switches apps before the fetch finishes, onStop comes first and the listener is gone. No lifecycle log from that day shows exactly when onStop arrived while the screen was off, so this step rests on the documentation and on reproducing the hang before and after the fix.

Nothing retried on return, either. The activity was still alive, so onCreate did not run again, and onStart only set system bar flags. The app stayed on the splash until the process was killed. On the test phone, the GA4 debug log showed first_open, session_start, screen_view and two app-open ad events, then nothing.

The [START fetch_config_with_callback] marker in the comment also appears in the Remote Config sample of Firebase's quickstart-android, which calls addOnCompleteListener(this) too. The marker and the line match, so the code most likely came from that sample. The other way this splash locked users out, through the RC force-update flag, is in "6.7" < "6.11" is false.

The first hang was force-stopped and set aside

The operator asked for a deeper device check before production. A Claude Code agent ran it on the S21 with ad domains blocked by DNS: an update install, rotations, 15 round trips to the home screen, and three 5,000-event monkey runs with zero app crashes and zero app ANRs.

Around 14:37 the agent woke the S21 from sleep and found vc95, installed about ten minutes earlier, stuck on the splash after the lock screen was dismissed. The log does not show when or how the app was launched. The agent force-stopped it, relaunched, saw the main screen, and noted in its own progress notes that this was a vc95 problem to check later on vc96. A relaunch after a force stop starts again from onCreate with the screen on, so that check could not show the cause.

Forty minutes later the agent deliberately launched vc96 with the screen off. It hung again, and only then did the agent open the code. The line was the same in both versions.

Unscope the listener, defer only the navigation

ab95e9a drops this from the listener so it no longer depends on the activity, and adds an isFinishing || isDestroyed check as its first line. Every call that opens the next screen goes through a new helper, whenStarted.

fun whenStarted(owner: LifecycleOwner, block: () -> Unit) {
    owner.lifecycleScope.launch { owner.lifecycle.withStarted(block) }
}

If the activity is visible (STARTED or later), the block runs now. If it is stopped, the block runs once when it becomes visible again. If the activity is destroyed first, it never runs. Five call sites were wrapped: three checkMyPermission() calls on the splash, the callback after the app-open ad wait, and goIntent on the logo screen (ActivityIntro). The agent wrote the three whenStarted unit tests first and ran them against an empty function, where 2 failed, before writing the body.

Removing this and nothing else was not enough. The listener would fire, but it would start the next activity from a stopped screen, and as the commit comment puts it, that startActivity is blocked or late. A user who went home during the splash might also see the app jump back over the home screen. The post-fix device check included "does not pop up over home".

Re-adding the listener in onStart would also work for the fetch: the reference says a listener added to a completed Task is scheduled immediately. It fixes only the RC Task, though. Two of the five wrapped sites, the ad-wait callback and the logo screen's Timer, are not Tasks. Using Task.await() in a coroutine would mean adding kotlinx-coroutines-play-services; the app's build.gradle has only coroutines-android and lifecycle, and the log shows no sign this path was weighed that day.

Don't hang navigation on addOnCompleteListener(this). Receive the result regardless of the activity, and defer only the screen change to the lifecycle.

whenStarted has its own limit: if the user never comes back, the next screen never opens. If the activity is destroyed in the meantime, the block is dropped, and reopening the app runs onCreate and a fresh fetch. That last part is a reading of the code, not something we tested on a device.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

One grep and a screen-off launch test

Start by finding listeners scoped to an activity. The first line below is the search the agent ran that day; it found nothing else in the main sources. The second line widens it to fragments' requireActivity() and Canceled listeners; it was not used that day. The risky ones are listeners that navigate.

git grep -nE "addOn(Complete|Success|Failure)Listener\(this"
git grep -nE "addOn(Complete|Success|Failure|Canceled)Listener\((this|requireActivity\(\)|activity)"

Then test on a device with an R8 release build. Steps 1-2 were run on vc96 before the fix and on the fixed build; steps 3-4 on the fixed build.

  1. Turn the screen off with adb shell input keyevent SLEEP, wait 3 seconds, and launch with adb shell monkey -p <package> -c android.intent.category.LAUNCHER 1.
  2. Wait 20 seconds, wake the phone and dismiss the lock screen. adb shell dumpsys window | grep mCurrentFocus should name the main activity. Before the fix it named the splash; after, the main screen.
  3. Launch, press Home right away, and launch again 12 seconds later. The phone should stay on the home screen in between and land on the main screen after. Repeat on the logo screen.
  4. Press Back during the splash and check for crashes.

The three whenStarted tests use Robolectric and LifecycleRegistry.createUnsafe to move the state from RESUMED to CREATED and back to STARTED. After the fix all 437 unit tests passed, and two monkey runs on the fixed build had zero crashes and ANRs. How the release carrying this fix, 1.6.029, went to 100% of users at once is in A 20% staged rollout went out at 100%.

How much of the 17% new-install drop-off this explains is unknown

A baseline written the day before the fix found that of 739 new users from September 12 to October 9, 611 (82.7%) reached the main screen within 24 hours. The CHANGELOG says only that this bug "may be part of" the 17% who did not.

A check on October 15 counted 107 of 120 new 1.6.029 installs (89%) reaching the main screen. That number cannot isolate the bug. The baseline used main-screen views, while 1.6.029 used the main_shown event added in 1.6.028; the same release also started an A/B test that removes the app-open ad from the first session for half of new installs; and the sample is 120 people. No event records a hang, so we cannot count how many users hit it.

The device check covered one S21 with ads blocked by DNS. We did not test live ads, other makers' lock screens, or returning after the process was killed in the background.

Still open: no test guards the five call sites

The unit tests cover whenStarted itself. The release notes say so: the wiring, whether ActivityEmpty and ActivityIntro actually call whenStarted, could not be guarded by unit tests and was checked on the device. If someone adds a new navigation call to the splash without whenStarted, today's tests still pass; only a device test that launches with the screen off or leaves the app during the splash would catch it.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

When does addOnCompleteListener(activity, …) remove the listener?

At the activity's onStop. The Task reference says so, and in this app a screen turning off during the fetch was enough to lose the result.

Doesn't an unscoped listener leak the activity?

Here the listener returns at once if isFinishing or isDestroyed, and whenStarted skips the navigation when the activity is gone. We did not measure leaks separately.

Why didn't monkey testing catch it?

That day's monkey runs kept the screen on and sent no Home key. The hang needs onStop to arrive before the fetch completes, so it only shows up in a test that turns the screen off or leaves the app during the fetch.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException
  • A market:// link opens a store chooser on SKT-sold Samsung phones: set the Play package first
  • "6.7" < "6.11" is false: comparing Remote Config versions as strings froze content updates
  • R8 kept 5 AdMob test IDs in our release build: one listOf().any line and a dex count
  • A reverse-construction generator and the gate behind 1,100 arrow-puzzle levels
  • Daily users rose after the redesign while organic D1 retention fell from 15.2% to 11.2%

item.title: Arrow puzzle level generator: 1,100 levels gated – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Method

A reverse-construction generator and the gate behind 1,100 arrow-puzzle levels

Once the move rule is written down and removal can only open paths, a board built in reverse is solvable without ever being played. Per-level gates then reject dull or unfair boards, and G2 checks the difficulty curve of the whole pack.

The generator built all 1,100 levels in Arrow Knots (the main game, 1 to 1000, plus an endless-mode fallback pack, 1001 to 1100), tutorials included; for the three tutorials the code fixes only the size and target windows. The pack first passed the G2 pack gate in commit e3c7781 at 18:32 on October 3, 2026, and in the current report all 1,100 levels pass the six structural gates checked per level. Two days earlier, generator v2 (6249b11) cut F0, the share of arrows you can remove the moment a board opens, from 0.50 to 0.11 in the hardest band of the generator benchmark.

Sources: the game repository's git history (ecedf0b, 6249b11, e3c7781, 9de89eb), ADR-0001, the level reports report-v2 and report-v3 (.md and .csv), the kickoff cross-check document, and session logs from October 1 and 3, 2026. Report numbers were re-read at HEAD on October 28, 2026.

Randomly placed boards were all stuck from 10×10 up

In Arrow Knots you tap arrows to slide them off the board. An arrow leaves along the line in front of its head (the code calls it the escape ray; below, just the ray). If another arrow sits on that ray, the tap bounces and costs a heart. The kickoff report of September 30, 2026 said boards would be generated and then checked with "an actual removal simulation" to see whether they could be cleared.

A cross-check simulation run the same day ruled that out. With arrows placed at random, 64% of 8×8 boards with 10 arrows could not be cleared, 92% with 16 arrows, and 100% from 10×10 with 25 arrows. Levels 861 to 1000 ship on 24×44 boards with a median of 73 arrows, a size a discard-and-retry loop would never reach.

The alternative is reverse construction. Start from an empty board and add arrows so that the k-th arrow placed is the k-th from last to leave. Accept an arrow only if its ray crosses no arrow already on the board, and the placement order, reversed, is a solution. A later arrow may sit on an earlier arrow's ray; that blocking is where difficulty comes from. In the same simulation, 200 of 200 boards built this way were solvable.

The move rule was fixed in an ADR before any generator work

Reverse construction depends on monotonicity: once an arrow can leave, it stays able to leave. The kickoff report never said how an arrow moves. A bent arrow could slide out snake-style behind its head, or the whole body could translate in one direction, and the two models block different cells. In the cross-check, 400 boards built for the head-following model were replayed under whole-body translation, and only 52 of them (13%) could be cleared.

ADR-0001 (an architecture decision record), accepted with the first commit (ecedf0b) on September 30, closed that gap. The ADR has the generator, the removal check, the hint and the animation share that one ray computation (the check and animation call Board.escapeRay; the generator calls the same computation inside it, size.ray). A blocked tap costs a heart and leaves the board unchanged. Together these make removal monotone, so a board is solvable exactly when its blocking graph (arrow i waits on j when j sits on i's ray) has no cycle.

Solvability then needs no search, only a peel: remove every arrow that can leave right now, repeat, and count the rounds, which gives the depth (layers). The release gate's solvability check asks for both a successful peel and a separate cycle search (DFS). Property tests, run before every commit, guard monotonicity with 300 generated boards and 1,000 runs that clear boards in random order.

Pin the move rule down in an ADR before you write a puzzle generator. Only 52 of those 400 boards were solvable under both models.

Half the arrows in v1 were free from the start

The v1 generator in ecedf0b, written with Claude, produced 300 solvable levels that were shallow. Even the hardest band in the v1 report, expert, had F0 at 0.494 and a depth of 5.6. Half the arrows could be removed from the start, and about five peels cleared the board.

At 22:32 on October 1, the main agent handed generator research to a sub-agent with a list of things to try: score candidates by how many existing rays they block, and add a final pass that turns free arrows into blocked ones. A ray-cover score was already in v1. The sub-agent worked out the direction: the last arrow placed leaves first, so new bodies should land on the rays of arrows that are still free. On 60 boards from the hard band (11×13), that score alone (freeWeight) gave F0 0.51, no better than v1 as it was (0.48). Late in a build there are almost no candidates in those spots, and the very last arrow is free no matter what. The final pass (blockerPlacements, which adds an arrow only if it blocks two or more free arrows) changed nothing.

What held F0 at 0.5 was empty rays. An arrow whose head sits on the rim pointing outward has a ray of zero cells, and nothing can ever block it. Rejecting arrows whose ray crosses no usable cell (minRay=1) brought F0 to 0.38 on its own. Adding tail growth took F0 to 0.30. If heads stay put and only tails extend into neighbouring empty cells, no ray changes and blocking edges are only added, so F0 can only fall and depth can only rise. Each extension runs a DFS to check that no cycle forms. Tails first grow only into the rays of free arrows, then into any empty cell to raise density (fill growth). Leftover holes get new arrows only when the blocking graph stays acyclic.

The research report came back 17 minutes later, and this combination is v2, committed as 6249b11 at 22:53. The commit message compares the expert band of the benchmark: F0 0.50 to 0.11, depth 5.8 to 14.6, density 0.74 to 0.97. Drawing long random paths up front, without growth, gave density 0.65 and F0 0.44, so it was dropped.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Defects found in 300 levels became G2 checks

At 15:48 on October 3 the operator asked whether the app simply ended after level 300, and seven minutes later asked for 1,000 levels. The agent re-analysed all 300 v2 levels. Boards were squeezed onto one screen as they grew, so the average cell size in levels 276 to 300 was 13.6 dp, and the smallest boards were down to 11.7 dp; after level 150 depth stayed between 16 and 21 while only the arrow count climbed. Counting again from the report CSV: level 293 had 94 arrows after 34 on level 292 (2.8×), and level 243 had 76 after 30. Even level 300, a regular level, had 109 arrows after 77.

The agent laid out two options, a board-size cap or large boards with zoom and scroll as competing games use, and recommended the cap. The operator chose large boards and set the ranges: one size cap for levels 1 to 200, then boards growing through 201 to 500, 501 to 700 and 701 to 1000. The agent turned that into keeping cell size fixed and letting the board outgrow the screen, and added the number: cells of at least 27 dp in Part 1.

The spec then turned each defect into a gate. Levels have roles: a ramp is a regular level on the difficulty curve, a spike is the one hard level in each cycle, and a breather is an easier level. T is an estimated solve time computed from arrow count and F0. The table shows the G2 results in the current report-v3.md.

Defect in the 300 levels, or new structureG2 checkResult (1,100 levels)
Cells averaged 13.6 dp, min 11.7 dpPart 1 cells ≥ 27 dp at 360 dp widthmin 27.3 dp
One hard level at 2.8× the level beforeSpike T over the preceding ramps' median: median 1.10 to 1.25, p90 ≤ 1.30101 spikes, median 1.12, p90 1.18
Arrow count flat for 50 levels (201 to 250), then up 40% in the 251sNon-spike, non-silhouette levels ≤ 1.15× the arrows of the previous regular level; breather T 0.60 to 0.90× the preceding ramps' median0 neighbour violations; 112 breathers, 0.61 to 0.88
Harder only by getting biggerMedian depth of 941 to 1000 ≥ 1.6× that of 101 to 20029 vs 14, 2.07×
Four parts with growing boards (ranges set by the operator)First 10 levels of a new part: arrows ≤ 1.10×, depth ≤ 0.85×All four transitions pass (201: 1.05×, 0.75×)

All 1,100 levels pass the six structural gates checked per level: L/A (depth per arrow, at most 0.60 on ramps), single-wave runs (no more than four rounds in a row that free only one arrow), F0, random-tap win rate, size caps and solvability. The random-tap win rate comes from 100 runs per level of tapping any arrow with three hearts. Counting in report-v3.csv, 1,071 of the 1,095 levels from level 6 on score 0, and every level from Part 2 on scores 0.

Random numbers come from the project's own SplitMix64 instead of Kotlin's Random(seed), which the cross-check flagged as unstable across versions, and e3c7781 records that two builds produced byte-identical packs.

What G2 missed: a repeating mask and per-level failures

Thirty minutes after the pack passed G2, at 19:02, commit 9de89eb fixed G2 itself. Endless-mode silhouettes reused the same mask a few levels apart on every 140-level cycle (castle at 1000 and 1005, fish at 985 and 1015, trophy at 995 and 1025). G2 grouped masks by the pair (name, mirrored), so a mirrored copy counted as a different picture.

128 levels missed their target window and shipped the closest candidate, and fallback level 1060 shipped while failing the per-level sawtooth check, because G2's sawtooth row looks only at the median and p90 of the 101 spikes. The random-tap cap of 0.5 is loose as well: level 7 sits at exactly 0.50.

G2 reads pack files on the JVM, so it could not see a packaging problem (aapt stripping .gz, which crashed the app on launch); that story is in "Use hundreds of agents" in practice. The pipeline also keeps going when G2 fails: it writes every pack, then prints "G2 FAILS" to standard error. What catches a G2 failure is CurveGateTest, which recomputes every level's stats from the committed pack, runs G2, and fails unless the recomputed CSV matches the committed report-v3.csv; the repository rule is that it passes before every commit.

ADR-0001 says that rotating arrows, arrows that stop on collision, keys and locks, or moving tiles break monotonicity and require a new ADR and a search-based verifier (BFS or SAT) first. T and random-tap win rate are model values; real play time was tuned separately in the par-time simulation that cut targets by 30%.

Seven steps, from a monotonicity test to a byte comparison

Any puzzle where removing a piece can only open paths can follow the same order.

  1. Write the move and removal rule as an ADR, and have the check, the hint and the animation share one ray computation.
  2. Test "removable stays removable" as a property: clear boards in random order, around 1,000 runs.
  3. If the rule is monotone, build in reverse. Accept the k-th piece only if its ray misses every piece already placed, and reject pieces with an empty ray.
  4. Raise difficulty by growing tails with heads fixed, checking for a cycle with a DFS on every step.
  5. Write F0, depth, L/A, single-wave runs and random-tap win rate for every level to a CSV.
  6. Enforce the pack gate as a test that recomputes the metrics from the boards and fails if they differ from the committed report.
  7. Derive seeds from the level number and a generator version, and bump the version when output changes. Build twice and compare bytes, then open the packaged app on a device.

Steps 3 and 4 and the depth count, as pseudocode:

place(a):                       # reverse construction
  if usable(ray(a)) == 0: reject  # an empty ray can never be blocked
  if ray(a) hits occupied: reject   # ray must miss every placed arrow
  accept(a)
growTail(a, cell):              # head fixed, ray unchanged
  waiting = arrows whose ray crosses cell
  if cell not empty or not next to a's tail end: skip
  if a at max length or cell on ray(a): skip   # never block its own ray
  if reaches(a, waiting): skip    # DFS: growing would close a cycle
  extend a's tail into cell
depth(board):                   # peel
  layers = 0
  while board not empty:
    if nothing removable: return unsolvable
    remove every removable arrow; layers += 1
  return layers

In this repository ./gradlew :arrow-engine:test :level-pipeline:test runs the property tests of step 2, the G2 test of step 6 and the determinism tests of step 7.

F0 and depth have not been checked against real play

The F0 and depth numbers here come from the generator and its reports; they have not been compared with where real players get stuck. With simulated players, the check that spikes clear at least 5 points less often than ramps in the same band failed in retune commit ab3f78c. At 22:28 the same day, spec commit 91d3c8c replaced it with a solve-time ratio of 1.10 to 1.25 and a rule that spikes clear no more than 3 points above ramps. Simulated clear rates are model values too, so how they match real play is still unknown.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can generated puzzle levels be guaranteed solvable?

They can if the rules are monotone. In Arrow Knots the reversed build order is a solution, and the release gate re-checks all 1,100 levels with a peel and a DFS cycle search.

What is F0 and why lower it?

F0 is the share of arrows that can be removed the moment a board opens. In v1's expert band it was 0.494: half the arrows could be removed from the start. The shipped pack sets a target window per level role (ramp, spike, breather); in report-v3.csv the median for Part 4 (levels 701 to 1000) is 0.11.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Testers said the time was "too long, so it's easy": checking that with a simulation before cutting puzzle par times by 30%
  • Puzzle game day-one churn: per-device event timelines, exact board math and four walls in chapter one
  • Block puzzle difficulty: how simulation bots caught a game you could never lose
  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException

item.title: App retention drop: five years of GA4 cohorts – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Daily users rose after the redesign while organic D1 retention fell from 15.2% to 11.2%

Day-1 retention of our spelling app's organic cohorts fell from 15.2% to 11.2% after an August 2025 redesign and has not come back in over a year. We have not pinned down the cause.

SugarSpeller, our Korean spell-checking app, averaged 780 daily active users in September 2025, the month after its redesign and its highest month of 2025. The release branch for version 1.6.007, which made a chat-style screen the default, was merged on August 18, and 3,053 new users arrived in September, close to twice the June and July numbers. We only saw that they were staying less on October 18, 2026, when we pulled five years of GA4 data. Organic monthly cohorts had gone from 15.2% to 11.2% on D1 (opened again the day after install) and from 4.2% to 2.6% on D30. The timing lines up with the redesign, but this data cannot separate the chat default, the ad changes and the surge of new users as causes.

Sources: the app repository's git history (02cbb15 to 61d6f15, a88ee55, eab1837, cb33385), the GA4 Data API scripts and output files committed with the October 18, 2026 strategy document (data through October 17, 2026), and the app's operations log. Cohort averages were recomputed from those output files on October 29, 2026.

26 months of organic cohorts: D1 from 15.2% to 11.2%

We built monthly cohorts by first session date with the GA4 Data API cohort request and kept only users whose first channel was Organic Search. Devices with no brand, OnePlus8 models and sdk_gphone emulators (Play's pre-launch test bots) were filtered out. Plain averages for the 14 months before the redesign and the 12 months after:

Organic monthly cohortsAvg sizeD1D7 (days 6-8)D30 (days 28-30)
Jul 2024 to Aug 2025 (14)1,06615.2%7.0%4.2%
Sep 2025 to Aug 2026 (12)90011.2%4.9%2.6%

Weighting by cohort size gives 15.4% to 11.2% on D1 and 4.3% to 2.6% on D30, so the picture holds. We also checked for a seasonal dip. In 2024 the September cohort's D1 fell to 14.7% and the October cohort was back at 16.3%. In 2025 the numbers were 13.6% in September, 12.3% in October and 12.3% in November, and every cohort through August 2026 stayed between 7.7% and 12.6%.

Weekly cohorts show where the step is. The 11 organic weekly cohorts from the week of June 2 to the week of August 11, 2025 averaged 16.4% on D1 (range 13.4% to 21.7%); the 13 from the week of September 1 to the week of November 24 averaged 12.6% (9.1% to 16.6%). A weekly cohort here is 176 to 423 people, so single weeks swing widely, and we made the call on monthly averages.

New users nearly doubled in September, and DAU went up

For months after the redesign, rising DAU kept the break out of sight; the repository has no record of the post-redesign cohorts being cut separately before October 2026. New users across all channels were 2,304 in August 2025 and 3,053 in September, against 1,381 in June and 1,596 in July. Monthly average DAU rose to 765 in August and 780 in September. It then dropped to 654 in October and kept sliding, from 582 in January 2026 to 408 in September.

Splitting DAU by first session date shows which users went missing. These are daily averages over the same calendar window, September 20 to October 17, in each year.

Time since first session202420252026
Same day (new)436434
1-7 days242612
8-30 days434115
31-90 days879533
91-365 days25316997
Over a year (1-2 years + over 2)293292251
Total DAU744688442

Each cell is rounded to the nearest user, so a column can be one off from its total. Of the 302 daily users lost between 2024 and 2026, 211 (70%) were people 31 to 365 days past their first session. Same-day new users fell by 9. Users older than a year went from 39% of DAU to 57%, yet their count fell from 293 to 251; the share rose because the younger group emptied out.

In the 2026 window, the 31-365 day group is made up only of people who first opened the app between late September 2025 and mid-September 2026, all of them post-break cohorts. That group fell 62%, from 340 to 130. New users across all channels in the two periods when this group first opened the app fell about 25%, from roughly 20,000 to roughly 15,100 (monthly new users prorated by day). Fewer arrivals cannot account for a 62% drop; the rest is people who came in and stayed less. We did not measure how much retention fell further after day 30.

Ad changes and a wave of new users landed in the same weeks

Version 1.6.007 was built from 27 commits (merges included) between August 7 and 18, 2025, touching 129 files with 6,864 lines added and 2,476 removed. Its first commit, 02cbb15, "ChatGPT-style UI, complete overhaul", is the first commit in this repository with a Claude Co-Authored-By trailer; six commits in the range carry one. One of their subject lines reads "UI/UX perfectly identical to ChatGPT, complete". How this app's commit messages changed over the following year is in A year of AI coding in 701 commits. Neither the commit messages in the range nor the working notes (progress.md) at the release say anything about watching retention or cohorts after shipping.

The screen was not the only change in that release. Three changes are worth setting against the retention data.

  • Default screen: getBoolean("opt.uiMode", true) made chat the default. Earlier versions had no such setting at all, so existing users who updated also opened into the chat screen.
  • An ad shown when the user exits the app with the back button (83bc49f).
  • Chunking, which splits long text into pieces before sending it to the checker (eb5aadc).

A separate hotfix for the app-open ad (a88ee55, version 1.6.008) shipped on August 26, and the surge in new users above fell in the same August and September. Weekly engagement time per user dropped from 377 seconds in the week of August 18 to 297 the next week and 253 by the week of September 8. Active users in those weeks rose from 3,072 to 3,400, though, so that metric mixes the screen change with a different set of users.

Four things we corrected in the AI-assisted strategy document

The break was first written up in a strategy document in commit eab1837 on October 18, 2026. The commit carries a Claude co-author trailer and includes the GA4 analysis scripts and their output files alongside the document. Recomputing from the same output files for this note turned up several things to fix; these are the four largest.

  1. The document labeled D30 as the day 28-30 average and gave 2.4%. That 2.4% was the average of the single day-30 values; the day 28-30 average is 2.5%. Its range also included the September 2026 cohort. The data ended on October 17, so anyone who joined after September 17 had not reached day 30, and that cohort showed a D30 of 1.0%. Without it the figure is 2.6%.
  2. The document listed 1.6.007's three changes and the August 26 hotfix, then called them "the only change that coincides with the break." It left out the surge in new users in the same weeks, and it reads as if the bundle were a single candidate cause.
  3. The document used engagement time per user, 377 to 253 seconds, as evidence of the break. The denominator changed under that metric; the organic cohorts are the cleaner evidence.
  4. The document said 80 to 97 users a day opened the quiz from a notification between October 9 and 17. The daily values were 70 to 97 (70 on October 13).

None of the four reverses the finding, but item 2 narrowed the candidates to one release when three changes and a wave of new users had landed in the same weeks. The document itself concluded that causation could not be established and left the decision to start a default-screen test to the operator.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

We are not switching the default back yet; a new-install A/B test comes first

The fastest response would be to make the older Classic screen the default again. On September 24, 2026 the operations log held the opposite proposal: remove Classic and move everyone to chat. That day's 28-day numbers showed Classic users running 7.6 checks per user against 4.5 for chat, and a return rate of 76% against 64%. In an app whose default is chat, though, Classic users are people who went looking for the switch, so the gap cannot be read as the effect of the screen. Moving existing users, who have had over a year on chat, back again has its own cost.

Comparing before and after on all-channel cohorts was also dropped. All-channel D1 fell as low as 8.0% in August 2023 and recovered to 12.5% to 15.1% in October to December of that year. Paid search brought 77% of new users in 2022 and 42% in 2023, and D1 moved along with that shift in channel mix. Paid (Cross-network) share was similar in 2025 and 2026, at 22% and 23%, but we compared organic users only.

What can separate the causes is an A/B test that gives half of new installs a different default screen. New installs run at about 185 a week, so detecting a 10-point difference needs about 350 per group, and two first-run experiments (judged on November 8 and around November 15) are already splitting those installs. Running three at once would leave all three unreadable, so the plan is to start after November 16. The bar is D7 up 2 points after four weeks.

When you ship a large redesign, cut out the D1 of the cohorts that install from that week on and track it for four weeks. In a month when installs jump, DAU will not show you the regression.

What we added while waiting: a morning quiz notification

Version 1.6.024 started sending a morning spelling-quiz notification on September 26, 2026. Before that, zero users a day opened the quiz from a notification; between October 9 and 17 it was 70 to 97 a day. Returning users per day, with bots excluded, went from 365 in the week of September 7 to 447 in the week of October 12, up 82 or 22%. How much of the 82 the notification caused is not measured yet; an experiment that sends more notifications to one group (qr_extra) reads that out in active days per user on October 31.

The notifications skewed another number. From version 1.6.030, events sent by a background alarm pushed GA4 totalUsers from 1,500 on October 17 to 2,400-2,900 on October 19-22, while activeUsers stayed near 500 (found on October 23). Every DAU figure in this note uses activeUsers. How we filter out test phones and bots is in GA4 said 19 installs yesterday and 8 were real.

A GA4 cohortSpec and filter JSON for organic cohorts

  1. Send a runReport with a cohortSpec. Give each cohort dimension: "firstSessionDate" and a one-month dateRange; set cohortsRange to DAILY, days 0 to 30, accumulate: false. Dimensions are cohort and cohortNthDay; metrics are cohortActiveUsers and cohortTotalUsers. We sent six months per request.
  2. Filter on first channel and bots with dimensionFilter.
    {"andGroup": {"expressions": [
  {"filter": {"fieldName": "firstUserDefaultChannelGroup", "stringFilter": {"value": "Organic Search"}}},
  {"notExpression": {"filter": {"fieldName": "mobileDeviceBranding", "stringFilter": {"value": "(not set)"}}}},
  {"notExpression": {"filter": {"fieldName": "deviceModel", "stringFilter": {"matchType": "CONTAINS", "value": "OnePlus8"}}}},
  {"notExpression": {"filter": {"fieldName": "deviceModel", "stringFilter": {"matchType": "BEGINS_WITH", "value": "sdk_gphone"}}}}
]}}
  3. Use day 1 for D1, and the day 6-8 and day 28-30 averages for D7 and D30. Say in the table header which one you used.
  4. If a cohort's last day plus 30 days falls after the end of your data, leave it out of the D30 average.
  5. Put each month next to the same month a year earlier, to see whether a September dip happens every year and whether the next month recovers.
  6. Line up weekly cohort D1 around the date of a large release to see when a break starts. Use the same filter as the monthly cohorts (our weekly script only had the brand filter).
  7. Pull DAU with both date and firstSessionDate, bucket the gap (same day, 1-7 days, 8-30, 31-90, 91-365, 1-2 years, over 2 years), and compare the same calendar window across years. A request like this is enough:
    {"dateRanges": [{"startDate": "2026-09-20", "endDate": "2026-10-17"}],
 "dimensions": [{"name": "date"}, {"name": "firstSessionDate"}],
 "metrics": [{"name": "activeUsers"}],
 "limit": 250000}
    For each row, bucket (date minus firstSessionDate), sum, and divide by the number of days in the window.
  8. Count users with activeUsers. If any feature sends events in the background, totalUsers will run high.

Organic users only, and it needs cohorts in the hundreds

Paid cohorts are not in this comparison. Monthly cohorts need a few hundred users before the averages settle. The staged rollout percentage and dates for 1.6.007 are not on record, so we could not confirm why the weekly break shows up in the week of September 1 rather than August 18. The script that split DAU by first session date had no bot filter, so the 34 same-day new users in 2026 may include pre-launch bots. That barely touches the conclusion about the 31-365 day group.

Search interest fell too. On Google Trends (South Korea), the 2026 average for "맞춤법 검사기" (spelling checker) was 38% below the 2025 average (checked October 18, 2026). That is a 2026 trend and cannot explain a step that starts with the September 2025 cohort, and we could not separate how much of it went into later drops such as the July 2026 cohort's D1 of 7.7%.

Numbers the notification readout and the default-screen test will log

At the October 31 qr_extra readout we will look at whether the group with more notifications gains at least 10% in active days per user while uninstalls and notification blocks stay within 2 points. Once the default-screen test starts after November 16, we will log D1, D7, checks in the first seven days, and uninstall rate per group for four weeks. Until those results are in, we will not call the chat screen the cause of the break.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Frequently asked questions

How do I see retention for organic users only in GA4?

Add firstUserDefaultChannelGroup = "Organic Search" to the dimensionFilter of a Data API cohort request. It is based on the first channel, so a user who later returns through an ad still counts as organic.

Why use the day 28-30 average for D30 instead of the day-30 value?

Single days swing with the weekday and small samples. This app's September 2024 organic cohort had a day-30 value of 2.8% and a day 28-30 average of 3.2%. Pick one, name it in the table header, and do not mix them.

Can DAU go up while retention goes down?

Yes. In September 2025 this app took in 3,053 new users and DAU rose to 780, while that month's organic cohort had a D1 of 13.6%, below the year before, and later cohorts did not recover.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.
