item.title: "6.7" < "6.11" is false: a version string bug – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Incident

"6.7" < "6.11" is false: comparing Remote Config versions as strings froze content updates

Kotlin's string < says "6.7" is greater than "6.11". Once the content version in Remote Config reached 6.10, that comparison stopped updates on every device with 6.2 to 6.9 stored.

The drawer of SugarSpeller, our Korean spelling app, showed content version (6.7/2.2) while production Remote Config held 6.11/2.3. The operator read both numbers off a device on September 25, 2026. The app compared the two versions as strings, so devices with 6.2 to 6.9 stored never received the quiz bank and notice updates sent through info_version after that. A commit at 12:14 the same day (7b997f8) added VersionCompare, which compares each dot-separated part as an integer, plus four unit tests.

Sources: the app repository's git history (d5ac5e2, 6d0f4f1, 5f082f8, 71c31ae, a4d5b9a, e9d6b9c, 079feab, 7b997f8, 31c082d, 844c828), CHANGELOG entries 1.6.019 and 1.6.023, the quiz bank review document and the monitoring script, rechecked on 2026-10-29. Remote Config template numbers and project identifiers are left out.

The drawer said 6.7; Remote Config said 6.11

The app ships its quiz bank, notices and FAQ as one JSON value in Firebase Remote Config (RC below). On the splash screen, ActivityEmpty compares RC's info_version and clip_version with the version stored in the device's Room database. If RC is newer, it deletes the local content and inserts the new set. The (6.7/2.2) at the bottom of the drawer is that stored version.

One suspect was the build. Debug builds of this app read the RC of a separate development Firebase project, so a debug build on the device could show numbers that differ from production. Production RC really was 6.11/2.3, which ruled that out and left the comparison code.

// ActivityEmpty, just before 7b997f8
if (res[0].infoVersion < infoVer || res[0].clipVersion < clipVer) {
    repo.setVersion(VersionT(infoVer, clipVer))
    // delete and re-insert content
}

infoVersion is a String field. Kotlin compares strings lexicographically, character by character, so "6.7" and "6.11" first differ at the third character: '7' against '1'. '7' is larger, "6.7" < "6.11" evaluates to false, and the app concluded that RC held the older version.

With one digit after the dot, both orders agree

String comparison has been there since the app first connected to Remote Config in 2020. The current form, infoVersion < infoVer, appeared on May 6, 2023 (6d0f4f1), when a commit flipped the comparison to the right direction; the clip condition was added two days later. While the minor part ran from 6.1 to 6.9, lexicographic order and numeric order were the same, and the check always gave the right answer. It broke when RC moved to 6.10. We recomputed what the old expression returns for each stored value:

Stored on the deviceRC at 6.10RC at 6.11
6.1updatesupdates
6.2 to 6.9skipsskips
6.10equalupdates

"6.1" is a prefix of "6.10", so the shorter string sorts first; 6.2 through 6.9 all win at the third character. From the day RC reached 6.10, a device stuck in that range ignored every info_version bump (unless clip_version also went up). The quiz bank review document also records that notices changed on September 13, 20 and 22 without any change to info_version, which stayed at 6.10. Those three notices reached no existing user, string comparison or not.

Fresh installs never showed the bug. On first run there is no stored version row, so the app inserts the RC content without comparing anything and starts on the latest set.

Three agent commits, none of them fixed the content check

Counting only the times an agent touched or reasoned about the version check itself, the git history shows three. On August 9, 2025 at 15:32, a commit generated with Claude Code (5f082f8) blamed a "persistent update notice" on the string comparison of app_version and switched major, minor and patch to integer comparison. The app was at 1.5.031, so major and minor were one character each and the string comparison gave the same answer anyway. At 17:51 that day a commit whose message just says "fix" (71c31ae) put the string comparison back. No reason was recorded. Neither commit touched the content version check.

On December 11, 2025, an RC sync refactor (a4d5b9a, co-authored by Claude Opus 4.5) added 11 tests (its message says 13). One of them, versionComparison_isCorrect, asserts that "5.0" < "5.1". It uses single-digit values and calls no app code, only Kotlin's String operator, so it passes whatever the production check does. How we find tests that stay green when the guarded code is deleted is in 3,066 green tests hid a line that breaks opening the database.

On the morning of September 25, 2026, the agent reviewing all 124 quiz items (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote into the publishing steps of its 11:08 commit (e9d6b9c): the splash screen compares versions as strings, so bump info_version to 7.0. Fifteen minutes later the value that went up was 6.11, and the document now said that 6.10 to 6.11 is larger even as a string, so 6.10 users would update. The document still said a 6.9 to 6.10 bump is not recognized, but said nothing about what to do for devices stuck below 6.10. The 11:23 commit (079feab) also added a rule to the project's CLAUDE.md, that a bump which changes the number of digits is not seen as an update, and left the comparison code as it was.

Devices below 6.10 surfaced only when the operator put the drawer's 6.7/2.2 next to production RC. The 12:14 fix (7b997f8) was also written by an agent (Claude Fable 5.1), this time after the operator had pointed out that the device and RC values differed. How this incident shows up in the commit messages is covered, along with other cases, in A year of AI coding in 701 commits.

One VersionCompare for both content and app versions

Setting RC to 7.0 would have unblocked 6.x devices for now, since "6.x" < "7.0" is true. It would break again at 7.10, and everyone editing content would have to remember never to make a bump that adds a digit, so we dropped it as a permanent rule.

Comparing all three parts as integers, as in August 2025, did not fit either. This app looks only at the major and minor parts of app_version and ignores the patch on purpose; comparing the patch would send every user on an older patch to the store after each patch release. 7b997f8 keeps one function and routes both the content version check and the major/minor checks of app_version through it.

object VersionCompare {
    fun compare(a: String, b: String): Int {
        val pa = parts(a); val pb = parts(b)
        for (i in 0 until maxOf(pa.size, pb.size)) {
            val x = pa.getOrElse(i) { 0 }; val y = pb.getOrElse(i) { 0 }
            if (x != y) return x.compareTo(y)
        }
        return 0
    }
    fun isNewer(remote: String, local: String) = compare(remote, local) > 0
    private fun parts(v: String) = v.trim().split('.').map { it.trim().toIntOrNull() ?: 0 }
}

The four tests in VersionCompareTest cover the values that failed ("6.11" against "6.7"), equal values, parts of different lengths or counts ("1.10.0" against "1.9.9", "6.11" against "6.11.0") and non-numeric input. The first test also asserts that "6.7" < "6.11" is false. 112 unit tests passed at that commit. Do not write a new version check with a string <; that rule is in CLAUDE.md now.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The force flag in the same JSON went on before adoption

The RC version JSON that holds the content versions also holds app_version and force, and since 7b997f8 the major/minor check of app_version goes through VersionCompare too. The splash screen decides in this order: if the installed version matches app_version character for character, let the user in; otherwise compare major and minor only; finally, if force is true, override the result and show the update dialog.

A September 18 commit (31c082d) records that a device with 1.6.017 showed "A new version has been released!", and the code was the first suspect. The real cause was an RC app_version that did not match the shipped version. A patch bump (1.6.017 to 1.6.018) is not rescued by the major/minor check, so the dialog goes away only when the RC value matches the shipped version exactly.

On that same September 18, force went on while few users had the new version, and sessions for the day were down 25% five hours later. A September 13 case is left out here: a note written that day corrected an earlier reading as GA4 standard-report lag rather than a lockout, while later documents list it as a lockout again. Since 1.6.019 (September 19), monitor.py --only rc reads the RC version JSON and prints, from GA4 for yesterday and today, the share of active users on exactly the app_version string. If force is true and that share is under 90%, it warns that the rest are stuck behind the splash dialog right now. A separate rollout incident, where a staged percentage went out wrong, is in A 20% staged rollout went out at 100%.

One git grep, a test with the failing values, a check on an old install

  1. Find lines that compare version-like names with < or >. In your own repository, drop the revision. In ours, with the revision just before 7b997f8 as below, the command finds the two lines in ActivityEmpty (248 and 270) and three lines in the a4d5b9a test (run on 2026-10-29). 
    git grep -nE '[Vv]er[A-Za-z]*(\[[0-9]\])?\s*[<>]=?\s*[A-Za-z.\[]*[Vv]er' 7b997f8^ -- '*.kt' '*.java'
  2. Move every hit into one function and test it with the values that failed. At minimum: "6.11" against "6.7" and "1.10.0" against "1.9.9".
  3. Do not verify on a fresh install. Install the build from before the fix and run it once with RC at 6.9 so the stored version is 6.9. Install the fixed build over it without clearing data, raise RC to 6.10, and check that the stored version shown on screen becomes 6.10. A bump that keeps the digit count, such as 6.15 to 6.16, passes under the old comparison too and proves nothing.
  4. When content changes, bump info_version.
  5. Before turning force on, check in GA4 the share of active users whose appVersion equals the RC app_version. Under 90%, leave it off.

Builds already installed still compare strings

The comparison runs on the device, so a device that has not updated to the fixed build keeps comparing strings. RC has since gone to 6.12 (October 1), 6.13 (October 9), 6.14 (October 10) and 6.15 (October 24), but on an old build with 6.2 to 6.9 stored, "6.7" < "6.15" is still false.

One server-side way to reach those devices is a one-time bump of the RC value to 7.0. On old builds "6.7" < "7.0" is true, and on new builds VersionCompare also sees 7.0 as newer than 6.15, so both paths update. We dropped 7.0 as a permanent rule, but as a one-time migration while old builds remain it is the right tool; after it, bumps should stay within 7.1 to 7.9 until old builds are rare enough. As of October 24 the RC value is 6.15, and there is no record of this app moving to 7.0. Because the old condition is an OR, raising clip_version would also make it true, but we do not know why those devices did not update at clip 2.3, so we do not count that path as a confirmed fix.

VersionCompare reads any non-numeric part as 0. A typo such as "6.l1" in RC would read as 6.0 and the update would be skipped silently; the test only confirms that "6.7" is newer than "abc" and raises no warning. "6.11" and "6.11.0" count as the same version.

For 1.6.023 a release APK on an API 34 emulator showed 6.11/2.3 in the drawer, but the record does not say whether that was a fresh install. If it was, the check never ran. clip_version is an open question too: stored 2.2, RC 2.3. "2.2" < "2.3" is true even as strings and the old condition was an OR, so the clip side should have triggered an update. The history does not say when clip became 2.3, so string comparison alone does not fully explain why this device stayed at 6.7/2.2.

Writing the version row before the content was another defect on the same update path. On September 28, on a physical S21, a first run while offline left the quiz bank empty until the next info_version; commit ce024cd now refills the bank when it is empty even if the version matches.

The old rule is still in CLAUDE.md

As of October 29, 2026, lines 206 and 207 of CLAUDE.md at HEAD still say the comparison is a string comparison and a bump that adds a digit is not seen as an update, while line 734 says versions are compared numerically with VersionCompare. An agent reading the first rule could believe the code still compares strings and pick bump values to suit that. The text from "the comparison is a string" on line 206 to the end of line 207 should become the one-time 7.0 migration rule for old builds; the "always bump info_version" rule on lines 205 and 206 stays. versionComparison_isCorrect, which calls no app code, is also still in the test suite; it should either be deleted or call VersionCompare.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Why is "6.7" < "6.11" false in Kotlin?

String comparison is lexicographic, character by character. At the third character '7' is greater than '1', so "6.7" sorts after "6.11".

Wouldn't bumping the version to 7.0 work with string comparison?

For now, yes. It breaks again at 7.10, and everyone editing content has to avoid bumps that add a digit.

When is it safe to turn on Remote Config's force flag?

Once at least 90% of active users run exactly the app_version string. This app turned it on with low adoption and lost 25% of the day's sessions.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException
  • A market:// link opens a store chooser on SKT-sold Samsung phones: set the Play package first
  • A splash that never moved on: addOnCompleteListener(this) and onStop
  • R8 kept 5 AdMob test IDs in our release build: one listOf().any line and a dex count
  • A reverse-construction generator and the gate behind 1,100 arrow-puzzle levels
  • Daily users rose after the redesign while organic D1 retention fell from 15.2% to 11.2%

item.title: Claude Code sessions in one repo: file owner table – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Several Claude Code sessions, one repo: the file owner table, checked against 13 merges

After one commit carried off 50 files another session was still writing, we started splitting parallel work with a table that gives every shared file exactly one owner.

Commit 32fca47 was supposed to fix a launch crash in release 1.0.3. It changed 74 files, and 50 of them belonged to the next app, which a second Claude Code session was building in the same working tree. That was September 23, 2026, in SugarMount's utility app repository (sugar-utils). Sixteen days later the family calendar app AXFamily wrote a plan around a shared-file owner table, and the next day merged 13 feature branches in 2 minutes 11 seconds. Seven of those merges needed hand-merged hunks. None were in the per-feature translation files; they came from committed translation output (four merges), names and error codes missing from the stub list (M1), an index file in R1's row (A1, A2), and test files (F2).

Sources: git history of both repositories (32fca47, ca1ade4, merges 3e9d0cb to e5f9798 and 58920b9 to ff0c975, a0351cf, 5d51b5b), AXFamily's release plan of 2026-10-09, memory notes the sessions left at the time, and this site's AGENTS.md. Hand-merge counts were redone with git show --cc on 2026-10-28.

A release fix shipped 50 files from a session next door

On the evening of September 23 two sessions shared the sugar-utils working tree. One was finishing the 1.0.3 release of the image compressor (U01); the other was building the next app, Flip & Rotate Image (U02). At 22:24 the U01 session committed 32fca47. Its message lists a fix for a constructor R8 had stripped, a release launch script, and analytics defaults. The diff added 3,946 lines across 74 files, including 50 files (3,313 lines) under apps/sugarflip/ and docs/store/sugarflip/ and 5 files (428 lines) in the shared image engine core/images, all of it U02 work in progress. The U02 session's memory note calls it a sweep "in git add -A style". U02's engine and screens got a commit with a real description the next afternoon, in 7821dbd.

The same commit added scripts/qa/release_launch.sh, and line 13 of that script was ./gradlew --stop. Per the Gradle docs, --stop terminates every daemon started with the same Gradle version. A session on the same PC was building the Korean spacing app, also on Gradle 9.6.0, and its memory note records two clean builds that day dying with Gradle build daemon has been stopped: stop command received.

Each session blamed the neighbour. The U02 session wrote that the stops came from the spacing app's build; the spacing app's session pointed at sugar-utils. Across the full history of both repositories, the only --stop is that line in 32fca47's script. Nothing records who ran it or when. The line stayed for 15 days, until ca1ade4 replaced it with --no-daemon on October 8.

In a shared working tree, git cannot tell your change from theirs

In one working tree git has no conflict to flag: both sessions' edits sit in the same index, and whichever session commits first becomes the owner of every file in the tree at that moment. With no per-file owner written down, an agent has no basis for deciding which changes are its own. The Gradle daemon had the same shape: not a file, but something every session on the PC used, and any session could stop it.

The U02 session wrote rules into its memory note that night. Re-read a shared file (AGENTS.md, the backlog, CHANGELOG, templates) right before editing it, and use a targeted Edit, not a full Write. Never commit, stash, reset or run gradlew --stop. Expect another session to kill a build, so check the timestamps on the test-result XML and rerun instead of trusting an exit code. The same rules now sit in the operator's global instructions, which apply to every project, next to a line saying long Gradle builds run with --no-daemon.

Separate worktrees still hand-merged AppContainer.kt in 3 of 4 merges

We had already tried separate working trees. On September 20 the repository was created at 23:10, and four foundation tasks (file handling, image engine, ads and billing, analytics) went to subagents, each in its own git worktree. Four branches merged between 23:28 and 23:40, two more by 00:26, six in all. git show --cc shows AppContainer.kt hand-merged in 3 of the 4 foundation merges. The repo's first ADR says "No DI framework; a manual AppContainer per app", so every foundation task had to add its own lines to that one file.

Worktrees keep work-in-progress files apart. A wiring file that every task appends to is still shared, and the conflict moves to merge time. The game repository gave each workstream an "exclusive files" column, described in "Use hundreds of agents" in practice: 10 workstreams, 59 commits in a day, three running at once. AXFamily wrote a separate table for the shared wiring files that column left out.

AXFamily's plan gave each shared file an owner and a route for everyone else

The October 9 release plan put this first in its conclusions: one Wave 0 agent lays down every shared file up front, and nobody edits those files from Wave 1 on. Section 2, "rules for parallel work conflicts", is a three-column table. Condensed:

Shared fileOwnerHow other packages work
Contract schema and generated codeW0 contract laneDon't touch; queue new contracts as follow-up PRs to W0
firestore.rules, index fileR1Put test JSON in rules-tests/fixtures/<pkg>/ only
Functions index.ts, errors.ts, etc.W0W0 registers every planned export as a stub (NOT_IMPLEMENTED); each package fills only its own handler file
App shell (pubspec, router, service registry, manifest, Gradle files)W0Routes, ad rules and channels ship as files in the feature folder; W0's registries collect them
Merged translations app_ko.arbW0's merge toolEach feature writes only parts/<f>_ko.arb; the tool merges
CI workflowW0Add one check file; it is auto-discovered
Gradle builds, devicesnoneOne at a time regardless of worktree, --no-daemon

W0 laid these files down serially (merged at 19:54 on October 9). Then the 12 packages in the Wave 1 table worked in parallel inside the folders listed in its "main files (exclusive)" column. Talking it out between sessions in one tree had produced 32fca47 and its 50 swept files; worktrees alone had hand-merged AppContainer.kt in 3 of 4 merges. One session doing all 12 packages in sequence would avoid conflicts; we never measured how long that would take.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Seven of 13 merges needed hand merging; the per-feature translation files never did

Between 01:51:06 and 01:53:17 on October 10, 13 feature branches went into the integration branch: the plan's 12 plus a design-system branch (UX0) that had no row in the plan. Listing, per merge, the files that still have combined hunks in git show --cc gives seven merges:

  • Four app-screen packages (A2 to A5): the merged app_ko.arb and app_en.arb plus three Dart files generated from them. A CI check fails when the merged file differs from the parts and says to run the merge tool and commit, so every branch regenerated and committed it. The parts/ files appear in none of the 13 merges.
  • The media package (M1): functions index.ts and errors.ts. M1 added confirmAssetUpload, which was not among W0's 16 planned exports, and both the account package (F1) and M1 edited the same error-code line.
  • A1 and A2: firestore.indexes.json, which R1 owns.

The rest were test files. Diffing each branch against its merge base with git diff --name-only and checking the table, 8 of 13 branches edited a file in someone else's row. That count leaves out the merged translations and the fixture files the plan assigned to each package; with B1's shared vector file it would be 9. Git merged two lines in the dependency file, two in a Gradle file and four in the manifest with no conflict; hand merges only exposed cases where two branches touched the same line. The plan's "nobody edits from Wave 1 on" did not hold; for some of the 8 (M1, F1), the reason was an endpoint the stub list did not name and error codes W0 had not put in errors.ts.

Six mismatches git never saw, and 12 review defects, sat outside the table

At 02:09, sixteen minutes after the merges, a0351cf ("minimal fix for Wave 1 integration breakage") repaired six package pairs. The app's paid-plan check (A4) disagreed with the billing server's (B1) subscription states, A4 and the settings package (A5) each declared their own ad-consent type, and the error copy didn't know the media package's new error codes. All six pairs lived in different files, so git raised no conflict. At 05:28, 5d51b5b fixed the 12 defects the integration review confirmed plus minor issues and a contract re-baseline, adding 2,088 lines across 115 files. Guardian checks were pulled into one function (isGuardianOf), and the three screen packages A2, A3 and A4 were made to read which family is being viewed from a single value, AppSession.currentHouseholdId. Two missing indexes went in with a new check that compares the app's orderBy queries with the index table.

The table named an owner for every shared file and none for concepts such as "guardian" or "current family". The double definitions showed up only in the integration review behind 5d51b5b. Use the owner table to cut text conflicts, and leave contract drift to an integration review plus the checks that review produces. We have not tried the table on work that cannot be split into rows, such as a refactor that cuts across many folders.

One table before splitting, two commands after merging

Write the shared-file list and its owners before you decide how many agents to run. Sessions that share a working tree get no commit rights.

  1. Find the files every task has to add a line to: DI container, router, endpoint list, dependency file, merged translations, CI config, database indexes.
  2. Give each one owner, and on the same row write the route others use instead (a parts file, a file of their own that a registry picks up). Shared things that are not files, like builds and devices, get a row too.
  3. The owner lays the wiring files down first and registers every planned name as a stub.
  4. Files a tool generates, like a merged bundle, are regenerated after the merge by whoever integrates. This site's AGENTS.md works the same way: content authors edit only <main>, the title and the description, never run tools/build.py, and leave generated files and everything outside <main> to the one build owner who runs the integration build. The agents drafting these notes each get their own copy of the site since October 26, 2026, when three of them shared one copy and mixed up and deleted each other's drafts.
  5. If sessions must share a working tree: re-read before editing, targeted Edits, no commit, stash, reset or --stop, Gradle with --no-daemon, and judge success by the test-result XML timestamps.
  6. After merging, count where the table leaked.
    # files that still have combined hunks in a merge
git show --cc --format= <merge> | grep '^diff --cc'
# files a branch changed, to check against the table
git diff --name-only $(git merge-base <base> <branch>) <branch>
    In AXFamily the first command found the 7 hand-merged merges; checking the second command's output against the table gave the 8 branches outside their rows.

How to phrase rules like these in an instruction file is covered in How to write AGENTS.md: only the rules an AI coding agent gets wrong.

Still committed: the merged translation files, and no row for concepts

AXFamily's develop branch still tracks the merged app_ko.arb and the three generated Dart files, and CI checks that they are current. Moving their regeneration to the integrator after each merge has not been done yet. Whether adding "concept" rows (guardian check, current family) to the owner table would cut defects like those in 5d51b5b is untested.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can two Claude Code sessions work in the same working tree?

They can, as long as neither commits unless the operator asks. In sugar-utils one session's commit, 32fca47, carried 50 files another session was still writing. Since then, sessions in a shared tree do not commit, stash, reset or run gradlew --stop.

Do git worktrees remove conflicts between parallel agents?

They stop work-in-progress files from mixing, but wiring files that several tasks edit still conflict at merge time. On September 20, AppContainer.kt was hand-merged in 3 of 4 merges.

Does gradlew --stop stop builds in other projects?

It does when their daemons run the same Gradle version. The Gradle docs say so, and two clean builds of another repository on the same PC, also on Gradle 9.6.0, died with "stop command received". Run long builds with --no-daemon.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • Commits without a Co-Authored-By trailer: the agent made 26 of the 29 we could check

item.title: Why R8 kept 5 AdMob test IDs in a release AAB – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

R8 kept 5 AdMob test IDs in our release build: one listOf().any line and a dex count

Four ad unit checks wrapped in listOf(...).any were something R8 could not fold, so 5 test ad strings stayed in the release dex. A plain || over the same constants left none.

The first real-ID bundle for Block Turn version code 2, built before upload at 17:16 on October 4, 2026, held 4 real ad unit strings and 5 Google test ad strings in its dex. It had passed the Gradle guard. A rebuild two minutes later overwrote it, so it was never uploaded, and the version code 2 we did upload has no test strings. With all real IDs present, either version of the code picks the real units at runtime.

Sources: git history of our game repository (575aaa1, 1aecbc2, 301bc9e), the launch rehearsal checklist and that day's agent session log. On 2026-10-28 we recounted three bundles and two APKs and built a small R8 reproduction. No ID value was printed.

The bundle passed the Gradle guard with 5 test strings inside

Money.kt gives a debug build, or a build with any empty ad unit field in BuildConfig, AdUnits.TEST, the set of Google test units; anything else gets the real ones. Version code 1, built at 12:25 that day, only checked the banner field, and when we counted that bundle on October 28 it had 4 real ad units and 0 test strings.

At 16:14 Claude Code widened the check to all four units, so that a build missing any one unit would treat itself as having no real IDs and use test units for all four. The comment it left says "never a half-real mix". This is the line:

units = if (BuildConfig.DEBUG || listOf(BuildConfig.AD_BANNER, BuildConfig.AD_INTERSTITIAL,
        BuildConfig.AD_REWARDED, BuildConfig.AD_APP_OPEN).any { it.isEmpty() }) AdUnits.TEST
    else AdUnits(BuildConfig.AD_BANNER, BuildConfig.AD_INTERSTITIAL, BuildConfig.AD_REWARDED, BuildConfig.AD_APP_OPEN)

In the same hour a review agent showed that the old Gradle guard, which decided by task name, could be bypassed. The agent moved the check into a checkReleaseAdIds task hooked to preReleaseBuild, which every release variant runs. That guard only looks at its input, ads.properties.

The agent committed at 17:14 (575aaa1) and built the bundle with the real IDs; the guard passed. The checklist's build step asked for the guard and the signature. The agent also ran grep -c over the dex strings, printing no values: 4 for our publisher number, 5 for the test publisher number. All 5 strings of AdUnits.TEST (banner, interstitial, rewarded, rewarded interstitial, app open) were in the dex.

The 16:14 comment and the review brief covered runtime behavior only; nobody checked whether R8 removed the branch until the dex of a build was counted.

R8 could not evaluate the listOf condition at build time

In a real-ID build the condition is always false, yet R8 could not work that out at build time and kept the branch that returns AdUnits.TEST. On October 28 we reproduced it in a small project: a BuildConfig of the same shape and a 5-string test set, all dummy strings, and both versions of the condition. We compiled it with Kotlin 2.3.21 and shrank it with R8 9.4.24, the version bundled with Android Gradle Plugin 9.4.1, using that plugin's proguard-android-optimize.txt unchanged. The listOf version left 5 test strings and 4 real ones in the dex. The || version left only the 4 real ones.

In javap output, kotlinc has already inlined the BuildConfig constants as string literals in both versions. The listOf version puts the four into an array, builds a list with listOf, and walks it with an Iterator, calling length() on each element. In R8's output dex the listOf call has become Arrays.asList, and the Iterator loop is still there. The || version calls length() directly on each literal; R8 computed those, folded the whole condition to false and dropped the test branch. Version code 1, which checked the banner alone, had the same shape and 0 test strings.

Write test-unit fallbacks as a plain || over BuildConfig constants, and don't wrap them in collection functions (we only measured any). Another case where we read R8's output by the numbers: Play Console said our DEX was 39% optimized.

The review agent made 19 findings and missed the test strings

The 16:49 review agent read the whole change without building it. Its brief listed "if any ad unit is empty, use TEST for all" and "what could break under R8 (keep rules for the Review API)". It came back with 2 high, 6 medium and 11 low findings, and none of them said the release would keep the test strings.

The Gradle guard only sees inputs, so it could not catch this. At 16:55 the agent had counted the dex of the measurement build (-PallowTestAds) the same way and logged "0 real, 5 test" in row 0-4 of the rehearsal checklist; at 17:16 it ran the same check on the real-ID build. The top of the checklist says not to write secrets down. Our full pre-upload checks are in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app.

The fix landed at 17:18 (1aecbc2). The agent described it as a change that removes the test ID strings from a real-ID build. The 17:42 commit (301bc9e) records the check that followed: 4 real, 0 test.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Why the debug source set is a poor home for the test units here

Moving the test units into the debug source set would keep them out of release builds entirely. It does not fit Block Turn. The -PallowTestAds build we use for device measurements and monkey runs is a release variant, and it has to ignore ads.properties and run on test units, because automated taps on real ads count as invalid clicks.

Left alone, every real-ID build would carry 5 test strings, "0 test strings" could no longer be the pass condition, and each time someone would have to work out whether those strings are dead code. So the condition was rewritten into a shape R8 folds. Today the input guard runs before the build, and the dex count is still run by hand after it.

Counting ad IDs in the dex without printing them

Don't decide what went into a release by reading code. Count it in the build output. These are the Git Bash commands we used for the October 28 recount; the publisher number is read into a variable and never echoed.

# 1. Read your publisher number into a variable (not printed)
MY_PUB=$(sed -n 's/^admob\.banner=[^0-9]*\([0-9]*\)\/.*/\1/p' app/ads.properties)
TEST_PUB=...   # the 16-digit test publisher number from Google's test ads page
A=app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab   # for an APK use 'classes*.dex'
# 2. Your ad units: must equal the number of units the app uses
unzip -p "$A" 'base/dex/*.dex' | grep -a -o "$MY_PUB/[0-9]*" | sort -u | wc -l
# 3. Test strings: must be 0 in a real-ID build
unzip -p "$A" 'base/dex/*.dex' | grep -a -o "$TEST_PUB[~/][0-9]*" | sort -u | wc -l

These commands give 4 and 0 for the vc1, vc2 and October 25 bundles, and 0 and 5 for the -PallowTestAds APK from October 25. For the check before the build, hook it to preReleaseBuild instead of guessing from task names:

tasks.matching { it.name == "preReleaseBuild" }.configureEach {
    if (!allowTestAds) dependsOn(checkReleaseAdIds)
}

Counting by prefix alone picks up one string from UMP

Counted by the ad ID prefix alone on October 28, each of the three bundles showed 5. Four were our ad units (the '/' form). The fifth was an app ID-shaped string ('~' form) under a different publisher. Searching 135 Google Play services, consent library (UMP, user-messaging-platform) and Firebase library files in the Gradle cache found the same string in UMP 4.0.0. Count with your own publisher number and the '/' to get 4.

A -PallowTestAds build is supposed to carry the 5 test strings, so the check only applies to real-ID builds. Because it runs after the build, all it can stop is the upload. The R8 reproduction covers one version (9.4.24) and one shape, a BuildConfig string constant; we did not test IDs read from resources or remote config. The manifest app ID is not in the dex; checklist row 1-7 covers it.

Arrow Knots still guesses from task names

Arrow Knots, the other game in the same repository, still checks only the banner field as of the October 27 commit, and its release guard still looks for "release" in task names. Moving it to the checkReleaseAdIds setup and turning the hand-run dex count into a script in the repository are the next jobs.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Does listOf().any change how the app behaves?

It doesn't. With all real IDs present, both versions pick the real units.

Would all or none instead of any also keep the branch?

We haven't measured those. Until we do, we write the fallback as a plain || over the constants.

Do these commands work on Windows?

Git Bash ships unzip, grep, sort and wc, so they run as written there.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Play Billing subscription screen 'temporary error' – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

A month of 'temporary error': our subscription details screen never waited for products, and 1 of 16 users started checkout

The details screen asked Play Billing for products, then checked on the very next line whether the list was empty, and sent anyone without cached products back to the main screen.

Over 90 days, 16 users opened the subscription details screen in our Korean spell checker app, and 1 started checkout. We pulled that funnel from GA4 on September 26, 2026, because of one Play review with 18 "helpful" votes: trying to subscribe to the premium plan gave a "temporary error", and had for a month. Commit 9290f91 that day made the screen wait up to 8 seconds for products. Version 1.6.025 shipped on October 1, and at the interim check on October 17, 4 of the 13 users who opened the details screen had started checkout (31%).

Sources: the app repository's git history (9290f91, 023dd3c, a839c87, 6eb49a1, plus commits from 2023 and 2024), the CHANGELOG entries for Sep 26 and Sep 30, the WATCH.md monitoring log, and the work session logs for Sep 26 to 30, 2026. User counts are GA4 users.

The 90-day funnel: 45 on the plans screen, 16 on details, 1 at checkout

On September 26 we pulled the subscription events for our Korean spell checker, SugarSpeller, counted by user, over 90 days. 45 users saw the plans screen, 16 went on to the details screen where you pick a billing period, and 1 started checkout. Fifteen of the sixteen (94%) left the details screen without starting a purchase. The details-screen events split 18 premium and 2 basic, spread across seven versions between 1.6.016 and 1.6.024.

The "temporary error" in the review is the app's generic retry toast, which in Korean reads roughly "A temporary error occurred. Please try again."

The function that requested products judged an empty list one line later

addSubsItems() on the details screen launched a coroutine in lifecycleScope that waited on the product flow with firstOrNull(), and then, further down the same function, checked the list size straight away. Trimmed, the old code looked like this:

getProductDetails(repo.premiumProductDetails)   // inside: launch { flow.firstOrNull() }
if (recyclerAdapterSubscription!!.mItemList!!.size <= 0) {
    Toast.makeText(..., R.string.string_common_error_retry, ...).show()
    startActivity(main screen)
}

If the billing manager's StateFlow already held the product, firstOrNull() returned on the spot and the list filled. If not, the coroutine suspended, the function moved on, and the size check saw an empty list. Every user whose products were not already cached got the toast and landed back on the main screen. The size check came in with a commit on January 4, 2024; the firstOrNull() call with one on October 3, 2024.

9290f91 turned the check into a wait. The screen now shows a progress dialog and waits inside withTimeoutOrNull(8_000); only if nothing arrives in 8 seconds does it show the toast and go back. The code comment gives the reasoning: connecting to billing and querying products usually takes 1 to 2 seconds, so wait several times that. We did not measure a latency distribution to pick 8 seconds.

The 2024 belief that Play 'sometimes splits the response' came from our own for loop

BillingClientManager stored the products Play returned only if(newMap.size >= 2), that is, only when basic and premium arrived in the same response. The commit that added the line, on October 4, 2024, says the product details response "intermittently comes in separately or together", so only store it when both arrive at once.

The split came from the app. Since December 30, 2023, queryProductDetails() had called queryProductDetailsAsync inside the loop that built the product list, once per iteration. With two products, that sent a one-product query and then a two-product query, and the responses came back as a one-item list and a two-item list. The 2024 fix hid the symptom by throwing away the one-item response. In exchange, whenever Play returned only one product (for example when one product's base plan is turned off), the map stayed empty for good.

9290f91 queries once and merges whatever arrives into the existing map. In Play Billing Library 9.1.0, QueryProductDetailsResult reports products Play could not return in unfetchedProductList; we now log it, which separates Play Console setup problems from app problems.

Three of the agent's first five tests stopped at Mockito

The fix was made with an AI coding agent (Claude Code), tests first: three Robolectric screen tests (waits while products are missing, lists plans when they arrive late, errors only when they never arrive) and two billing manager tests (single-product response, split responses merged). All five failed on the first run, but three of them were not reproducing the bug:

java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "org.mockito.plugins.MockMaker$TypeMockability.mockable()" because "typeMockability" is null

The agent had mocked ProductDetails with Mockito. The class is final, and this project's test classpath mixes in mockito-android, so final mocks could not be created, and we dropped the mock. ProductDetails has a package-private constructor that takes a JSON string, so a test helper, TestProductDetails, lives under the same package name, com.android.billingclient.api, and builds real objects from the JSON shape Play sends (productId, type, subscriptionOfferDetails, pricingPhases). On the next run all five failed for the intended reasons: the screen test with "sent the user to main even though products simply had not arrived yet", the merge test expecting basic and premium and getting an empty set. After the fix they passed. A trimmed version of the helper, with product IDs and price replaced by placeholders:

package com.android.billingclient.api   // test sources; the constructor is package-private
fun subscriptionMonthly(productId: String, basePlanId: String): ProductDetails {
    val phase = JSONObject().put("priceAmountMicros", 1_000_000_000).put("priceCurrencyCode", "KRW")
        .put("formattedPrice", "KRW 1,000").put("billingPeriod", "P1M").put("recurrenceMode", 1)
    val offer = JSONObject().put("basePlanId", basePlanId).put("offerIdToken", "token-$basePlanId")
        .put("offerTags", JSONArray()).put("pricingPhases", JSONArray().put(phase))
    val json = JSONObject().put("productId", productId).put("type", "subs")
        .put("title", productId).put("name", productId).put("description", "test")
        .put("subscriptionOfferDetails", JSONArray().put(offer))
    return ProductDetails(json.toString())     // a real object, not a mock
}
// usage: subscriptionMonthly("premium", "premium-monthly")

On a Galaxy S21 the screen still bounced, and a rebuild from the Sep 26 evening code did the same

On September 28 we opened the details screen on a Galaxy S21. The progress indicator spun, the screen closed, and the app went back to main. The first suspect was the changes from the past two days, so we built a release APK from the Sep 26 evening code (which already had 9290f91) and installed it on the same phone. It failed the same way, after 8 seconds. The billing connection's error was In-app billing API version 3 is not supported, and the phone's Google Play services build was from December 2024.

The phone was the cause, but two app defects showed up with it. When billing setup ended in failure, no disconnect callback followed, so nothing ever reconnected; until the app was restarted, the screen waited the full 8 seconds every time and then showed a "please try again" that had nothing to do with the cause. Commit 023dd3c the same day made the billing manager expose a connection state (connecting, ready, or unavailable with a response code). In 1.6.025 the wait looks like this:

repo.ensureConnected()                       // reconnect if an earlier attempt failed
popupDialog.showDialog(POPUP_TYPE.PROGRESS, true)
lifecycleScope.launch {
    val outcome: Any? = try {
        withTimeoutOrNull(PRODUCT_LOAD_TIMEOUT_MS) {   // 8_000L
            merge(source, repo.connectionState.filterIsInstance<BillingConnectionState.Unavailable>())
                .firstOrNull()                        // products or a failed connection, whichever comes first
        }
    } finally { popupDialog.stopDialog() }
    // Unavailable: (on BILLING/SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE) "check the Play Store" + subscription_unavailable / null (over 8 s): retry toast / else: list the plans
}

On BILLING_UNAVAILABLE it skips the wait, tells the user to check the Play Store, and sends a subscription_unavailable event to GA4.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The day after 'ready to ship', the operator's own test on an S23 led to seven more billing defects

On September 29, version 1.6.025 was logged as ready to ship (the review process that day is in 84 agents reviewed a release). The next morning the operator installed the latest build on a Galaxy S23, tried subscribing, reported that it was not working, and said the release could not go out like this. That prompted another round on the S21 with agent cross-checking: three analysis agents, two refutation passes, three fix agents and two adversarial reviews. It found seven billing defects that had been in the app since 1.6.024 or earlier:

  1. When the purchase sheet failed immediately, the progress indicator never went away, and a background thread kept one CPU core busy.
  2. The billing setup callback wrote OK into the same global value as purchase results, which read as "subscription complete".
  3. A PENDING purchase was treated as a success.
  4. Every return to the app created a new BillingClient (a leak), and the Classic screen saw an empty purchase list before the query finished and saved subscribers as free users.
  5. The Chat screen did not apply benefits after a purchase.
  6. Starting checkout without knowing the current purchases let an existing subscriber buy a second subscription.
  7. A screen's onDestroy closed the billing connection the whole app shared.

a839c87 moved purchase results into their own flow, separate from connection state, and read purchases from a signal that fills only after a successful query, so a user is downgraded only when the query succeeded and found no active subscription. 6eb49a1 re-queries purchases right before checkout and does not open the purchase sheet when they are unknown. Counting every fix that day, unit tests went from 250 to 292.

We never read the S23's logs, but the same test on the S21 showed the problem was how we were testing. A sideloaded release build that was never uploaded to Play gets Play's "Google Play billing is not available for this version" message, and the debug build, whose package name ends in .debug, has no products registered in Play. The only way to run a real purchase end to end is to upload to the internal testing track and install from Play with a license tester account, so that check became a step in the release procedure (b88e9bf).

Judge now, wait forever, or wait 8 seconds

Judging right away, the old behavior, treats "the list is empty the moment the screen opens" as an error, so it went. Waiting forever was already half there in the old code: firstOrNull() never returns if the product never comes, so deleting only the size check would have left users staring at an empty screen. We also wrote down the next move in case the 8-second wait was the wrong fix: if checkout starts from details were still 0 to 10% 30 days after release, the product query itself is failing, and the next step is retrying the billing connection.

Do not judge asynchronously loaded product details the moment the screen opens. Set a ceiling on the wait, and when the failure already has a known cause, such as an unavailable billing connection, report it right away instead of waiting. The same two rules now sit in the subscription section of the agent instructions (CLAUDE.md) in this app's repository.

4 of 13 is an interim number, and device-side billing failures stay

The other half of the September 26 rule: 30 days after release, if more than 30% of details-screen users start checkout, the cause is confirmed. The interim 31% on October 17 clears the bar, and two purchases went through, but it rests on 13 users. A log entry on October 18 found that Play's pre-launch robots had inflated version 1.6.030's subscription screen numbers; whether any of these 13 were robots is not recorded. (How we filter those devices in GA4 is in GA4 said 19 installs yesterday and 8 were real.)

On the same day, subscription_unavailable fired for 2 of the 13 (15%). Users whose device cannot bill, through outdated Play services or a sign-in problem, are still there after the fix, and the most the app can do is say so clearly. We have only used TestProductDetails with Play Billing Library 9.1.0, and the Robolectric tests never see a real purchase or Play's signature check.

Checking whether your own subscription screen turns users away

  1. Put the plans-screen, details-screen and checkout-start events side by side in GA4, counted by user. If checkout starts from details are in single-digit percent, open the details screen code first.
  2. In any function that launches a collector on the product flow, look for a list-size check further down the same function.
  3. Check whether queryProductDetailsAsync runs inside a loop and whether the response handler stores products only when all of them arrive. Merge what arrives, and log unfetchedProductList.
  4. Have the details screen wait with a progress indicator and a ceiling, and end immediately with a "update Play" message when billing setup finishes with BILLING_UNAVAILABLE or SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE.
  5. Create a com.android.billingclient.api package in your test sources with a helper that builds ProductDetails from JSON. Make the three screen cases (waiting, late arrival, never arrives) and the two manager cases (single and split responses) fail first, then fix.
  6. Verify real purchases through the internal testing track and a license tester.
  7. Before release, write down the decision rule with a date: above what rate the cause is confirmed, below what rate it is something else.

What the October 31 check has to answer

The final check is due on October 31, 30 days after 1.6.025 shipped. First we check for pre-launch robots among the details-screen users. Then we look at two numbers: checkout starts against the 30% line, and subscription_unavailable against 5%, above which a button that goes straight to the Play Store is on the table. The records do not show whether the internal-track real purchase check we added to the release procedure was done before 1.6.025 shipped.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Frequently asked questions

My subscription screen keeps showing a "temporary error". Is Google Play down?

Check your own code first. Our details screen decided the product list was empty before the asynchronous product details arrived, and sent every user without cached products away. If retrying always gives the same result, it is not a temporary outage.

How do I test with ProductDetails when Mockito cannot mock it?

Create the com.android.billingclient.api package in your test sources and call the package-private constructor with JSON shaped like Play's response, which gives you a real object. We ran five tests this way on Play Billing Library 9.1.0.

Is "Google Play billing is not available for this version" on a sideloaded APK a bug?

No. Builds that were never uploaded to Play, and debug packages, cannot bill. Upload to the internal testing track and install from Play with a license tester account to check a real purchase.

item.title: Android 16 KB page size, NDK 27 and a blue tint – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

16 KB page size support: a blue tint that only NDK 27 and 29 produced, and 12 .so files measured again

In our video app, 16 KB alignment came from one linker flag, not from the NDK upgrade that came first, and that upgrade is where a blue color regression came in.

Six of the twelve arm64 native libraries in SugarAlbum, the ones we build ourselves, were 4 KB aligned (0x1000). Commit aedf831 on January 3, 2026 rebuilt them with NDK 26.3 at 16 KB (0x4000). Along the way, builds made with NDK 27.0 and 29.0 put a blue cast on photo transitions. On October 27, 2026 we rebuilt the libnative_filter source (two C files) with four NDK versions: NDK 25.1, which the commit lists as "16KB unsupported", gave 0x4000 once the linker flag was in.

Sources: the SugarAlbum git history (c3e09b1, d73db50 to 7efd9c1, aedf831) and the work notes committed with it, .so alignment values rechecked with llvm-readelf on 2026-10-27, and the official Android Developers documentation.

The three .so files rebuilt for targetSdk 36 were still 4 KB aligned

SugarAlbum turns a set of photos into a video. At aedf831 the app has 763 Java files and 32 Kotlin files, and the video and filter work runs in C/C++ libraries built with ndk-build. We raised targetSdk from 33 to 34 on July 15, 2024 (c3e09b1) and from 34 to 36 between August 27 and September 1, 2025 (d73db50 to 7efd9c1). On August 31 (3e7e099) we rebuilt the three arm64 libraries of the multimediaFramework module (libBeatTracker, libPixelCanvas, libPixelUtils) without telling the linker about page size, and the other three (libnative_filter, libFFmpegProcessor, libKwpFFmpegMuxer) were still the November 2022 builds. So right before aedf831, all six had LOAD segments aligned to 0x1000.

Google announced on the Android Developers Blog on May 8, 2025 that starting November 1, 2025, new apps and updates targeting Android 15 or higher must support 16 KB pages. The current page size guide (updated 2026-10-16) says that starting February 1, 2027, updates without 16 KB support can't be released. Our repo notes say a Play Console warning asked for a fix "by May 2025". That date appears in neither official source, and the warning text itself isn't saved anywhere in the repo.

The January work was done with Claude Code; the commit carries its Co-Authored-By line. A work note committed alongside it, ffmpeg.md, records the first move: "After: NDK 27.0.12077973. Reason: the APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES flag is only supported in NDK r27 and later." The final commit used 26.3, and ffmpeg.md went in still saying 27.0.

NDK 27.0 and 29.0 builds tinted photo transitions blue

The commit message has a three-line NDK table: 25.x does not support 16 KB, 26.3 works (adopted), 27.0 and 29.0 show "a blue tint bug with -O3 optimization". progress.md, in the same commit, describes the symptom as a bluish cast during photo transitions, places it in the PixelUtils and libyuv code of the multimediaFramework module, and notes that an -O0 build looks normal. All five modules in that module's Android.mk (libYUV, libMasp, PixelCanvas, PixelUtils, BeatTracker) compile with -O3.

No automated check caught it. The only tests in the repo are the two placeholder tests Android Studio generates (ExampleUnitTest and ExampleInstrumentedTest); nothing compares colors or rendered frames. NDK 27.0 and 29.0 both built cleanly and both produced aligned libraries. The tint showed up only when someone ran the app and watched a transition.

progress.md names the cause as "a Clang -O3 optimization bug". The only evidence on record is that -O0 looks fine. The bundled compilers are clang 17.0.2 in NDK 26.3, 18.0.1 in 27.0 and 21.0.0 in 29.0, so the tint lines up with clang 18 and later. A clean -O0 build is also what you'd see if our own code had undefined behavior that the newer optimizer treats differently, and nobody narrowed it down to a function.

The same commit tidied the libyuv NEON lines in Android.mk, so we checked that too. libPixelUtils.so exports 198 symbols with NEON in the name both before and after the commit. The NEON code was already in the old build, so it isn't the variable.

NDK 26.3 ignores APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES

The final commit sets alignment in three places: android.ndk.maxPageSize=16384 in gradle.properties, APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES := true in three Application.mk files, and LOCAL_LDFLAGS += -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 in six Android.mk modules. To see which one did the work, we searched each NDK's build/core for the flag name. It isn't in 25.1 or 26.3; it's only in build-binary.mk of 27.0 and 29.0. In 27.0, a true value adds max-page-size=16384 to the link. In 29.0, 16 KB is the default and a false value sets it back to 4096.

Then we rebuilt the libnative_filter source from aedf831 with each NDK and read the LOAD alignment with llvm-readelf -lW on 2026-10-27.

NDKLinker flag in Android.mkarm64-v8a LOAD alignment
25.1.8937393no0x1000
25.1.8937393yes0x4000
26.3.11579264no (Application.mk flag only)0x1000
26.3.11579264yes (as committed)0x4000
27.0.12077973no (Application.mk flag only)0x4000
29.0.14206865no0x4000

Under 26.3 the 16 KB alignment came from the Android.mk linker flag; the Application.mk line did nothing. The same flag gave 0x4000 under 25.1. The commit's "NDK 25.x: 16KB unsupported" was never tested with the flag in place, and it follows from the first assumption that the feature needs r27. The official guide's "Android NDK r27 and lower" section also gets 16 KB alignment from the max-page-size and common-page-size linker flags and never mentions APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES.

The six prebuilt FFmpeg libraries pass the LOAD check and fail the RELRO formula

progress.md left six prebuilt FFmpeg libraries (libavcodec-56, libavfilter-5, libavformat-56, libavutil-54, libswresample-1, libswscale-3) marked as needing a separate 16 KB rebuild. Their LOAD segments were already aligned to 0x10000 (64 KB) before the commit. 64 KB is a multiple of 16 KB, so they pass the guide's rule that no LOAD segment may be below 2**14.

The guide has a second check. (VirtAddr + MemSiz) of the GNU_RELRO segment should divide evenly by 0x4000. If it doesn't, and RELRO shares a LOAD segment with writable data that follows it (.data, .bss), the app can crash at runtime with a segmentation fault. A LOAD segment holding only RELRO data, followed by a writable LOAD that starts on a separate 16 KB page, is a case where the formula doesn't apply; the guide's example of that layout is still 16 KB compliant. We ran all twelve arm64 libraries from aedf831 through that formula.

LibraryRELRO end % 0x4000Result
libnative_filter, libBeatTracker, libFFmpegProcessor, libKwpFFmpegMuxer0x0pass
libPixelCanvas, libPixelUtils0x1000formula doesn't apply (RELRO-only LOAD)
six prebuilt FFmpeg libraries0x1000 to 0x3000RELRO shares a LOAD with .data/.bss

In libavcodec-56, the writable LOAD segment is 0x257f00 bytes in memory and only its first 0xfbf8 bytes are RELRO, which is the shape the guide uses as its crash example. The commit added only max-page-size; the guide's examples also pass common-page-size=16384. Our six self-built libraries passed without it. The repo has FFmpeg's source and build scripts, but nothing records which flags produced the .so files it ships. ffmpeg.md says -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 was added to ADDI_LDFLAGS in both build scripts; in this commit the two scripts were only moved, and ADDI_LDFLAGS on line 28 of build_arm64-v8a.sh doesn't have that flag.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Keeping NDK 25.1 and adding the linker flag would have worked

There were three ways to go in January. We pinned NDK 26.3 and wrote "do not use NDK 27 or later" into the notes.

  • Stay on NDK 25.1 and add the linker flag. The table above says alignment would have been fine, and since the records show no tint on 25.1 and the compiler would have stayed the same, there was no reason to expect a color regression. It was ruled out by the "25 unsupported" call.
  • Use NDK 27 or 29 and lower -O3 only in multimediaFramework. -O0 is recorded as looking fine, but nobody measured how much slower video processing gets.
  • Find and fix the function that shifts the color. There's no record of an attempt.

Don't upgrade the NDK first. Put the linker flag into the NDK you already use and check the alignment with readelf. If you have another reason to move to a newer NDK, do it as a separate change and compare rendered output against the previous build.

CMake builds and NDK r28 or later need a different procedure

This is an ndk-build project (Android.mk, Application.mk). With CMake, the guide puts the flags in target_link_options, and the Android.mk line is irrelevant. NDK r28 and later align to 16 KB by default, so the flag isn't needed at all; our 29.0 build gave 0x4000 on arm64 with no flag.

There's no basis for saying NDK 27 will do the same to other code. We didn't check 32-bit (armeabi-v7a) libraries; the guide's requirement covers 64-bit devices.

Checking with readelf twice and the same set of photos

  1. For each arm64-v8a .so that ships in the APK or AAB, read the LOAD alignment. The last column must be 0x4000 or larger.
    llvm-readelf -lW libfoo.so | grep -E "LOAD|GNU_RELRO"
  2. If there's a GNU_RELRO line, add VirtAddr and MemSiz and take the remainder mod 0x4000. If it isn't zero, check whether the LOAD segment holding RELRO also holds .data/.bss (its MemSiz is much larger than RELRO's).
  3. Before changing the NDK, add both flags from the guide to Android.mk in your current NDK and repeat step 1.
    LOCAL_LDFLAGS += -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 -Wl,-z,common-page-size=16384
  4. APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES is read only by NDK r27 and later. On r26 or older, that line alone does nothing.
  5. Delete the .so files in jniLibs and rebuild every time you change the NDK or the flags. Our notes record that Android Studio's Clean Project doesn't remove jniLibs, so the build script deletes them first.
  6. Export a video from the same photos with the old build and the new one, and watch the transitions side by side.
  7. If you ship uncompressed .so files, confirm Android Gradle Plugin 8.5.1 or later and run zipalign -v -c -P 16 4 app.apk. SugarAlbum uses AGP 8.12.0.

Another Play Console warning we traced is in Play Console said our DEX was 39% optimized. The culprit was a keep rule for an SDK we never used. The app itself is on the SugarAlbum page.

Not done yet: a 16 KB emulator run and a per-module -O3 check

Video export has to run end to end on a 16 KB page emulator image to see whether the FFmpeg libraries crash on RELRO. If they do, FFmpeg needs a rebuild with common-page-size=16384. We still don't know which module the tint comes from; one way to narrow it down is to take the five multimediaFramework modules off -O3 one at a time. The NDK 27.0 in ffmpeg.md should be corrected to 26.3.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Do I need NDK r27 or later to support 16 KB pages?

Not for the alignment itself. With -Wl,-z,max-page-size=16384 in Android.mk, NDK 25.1 rebuilt libnative_filter.so (arm64) with 0x4000 LOAD alignment (measured 2026-10-27). r27 is only needed for the one-line APP_SUPPORT_FLEXIBLE_PAGE_SIZES approach.

How do I check whether a .so is 16 KB aligned?

Run llvm-readelf -lW or llvm-objdump -p and confirm every LOAD segment is aligned to 0x4000 (2**14) or more. If GNU_RELRO shares a LOAD segment with writable data, also check that (VirtAddr + MemSiz) % 0x4000 is zero.

Can I keep a prebuilt .so that is 64 KB aligned?

It passes the LOAD alignment check. SugarAlbum's six FFmpeg libraries are 0x10000 and pass that check, but their RELRO remainders are 0x1000 to 0x3000.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException
  • A market:// link opens a store chooser on SKT-sold Samsung phones: set the Play package first
  • A splash that never moved on: addOnCompleteListener(this) and onStop

item.title: Puzzle game time limits: 3-star par by simulation – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Measurement

Testers said the time was "too long, so it's easy": checking that with a simulation before cutting puzzle par times by 30%

We picked the size of the par-time cut from simulated three-star rates per level band. The first proposal, a 45% cut, left casual players a 1% three-star rate on later levels, so we cut 30% instead.

On levels 41-200 of Arrow Knots, the median par was 65 seconds while our simulated casual player finished in a median 41. On the afternoon of October 4, 2026 the operator passed on feedback from three real testers: the time was too long, so the game was easy. That evening commit efe26ae multiplied every par by 0.7. The cut we first agreed on was 45%. The coding agent recommended it and the operator approved it. A rerun over 158 levels then showed casual players earning three stars on 1% of attempts past level 500. At 30% that rate is 30%, and par lands next to the casual median (45 s against 41 s, 190 s against 188 s).

Sources: the game repository's git history (efe26ae, 632adb5, 89dc35a and others), design docs 05, 06, 09a and 09b, the October 4 agent session log, and an October 27 GA4 check. The simulation tables are copied from that session's output; constants were rechecked at HEAD on October 27, 2026.

Eight par scales applied to one set of simulated runs

Par in Arrow Knots is a countdown at the top of the screen, but nothing happens when it reaches zero; the level keeps going. It matters for stars: a three-star clear needs at most one mistake per 12 arrows and a finish inside par. Shorter par means fewer three-star clears, and how many fewer depends on where in the game you are.

The simulator has two players. The casual one checks arrows in random order at 120 ms per arrow; the skilled one checks outward from its last tap at 60 ms. Tap time follows Fitts's law (far and small targets take longer), and mis-touches and taps on blocked arrows happen with set probabilities. The agent took every 7th level from 1 to 1,100 (158 levels), ran each 30 times as the casual player and 15 times as the skilled one, then rescored the same runs under each candidate scale and floor. The candidate scales were split into two batches and run twice, taking about 5 and 3 seconds.

Scale (floor)Par, 41-200Par, 501-1100Casual runs inside par, 501-1100Casual 3-star (41-200 / 201-500 / 501-1100)
1.0 (20 s, shipped)65 s265 s88%50 / 45 / 40%
0.8 (15 s)55 s215 s88%50 / 44 / 40%
0.75 (15 s)50 s200 s81%50 / 43 / 39%
0.7 (15 s)45 s190 s52%50 / 38 / 30%
0.65 (15 s)45 s175 s17%46 / 27 / 12%
0.6 (15 s)40 s160 s3%37 / 16 / 2%
0.55 (15 s)40 s150 s1%23 / 9 / 1%
0.5 (10 s)35 s135 s0%14 / 2 / 0%

Par figures are medians across the levels in each band. In the same runs the casual median was 41 s for levels 41-200, 93 s for 201-500 and 188 s for 501-1100, and the skilled three-star rate was 67 / 71 / 77% on every scale. On levels 41-200 the casual three-star rate is 50% at both 1.0 and 0.7: runs inside par fell from 88% to 84%, yet three-star clears did not move, so the runs pushed past par were mostly runs that had already lost the third star to mistakes.

The agent called par "about 2x" the casual median and proposed a 45% cut

The testers' list had 11 items; the timer was item 4: shorten the time because it is too long and therefore easy, and when time runs out, restart the level or show the watch-an-ad prompt. The operator pasted the list at 14:41 KST. Two minutes later the agent, having read the code, answered that par was "about 2 times" the casual median solve time and "about 3.5 times" the skilled one. The example in that same answer was a 22-arrow board with a 54 s par, a 41 s casual median and a 24 s skilled median. Those numbers give 1.3 and 2.3.

Working from that "about 2x" figure, the agent recommended cutting every par by about 45%, bringing par down to roughly the casual median. At 14:54 the operator picked that option, which also limited real time-out failures to one or two levels per world.

What stopped the 45% was a done-condition the agent wrote onto the task card a few minutes later: "recompute 3-star rates per band by simulation: skilled 60-75%, casual 25-40%." The agent ran that check before touching the code. At 0.55, casual runs on levels 501-1100 finished inside par 1% of the time and earned three stars 1% of the time. On levels 41-200, par (40 s) dropped below the casual median (41 s).

Par was 1.6 times the casual median on 41-200 (65 s against 41 s) but only 1.4 times on 501-1100 (265 s against 188 s). A single scale taken from one board's ratio pushes the later bands, which had less slack, under the median first. Take the direction from testers, and pick the amount from a per-band three-star table.

At 15:06 the agent asked again with three options: a 30% cut (recommended; casual three stars 30-50%, skilled 67-77%), 35% (later-band casual 12-27%) and 45% (the first plan; later-band casual 1-9%). It had also simulated 0.75 and 0.8 but did not offer them. The operator chose 30% at 18:44, and the commit ten minutes later applied the 0.7 scale and lowered the par floor from 20 s to 15 s.

The design docs made par generous on purpose

The October 2 design doc (05) made par a soft countdown: run past it and you lose only the third star. It cited a fan-wiki summary saying Candy Crush removed its timed levels in May 2018 (the doc notes the original page was blocked and never read) and the Two Dots help page line "Two Dots is not timed!", and it followed the game's earlier positioning as a relaxing puzzle (doc 00).

The solve-time model doc (06) multiplied its fitted formula by 1.42 so that casual players would have 30% of the clock left on average. The October 3 check gate for the 1.1.0 expansion to 1,000 levels plus an endless mode, called G1, required the same thing: casual mean time left of at least 30%. Big boards add a per-screen term, PAR_SCREEN_S, which the spec allowed to be 2-4 s. The model spent 12.4 s per extra screen on camera pans and off-screen checks, and 2-4 s left only 13-22% of the clock, so the term was frozen at 19 s (632adb5).

That 19 s is item 1 under "Spec deviations" in the G1 report, with its reason, because the workstream rules (09b) said: "Never weaken a test to make it pass. If the spec looks wrong, record it under 'Spec deviations' in your final report, with the reason." The G1 report's check table lists part 3 casual mean time left at 30.6%, against a 30% minimum.

None of the model's constants were fitted to real players. Doc 06 took search and tap speeds from ranges in visual-search and Fitts's-law studies, and marked the chance of tapping a blocked arrow as "an estimate, to be calibrated with telemetry." Doc 05 planned to reset each level's par to the 70th percentile of real mistake-free clears after launch, but on October 4 there was no such data.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Time-out failure went into a boss time attack, not the main levels

The second half of the testers' suggestion, failing the level when time runs out, was not adopted as asked. It was option two in the agent's 14:44 question ("every level fails from world 2", i.e. from level 31), described as more rewarded-ad views but a risk of losing players who like to solve calmly. The task card that day also recorded the agent's market check: the top two apps in the genre advertised "no timer" in their store text, and one app used a hard timer with a +60 s ad.

A real time limit went into the code that night as a mini game. Commit 89dc35a at 23:15 added four mini games every 25 levels, one of them a boss time attack where the clock can run out and a rewarded ad buys 30 more seconds. Main levels still never fail on time; efe26ae's message says: "Missing par still never fails a level."

Even at 0.7, early levels and skilled players missed the done-condition

The skilled three-star rate did not move between scales 0.5 and 1.0. Skilled runs finished inside par 97-99% of the time on every scale; mistakes were what cost them the third star. Casual three stars on levels 1-40 also stayed at 56% (55% at 0.5).

Against the task card's done-condition, 0.7 was inside 25-40% only for casual players on levels 201-500 (38%) and 501-1100 (30%). Casual players on levels 1-200 sat at 50-56% and skilled players on 501-1100 at 77%, both outside the range. The commit message says only "casual 3-star 30-50%", and the mistake allowance (STAR3_DIV 12) was left alone.

The sample is thin at the start: levels 1-40 contributed six levels (1, 8, 15, 22, 29 and 36). If running out of time fails the level, don't tune to the median, since that fails half of all attempts; the time attack in doc 05 set its limit at 1.3 times the median.

Storing simulated runs and rescoring them per candidate scale

  1. Make the game and the simulator use the same par function. Here pace.py reads its constants out of the app's Pace.kt, so the model plays the shipped numbers.
  2. Run a sample of levels with at least two player types and keep (cleared, time, mistakes) for every run.
  3. Write the target three-star range per band before you look at results.
  4. Rescore the stored runs under each candidate scale and floor, and tabulate per band: median par, casual median, share inside par, and three-star rate.
  5. Give the person deciding two or three options, each with its later-band numbers.
  6. When the constant changes, regenerate the par column of the level data and update the checkpoint tests and the all-levels comparison in the same commit. efe26ae changed 13 checkpoints (level 1000 went from 380 s to 270 s) along with the 1,100-level table.

The rescoring in that day's script centres on these lines (variable names spelled out):

def par(base, scale, floor):
    t = base * scale + AUTOSTART_SLACK_S   # 5 s before the first tap
    return min(max(round(t / 5) * 5, floor), PAR_MAX_S)
three_star = cleared and time <= par(base, scale, floor) and mistakes <= arrows // 12

We also had bots play a block puzzle before players did; that write-up is Block puzzle difficulty: how simulation bots caught a game you could never lose.

What's left

We have not measured real players' three-star rate yet. An October 27, 2026 check found the GA4 custom dimensions level, stars and world reading (not set) for all time (1,258 level_up events in Arrow Knots). The app appears to send these integers as numeric parameters that the dimensions don't pick up, and sending them as strings too is proposed for the next release. There is no record yet of the G1 checks being rerun after 0.7 (the report is unchanged since October 3).

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

How do you set a three-star threshold in a puzzle game?

Arrow Knots gives three stars for at most one mistake per 12 arrows plus a finish inside par. We chose the par scale, 0.7, so that simulated casual players earn three stars on 30-38% of attempts in the later level bands.

Should a level fail when the timer runs out?

Not in this game's main levels: running past par only costs the third star. A fail-on-timeout rule exists only in the boss time attack, one of four mini games that rotate every 25 levels (so it comes every 100 levels).

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • Block puzzle difficulty: how simulation bots caught a game you could never lose
