item.title: AI commit provenance: what Co-Authored-By misses – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Commits without a Co-Authored-By trailer: the agent made 26 of the 29 we could check

Do not report a Co-Authored-By count as the share of AI-written code. Of 29 commits without the trailer that we could check against session logs, the agent made 26. Have it add the trailer to merges and reverts too.

In the repository of our Korean spell-checker app, 26 commits whose times match git commands the agent ran (25 merge commits, 1 revert) carry no Co-Authored-By: Claude trailer. The window is the one covered by Claude Code session logs, from the evening of September 13 to October 24, 2026; of the 29 trailer-less commits in it, only 3 have no matching command in the logs. Since August 2025 there are 89 commits without the trailer, and sorted by subject line and date, 52 of them are merge commits or stash entries. If the agent runs your merges and reverts, tell it in the instruction file to pass -m with the trailer.

Sources: git history of four repositories (recounted on October 25, 2026 with the cutoff fixed at the end of October 24, KST), Claude Code session logs kept on this PC, and the GitHub pull request list. Author names and session IDs are left out.

After September 13, 26 of the 29 commits without a trailer match an agent git command

A missing trailer says nothing about who made the commit. So we went through the Claude Code session logs (JSONL files) and collected every shell command the agent ran that contained git commit, merge, revert, stash, tag and the like, and that mentioned this repository in its working directory or command. A commit counted as "agent command found" when such a command ran between ten minutes before and 30 seconds after the commit time.

The agent's first git write command for this repository ran at 20:41 on September 13, 2026. From then to October 24 there are 282 commits, and all 253 with a trailer matched an agent command, so the method found every trailer commit in that window.

In this window 89.7% of commits carry the trailer, while 279 commits, 98.9%, match a git command the agent ran (on the trailer-less side, 25 merge commits and 1 revert). The revert d378829, at 10:47 on September 30, sits in the log as git revert --no-edit aa2d224. The commit it reverted had gone in 28 minutes earlier with a trailer; the revert has none. The merge 2b9d3a1 on October 17 was git merge --no-edit main. On the same day the agent wrote its own -m message for merge b356c72 and still left the trailer line out.

The remaining three are a version commit (16d9917) and the two v16024 release merges, made at 20:07 and 20:08 on September 26. No matching command is in the logs, so we left them undecided.

Matching on time alone could produce coincidences, so we shifted every commit time by three hours in each direction and ran the same match. Only 17 and 15 of the 253 trailer commits matched (6 to 7%), and 0 and 1 of the 29 without a trailer.

All three merges in the same period that do carry a trailer (857326b, 08b1f7a, 0458820) have an agent command in the logs that put the trailer in. For 08b1f7a and 0458820 it was git merge … -m "… Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 …"; for 857326b the agent resolved a merge conflict and then added the same line with git commit -m.

The 89 trailer-less commits since August 2025: 50 merges, 2 stash entries, 7 early commits, 30 others

We matched Co-Authored-By: Claude at the start of a message line, then recounted with git's own trailer parser (%(trailers:key=Co-authored-by)); the two counts were identical in all four repositories. Up to October 24, 2026, git log --all on the spell checker lists 725 commits, and 345 of the 434 since August 1, 2025 (79.5%) carry the trailer. The 701 commits in our note on 701 commit messages were counted on the develop branch only, up to October 19, minus one submodule commit, which is why the totals differ.

GroupCountHow we sorted it
git-flow release merges37Subject Merge branch 'release/…', 'hotfix/…' or Merge tag …
Feature, sync and PR merges139 feature branches, 3 syncs between develop and main, 1 pull request
Stash entries2On main: … and its index on main: …
Before the first trailer7August 3 to the morning of August 7 (the first trailer is 02cbb15, August 7 at 22:01)
Other single-parent commits3024 code, 5 data or config, 1 revert

The two stash entries are not commits anyone meant to count. git log --all follows refs/stash as well, so of the five stashes in this repository, the newest one (September 10, 2026) and its index commit show up. Put --exclude=refs/stash before --all and the numbers become 345 of 432 (79.9%), with 87 lacking the trailer.

Drop merges and start the window at the first trailer, and the share rises to 342 of 372 single-parent commits (91.9%).

Of the 30 single-parent commits, the five data or config ones are 9 image and PSD files (94773fa), 4 image and PSD files plus a few string and DB-version lines (417259d, 9 files, +8/−8), collapsing eight .gitignore lines into one (3c1bdca), a two-line version bump in build.gradle (36a6c23), and 906 lines of quiz data plus a two-line version bump (16d9917). All 24 code commits fall between August 9 and September 13, 2025. One of them, f43dada, is the operator reverting source the AI had changed wrongly; its Korean message roughly reads "restore the existing source that was edited wrongly (Claude Code…)", and the story is in our note on 701 commit messages.

The mining memo counted about 40 merges and called the rest hand commits

This topic came from a mining memo an agent wrote while scanning the repository. It said about 40 of the 89 were git-flow merges and the rest were hand commits. The recount found 51 merge-shaped commits (one of them a stash) and 7 commits from before the first trailer inside the window. Of the 29 commits we could check against the logs, the agent's own commands made 26.

The memo's totals (728 and 348) had no cutoff either. Five new commits arrived in this repository on the morning of October 25 alone, and the same command then returned 730. Every number in this note uses --until=2026-10-25T00:00:00. The memo also said our peer-to-peer chat app repository started in September 2026; its first commit is from August 21, 2025 (8 commits that month, 95 in September 2026).

In the utilities app (7) and the puzzle game (10), every trailer-less commit matches an agent command

RepositoryFirst commitCommitsTrailerShareNo trailer (merges)
Spell checker, all history2020-12-1672534547.6%380 (205)
Spell checker, since Aug 202543434579.5%89 (51)
Utilities app2026-09-20878092.0%7 (6)
Puzzle game2026-09-3017016094.1%10 (10)
P2P chat app2025-08-2110310299.0%1 (0)

Even in repositories built with the agent from day one, the gaps are mostly merges. All 10 trailer-less commits in the puzzle game are merges, and all 10 line up with an agent git command in the session logs. The same repository has 9 merges that do carry the trailer.

In the utilities app, 5 of the 6 merges are Merge branch 'worktree-agent-<id>'. All five are in the session logs as git merge --no-edit worktree-agent-<id> commands the agent ran, and the git worktree list output in the first of those commands shows the branches sitting in .claude/worktrees/agent-<id>, the worktree folders Claude Code created for its subagents. The one single-parent commit, 1171dee, is the agent's own git commit -m "Ignore local upload keystores", written without the trailer line. The single gap in the P2P chat app is its root commit, "first commit", three minutes before the first trailer commit.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Two pull requests labeled codex never appear in git log --all

The author field is no help. All 89 trailer-less commits since August 2025 in the spell checker come from one account, which also authored 338 trailer commits.

Pull request labels live only on GitHub. The spell checker has three pull requests. #1 and #2, from June 29, 2025, have a codex label and codex/… branches, and both were closed without merging. Their commits (09cb9b5, d318e22) are on no branch, so git log --all never shows them, and their messages have no trailer either. #3, merged with 20 commits, has no label.

Branch names such as worktree-agent- and codex/ survive a merge only in the merge commit's subject. Wording differs too: between the night of August 7 and September 13, 2025, the median subject length was 38 characters for trailer commits and 20 for the rest; we did not use it to decide who made a commit.

Session logs matched 253 of 253 trailer commits in the checked window, which makes them the strongest signal we have. They exist only on this PC, and for the spell checker they start on the evening of September 13, 2026.

Six git log lines with --exclude=refs/stash

These run as-is in Git Bash or a macOS or Linux shell. Change the cutoff and the trailer text to match your repository.

U=2026-10-25T00:00:00; S=2025-08-01T00:00:00
P='^Co-Authored-By: Claude'
# 1. total and trailer commits (stash excluded)
git log --exclude=refs/stash --all --since=$S --until=$U --format=%h | wc -l
git log --exclude=refs/stash --all --since=$S --until=$U -i -E --grep="$P" --format=%h | wc -l
# 2. commits without the trailer, merges among them
git log --exclude=refs/stash --all --since=$S --until=$U -i -E --grep="$P" --invert-grep --format=%h | wc -l
git log --exclude=refs/stash --all --merges --since=$S --until=$U -i -E --grep="$P" --invert-grep --format='%h %s'
# 3. cross-check with git's trailer parser
git log --exclude=refs/stash --all --until=$U --format='%(trailers:key=Co-authored-by,valueonly)' | grep -ci claude
# 4. single-parent commits without the trailer, with size
git log --exclude=refs/stash --all --no-merges --since=$S --until=$U -i -E --grep="$P" --invert-grep --stat --format='%h %ad %s' --date=short
  1. Fix the cutoff with --until. In a repository that gets commits every day, the totals change within hours.
  2. Find the date of the first trailer (first line with --reverse) and start the window there.
  3. Sort the commits without a trailer into merges, stash entries, data or config, and code.
  4. If you have session logs, match commit times against the times of the agent's git commands, and shift the times by a few hours to measure how often they match by chance.
  5. If the agent runs your merges and reverts, add a rule to its instruction file to pass -m with the trailer.

Periods without session logs and squash merges cannot be settled

In the spell checker, the 51 trailer-less commits made after the first trailer but before the session logs start (23 merges, 28 single-parent commits) stay undecided. The 24 code commits among them added 5,749 lines of Kotlin and Java, while the 39 trailer commits of the same weeks (the night of August 7 to September 13) added 14,762. Why a trailer is not a share of code lines is covered in the 701-commit note.

Some repositories will not fit this method. With squash merges, one pull request becomes one commit, and the trailer depends on the tool of whoever presses the merge button. In repositories with many contributors, each person's commit habits make the ratio harder to read. Tools that keep no session logs, or setups that delete them, rule out the cross-check entirely. In a GitLab survey of 1,528 developers and technology buyers in six countries, released on June 23, 2026, 43% said they cannot reliably distinguish AI-generated code from human-written code, and 39% pointed to systems that don't track code origin (GitLab press release).

What we will check next

Neither the spell checker's instruction file nor the global instructions say anything about trailers (checked October 25). Once a rule for merges and reverts is written down, the trailer-less merges have to be counted again to see whether it worked.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Frequently asked questions

Does a commit without a Co-Authored-By trailer mean a person wrote it?

No. When the agent runs git merge or git revert --no-edit with git's default message, or passes -m without the trailer line, the commit it makes has no trailer.

What extra commits does git log --all count?

Besides every branch and tag, it follows refs/stash, so the newest stash and its index commit count as two commits. git log --exclude=refs/stash --all leaves them out.

Can a merge commit carry a Co-Authored-By trailer?

It can if you pass the message yourself with git merge --no-ff -m "message" and put the trailer on its last line. After a merge conflict, add the same line to the git commit -m that concludes the merge.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Several Claude Code sessions, one repo: the file owner table, checked against 13 merges
  • Three agent designs, three judges: the market judge alone would have picked the one that crashed on every KakaoTalk file
  • Running an AI marketer on a schedule four times a day: the permission table that leaves money, accounts and policy to a person
  • 84 agents reviewed a release: three refuters per finding, and only the 20 survivors got fixed
  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException

item.title: AI coding agents and secrets: chat, logs, tokens – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

AI coding agents and secrets: one rule in chat, logs and token permissions, and the two exceptions a copied masking regex missed

Give the agent commands that check without printing values, keep log masking in one function guarded by a test that fails on copies, and give deploy tokens only the permissions the code needs.

Four copies of a log-masking regex were being merged into one function when two exceptions in one of those files turned out to carry the auth token in clear text. That was in a peer-to-peer chat app on September 13, 2026, six days after the defect had been marked fixed. The same pattern showed up twice more: on October 2 an agent printed the last 150 lines of the shell history and an API key landed in the session log, and on October 10 the deploy plan for a family app asked for a wider Cloudflare token.

Sources: git history and tests from three repositories (the chat app, a Korean spell checker app, and a family app still in development) and the agent session logs. Session-log counts were redone on October 25, 2026. Every secret shown below is a placeholder such as XXXX.

One rule, three places it has to hold

The rule fits in a sentence: never copy a secret's value anywhere; say where it is and what kind it is. With a coding agent in the loop it has to hold in three places. Whatever the agent reads ends up in the session log, the code it writes can put values into logs and exception messages, and the deployments it designs can ask for broader tokens than the code needs.

In all three places the agent did the fixing. The person running these projects (the operator below) made two main decisions: the rule should apply to every session, and the agent should stop handing work back and do it itself.

Chat: the first secrets rule was written 47 seconds after a key reached the session log

The agent printed the last 150 lines of the shell history at 8:47 on October 2. The operator had asked it to fill in the shared instructions every session reads, and it wanted to learn the setup. One of them exported an AI API key. Tool output is saved verbatim in the session log, so the key was now part of the transcript.

At that moment the instruction file held only rules about reply format. Forty-seven seconds after the key was printed, the agent wrote the first secrets rule into it: one line saying secrets stay out of any output. It said what not to do and nothing about how to check, and for an agent, reading a file and printing it are the same action. Eighteen seconds later the agent told the operator that an AI API key sat in plain text in the shell history, giving the location and kind but not the value.

At 8:55 the operator asked for a rule that keeps passwords and personal data out of every session's chat, and the agent replaced the one line with a rule that also says how to check. The gist: never write a value, only where it is and what kind. Files are checked with commands that show key names and line counts (grep -c, cut -d= -f1), and commands take environment variables or file references instead of values. It covers commits, docs and memory files as well as chat, and a value someone pastes in is not quoted back; the agent recommends rotating it. The scope also widened from secrets to personal data.

The agent deleted the four history lines that held the key (three export lines and one secret-registration command that took the value as an argument) and counted again: zero. It reported two places it left for later: the log file of the session still running, which could break if edited mid-session, and the terminal window where the key had been typed. The report ended by saying that deleting doesn't undo the exposure and rotating the key is the only sure fix, and that a new key should be registered by name with the value typed at the prompt.

On October 25 we recounted across the 109 main session logs. The key-names-only command cut -d= -f1 appears 24 times, every dated one from October 3 on; with subagent logs included it is 2 in September and 179 in October. Counting .env lines with grep -c was already a habit in September (25 times), so what grew is the names-only check. Lines matching three known key shapes (the newer AI API key format, GitHub tokens, sk- keys) came to exactly one across all 2,567 logs including subagents: that 8:47 output.

# .env: line count and key names, no values
grep -c '=' .env
cut -d= -f1 .env
# shell history: how many lines mention that key name
grep -c 'API_KEY' ~/.bash_history
# commands reference values instead of containing them
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" https://api.example.com/v1/ping
wrangler secret put SIGNING_KEY < secrets/signing-key

Logs: four copies of a masking regex, and two exceptions that never masked

The chat app (Flutter) passes a shared token as ?token= in the signaling server URL. On September 7, the agent reviewing platform security before release rated this High: the discovery logs went through debugPrint, which prints in release builds too, and four connect-log lines wrote the whole URL.

The reviewing agent proposed Uri.parse(url).replace(query: null). The agent assigned to fix it reported that this keeps the query: in Dart's Uri.replace, a null argument means "keep the existing component". It switched to a one-line regex instead.

The copies came from how the work was split. Several fix agents each owned a set of files that day. The mobile owner's scope was "one masking line" in its two files, and the two web files went to another owner as a request. Shortly after midnight, the web side got its own _maskToken wrapping the same regex. A docs pass on September 8 and 9 wrote down "regex duplicated in 4 files; extracting a shared helper is still open", while the defect list already said Fixed, dated September 7.

On September 13 (555680e), writing the shared function meant looking at every place each file turned the URL into a string. Two HttpException sites in the mobile HTTP client had no masking at all: a failed SSE connection put the token into the exception's uri, and a failed POST put it into both the message and the uri. The mobile owner's first fix had covered the success log line only, and the failure exceptions in the same file were outside it. The web copies masked their failure messages too.

String maskSignalingUrl(String url) =>
    url.replaceAllMapped(_signalingToken, (m) => '${m[1]}***');
final RegExp _signalingToken = RegExp(
  r'([?&](?:token|secret)=)[^&#\s]*',
  caseSensitive: false,
);

The new pattern ignores case, also covers secret=, and stops at # or whitespace. We ran the old pattern ([?&]token=)[^&]* and the new one through Python's re on placeholder values to see the difference:

InputOld regexNew regex
ws://h/ws?TOKEN=XXXXunchanged?TOKEN=***
ws://h/ws?secret=XXXXunchanged?secret=***
ws://h/ws?token=XXXX#frag?token=*** (fragment eaten)?token=***#frag
http://h/api/token/listunchangedunchanged

Three kinds of tests went in with it: 7 rule tests, 1 source guard, and 1 real failure path. The failure-path test starts an HTTP server on the loopback address that answers 401 and checks that the client's exception text contains token=*** and not the value. The source guard, shortened:

test('no copy of the masking regex comes back in discovery', () {
  final offenders = <String>[];
  for (final f in Directory('lib/core/discovery').listSync()) {
    if (f is! File || !f.path.endsWith('.dart')) continue;
    if (f.path.endsWith('discovery_log.dart')) continue; // the definition
    final src = f.readAsStringSync();
    if (src.contains('token=)') || src.contains('_maskToken')) {
      offenders.add(f.path);
    }
  }
  expect(offenders, isEmpty);
});

It fails if the regex fragment token=) or the old helper's name shows up in any file other than the definition. The duplication stayed for five days after it was written down on September 8, so copies are now blocked by a test rather than left to review. Keep one masking function, and commit a test that fails when a copy appears.

The same commit replaced the peer's public-key fingerprint in the diagnostics map with a yes/no flag. That map goes straight to the diagnostics screen, reports and logs; the fingerprint is meant for a person to compare by eye, so the confirmation dialog reads it on its own.

Release logcat also carried what users typed

On October 17, QA on the SugarSpeller spell checker found the same class of bug in its release logcat (21895f6). Up to version 1.6.030, release builds logged the check request URL (which contains the user's text), the first 500 characters of the raw response, a session key for the external checking service on every resume, and the FCM push token. In the app's logging wrapper, log.e prints regardless of BuildConfig.DEBUG.

The fix followed the chat app: diagnostic lines moved to log.d, and keys and text are logged only as a length or a present/absent flag. ReleaseLogSecretsTest scans all main sources for log calls that print in release and looks only at interpolations and arguments outside string literals. Its first test feeds in the 7 old leaking lines and requires all 7 to be caught; the test comment says that if these are missed, the scan below is fake too. A release build of 1.6.031, the next development version, went onto a Galaxy S20, and logcat showed zero such lines. The same yardstick first appeared in 3,066 green tests hid a line that breaks opening the database: checking tests by deleting the guard.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Permissions: the Worker was redesigned instead of adding permissions to the token

The family app keeps photos in Cloudflare R2, with a media Worker handling uploads and reads. The deploy notes from the afternoon of October 10 listed three jobs for a person: add Workers KV edit and billing read to the deploy token, create a separate token for the usage analytics API, and issue an R2 S3 key pair so Firebase functions could delete objects. The reason was a free-tier guard that read Cloudflare's analytics API every hour and wrote a pause flag to KV.

At 22:52 that night the operator told the agent to do the work itself instead of handing it over. At 23:13 the agent reported that work to make the Worker run without any extra token was already under way, and at 00:04 it committed 2c906c7: 33 files, 1,238 lines added and 1,146 removed. The first design, one new credential per feature, had been the agent's own; this time it rebuilt the same features on the R2 binding, the Durable Object and the shared key it already had. By design the token needs 2 permissions: Workers Scripts Edit and R2 Edit.

  • A Durable Object (a stateful object that runs next to the Worker) now counts the day's Worker requests, Durable Object requests and R2 reads and writes itself. When the total passes 25 to 50% of the free allowance (the share moves with the time of day), uploads and reads close for the day and reopen at the next midnight, Korea time. The 248-line cron file that read the analytics API is gone.
  • Functions delete R2 objects through a signed DELETE request to the Worker instead of S3 credentials. The signing key is derived from an HMAC key the functions and the Worker already shared; the signature covers method, path, keys, timestamp and nonce. Timestamps must be within ±60 seconds, a nonce works once, there is a daily cap of 3,000 requests and 30,000 objects, and only paths under the requesting family's folder are deleted.
  • Worker secrets went from 3 to 1, and billing read was never added. Checking once in the dashboard that the account is on the free plan was left to the operator.

The cost is written down in the ops notes. Because the delete-signing key comes from the shared HMAC key, all 4 function service accounts that can read that key could in theory sign a delete. Before, only the delete function's account could read the R2 token. Narrowing it again means a separate delete key, which is one more Worker secret.

A read-only ops check on October 11 looked at the real token and found 3 permissions, one more than the design: Workers Scripts Edit, R2 Edit and Account Settings Read. With no billing read, the plan API answered with auth error 10000, which also confirms this token cannot change the plan or billing.

A copy written another way passes the source guard, and masking does not protect the token

The source guard looks for two strings in one folder. A regex written another way, or a copy in another folder, passes. The spell checker's log scan works line by line, so a log call split across lines gets through.

Masking does not protect the secret itself. The chat app's token is a constant in the app binary and can be extracted, which is why the app treats it only as spam control. The server also accepts the token in a header, but the client still sends it in the query; the review found the web client cannot set that header, so the fix closed the path from URL to log instead.

The chat rule works only while the agent follows it, and the count only finds key shapes we know.

The same night the Worker was reworked to need no extra token, the agent's own tool permissions grew. The agent's permission checker blocked the IAM grant commands, and approval in chat did not lift the block; an allow rule in the settings was required. The agent asked for two lines, one script and all gcloud commands, and the operator replied four minutes later that they were added. At 23:13 it asked for three more lines allowing the workflow tool and all npx firebase-tools and curl commands. How we scope what an agent may do on its own is in Running an AI marketer on a schedule four times a day: the permission table that leaves money, accounts and policy to a person.

Checks to add to agent instructions, masking code and token scopes

  1. Put checking commands next to the prohibition in your agent instructions: grep -c, cut -d= -f1, and $NAME references in commands (on the file itself: How to write AGENTS.md: only the rules an AI coding agent gets wrong).
  2. Don't let the agent read the shell history or .env whole. Have it count the lines that mention a key name; delete any key it finds there and rotate it. Pass new values through a prompt or a file, not a command argument.
  3. For each kind of string that carries a secret (a URL, say), keep one masking function and call it everywhere that string is built: logs, exception messages, exception uri fields, diagnostics maps.
  4. Write three tests: the rules (case, other key names, fragments, the same word in a path), a source guard (regex fragments outside the definition file), and a real failure path (a 4xx from a local server).
  5. Feed a log checker the old leaking lines first and confirm it catches them.
  6. Install a release build on a real device and search logcat by key name or marker. Grepping for the value puts the value back into your shell history.
  7. For tokens, write down the permissions each feature needs, and before adding a credential check whether an existing binding or key can do the job. Confirm the real scope with read-only calls.
  8. Where something got wider, write one line: what widened, and what it would take to narrow it.
# release logcat: count token= lines that are not masked
adb logcat -d | grep 'token=' | grep -vc 'token=\*\*\*'

One stale doc line, one transcript line, one undeployed Worker

The chat app's security doc still says "regex duplicated in 4 files" as of its September 16 commit; the code changed and that line did not. The key-shaped line in the October 2 session log has not been deleted, and the logs don't show whether that key was rotated. For the family app, once the Worker is deployed, we need to confirm uploads and deletes work with the 2 designed permissions and whether the extra Account Settings Read is needed at all.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Is it safe to let an AI coding agent read my .env file?

Not in a way that prints values. Agent tool output is stored in the session log as is. With cut -d= -f1 .env for key names and grep -c for counts, the agent can still tell whether a setting is missing.

Why is a masking regex copied into several files a problem?

What one copy handles doesn't carry over to the others. In this chat app the web copies masked failure messages too, while two failure exceptions in the mobile file sent the token unmasked. One function plus a source-guard test that fails on copies prevents it.

How do I cut down the cloud token permissions an agent uses?

List the permissions each feature needs, and before creating a credential, check whether an existing binding or shared key can do the same job. That way the family app's Worker was redesigned to run without KV edit or billing read permissions, a usage-API token or S3 credentials; by design its token needs 2 permissions.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

  • Our contrast checker passed while skipping 40% of the text: make it print how much it measured

item.title: We checked the market after 3 apps: median 1,166 – SugarMount
item.description:
AX note · Retrospective

We built three photo apps before checking the market: this year's new apps had a median of 1,166 installs

A four-minute scrape of top Google Play search results showed that the 32 photo-compress apps released in 2026 had a median of 1,166 lifetime installs, and we recorded the next 11 planned apps as on hold.

On the morning of October 3, 2026, three of our Android photo apps were already built and uploaded to Play. Compress Image was waiting on the production track; a flip-and-rotate app and an image format converter sat on the internal test track. The operator asked a blunt question that morning: there must be hundreds of AI-built photo apps by now, so had anyone looked at the market? Nobody had. We had the coding agent scrape Play search results, and the first report came back four minutes later. Of 71 compress-and-resize utilities in the top 30 results, 32 had been released in 2026, and their median lifetime installs were 1,166. Our own app was not in the top 30 for any of the nine queries.

Sources: three market research documents in the SugarMount app repository (sugar-utils), written on 2026-10-03 and committed in 7b0e567; the daily ops check of 2026-10-23; git history; and the work session log. Install counts are the worldwide lifetime numbers Play exposes. Checked on October 24, 2026.

26 of the 32 compress apps released this year had fewer than 10,000 installs

The compress category came first. Six Korean and three English queries, top 30 results each, gave 103 apps. Keeping only utilities whose titles mention compressing, file size or resizing left 71. Of those, 47 were released in 2025 or 2026, and 32 in 2026.

Those 32 topped out at 73,286 installs. None had reached 100,000, and 26 were under 10,000. One 2026 app that aimed at exactly our pitch, getting photos ready for upload forms, had 0. The top of the list belonged to apps released between 2013 and 2022; the leader had 43.06 million installs.

About ninety minutes later the agent ran the same scrape for the other two categories. Flip and rotate: 46 utilities, only 7 released in 2026, median 373. Format conversion: 71 utilities, 38 from 2026, median 136. In none of the three categories had a 2026 app passed 100,000.

Twenty days later, in the October 23 ops check, the download badges on the public Play pages read 5+ for Compress Image, 1+ for the flip app and 0+ for the converter. Those are 20-day-old apps, so they cannot be lined up against lifetime counts that had up to ten months to build. We read them only as a slow start.

We skipped the check because building looked cheaper than checking

The missing check had a chain of causes behind it.

The lineup was chosen by feature. The product spec revised on September 21 fixed a list of 14 apps and paired each candidate with a "reference app" from one established developer. The same section said, in its own words, that the order was not a download ranking or a revenue forecast.

The reference apps then created an illusion. The reference compress app had 3.89 million installs, and the top of the search results was apps from 2013 to 2022 with millions to tens of millions of installs. If you only look at survivors, "build the same thing, but cleaner" sounds like a plan. Nobody looked at what happened to the apps that arrived this year.

The biggest link was cost: building had become very cheap. The flip-and-rotate app went from its engine commit (7821dbd, September 24, 13:29) to the internal test track (bc0ea78, 20:51) in 7 hours 22 minutes, and the converter reached the internal track at 22:39 the same night (7b9fd55). Leaving out review and store listing work, an app took less than a day, so "ship it and read the numbers" sounded reasonable. The scrape took four minutes.

Underneath all three: the workflow had no gate that said "look at the market before you build". It had a release gate and on-device checks, both described in How we shipped four Android apps in 20 days with an AI coding agent, but nothing upstream of the code.

None of our three starting assumptions was supported by the data

Assumption one: an app that fixes what users hate about the incumbents will get installs. In the newest reviews of the top six compress apps, 127 were rated 3 stars or lower. Keyword tagging put 39 of them under too many ads, 19 under errors, 17 under paid plans and subscriptions, and 12 under output that missed the target size. Our app has no subscription and never writes a file larger than the original. Yet 26 of this year's 32 entrants had not reached 10,000 installs. That figure does not split apps that fixed the complaints from apps that did not, so it cannot refute the assumption directly. It does not support it either. (The top complaint applied to us too: the agent reported that the app-open ad turned on in 1.0.3 on September 23, an operator decision, was the same type. The operator kept it.)

Assumption two came from the operator: merge the three apps into one photo toolbox and people will look for it. The agent searched Play for Korean phrases meaning "photo tool set", "photo utilities" and "image tools", plus "image toolbox" in English. The top results were the default photo app, gallery apps and big photo editors. What the data shows is that general apps own the category-name searches. Play hides search volume, so we do not know how many people search that way.

That afternoon the same question went to document viewers. One developer had three apps: a viewer for HWP files (the Korean word processor format that government offices use) at 436k installs, a PowerPoint viewer at 469k, and an all-in-one office app at 13k. Three apps from one developer, with HWP demand boosted by a policy change, cannot prove that single-purpose beats all-in-one; we treated it as a directional signal. Assumption three, that AI features would make a viewer stand out, was checked against reviews. Of 15,043 Korean reviews of document viewers, 0.36% asked for AI, summaries or translation. That says reviewers rarely ask for it, not that AI cannot set an app apart. Both signals pointed the same way, so the next app became a single-purpose HWP viewer, HWP Viewer SugarDoc.

The agent followed the spec's order, and got the median wrong

The coding agent executed the spec's order as written. While shipping the third app it never suggested looking at the market before the next one. When the operator asked, the agent admitted no market analysis had been done and pointed at the spec's "not a forecast" line.

The numbers had a small error too. Re-reading the scrape script for this note, we found the median computed as s[len(s)//2] on the sorted list s. With 32 values that returns the upper of the two middle values, 1,304. The true median, the mean of 1,028 and 1,304, is 1,166, and that is the number this note uses. The conclusion stands. The flip category has 7 values, so its 373 is exact. The converter category has 38, so its 136 is also an upper median; the value list was not kept, so we could not recompute it, and the true figure is 136 or lower.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

We recorded 11 planned apps as on hold and changed category

There were four options on the table.

  • Keep building U04 to U14 as planned. If those categories look like the three photo ones, that repeats the same result eleven times. We have not scraped any of them yet, though. The hold was recorded in the backlog on October 4.
  • Buy installs with ads. Not until we have measured what one install is worth.
  • Unpublish the three apps. Keeping them up costs almost nothing, and the search terms people actually used only show up in Play Console after an app is public. They stay up for a 30-day measurement.
  • Move to a category where demand is shifting. From October 2026, Korean government mail systems block .hwp attachments, which pushes documents to the newer HWPX format. One viewer released in May 2026 had already reached 417,538 installs. This is the one we chose.

There were other ways to check the market, too. Paid app-intelligence services show install trends and estimated keyword data, for a subscription fee. Keyword tools can only estimate Play search volume, because Play does not publish it. Skimming the top-chart pages by hand is free, but the chart tops do not show how this year's entrants are doing. The record does not say why a script was chosen. What it does show is that the agent was already working in the repository and the cost was a few minutes.

The HWP viewer was started on October 4, went public on October 10, and shipped with no ad SDK. The difference from the photo apps is that review data and a rendering spike came before the first line of app code. (The rendering spike is written up in Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents.)

Before you build your next app, look at the median installs of this year's entrants in the same category.

The 15-minute check to run before building

This is the order we ran on October 3, plus step 2 (writing the rule first), which we skipped that day. Collection used the Python library google-play-scraper, which reads Play's web pages; it is not an official Google API.

  1. Write 6 to 9 queries in task words, the way a user would type them. We used six Korean queries and three English ones, such as "compress image" and "image resize kb".
  2. Write the decision rule before looking. For example: if this year's entrants have a median in the low thousands and none has passed 100,000, do not build a single-feature general utility.
  3. Collect the top 30 app IDs per query. For each app read lifetime installs, release date, rating count, and whether it has ads or in-app purchases.
  4. Keep only apps whose title names the same task. We excluded general photo editors, video apps and PDF apps with a deny list. 103 became 71.
  5. Take the apps released this year and count them, plus their median installs (mean of the two middle values when the count is even), maximum, how many are under 10,000 and how many are over 100,000. Note the release years of the top 10.
  6. Check whether your own app ID appears anywhere in the results.
  7. Pull up to 200 of the newest reviews for each of the top six apps, keep 3 stars and lower, and tag them by keyword: ads, payment, errors.
  8. Search once more with the category name ("photo utilities"). If you are considering an all-in-one app, look at that result first.

Below is a cleaned-up version of the collection code from that day, arranged to follow steps 3 to 6. We have not run this cleaned-up version, only syntax-checked it, so adapt the queries and both regexes to your category. The median comes from statistics.median, the line that prevents the upper-median mistake described above.

import re, statistics, time
from google_play_scraper import search, app
QUERIES = [("사진 용량 줄이기", "ko", "kr"), ("사진 KB 줄이기", "ko", "kr"), ("compress image", "en", "us")]
KEEP = re.compile(r"압축|용량|크기|사이즈|compress|resiz|kb|size", re.I)
DROP = re.compile(r"video|동영상|pdf|editor|편집", re.I)
YEAR, MY_APP = 2026, "com.example.myapp"
ids = set()
for q, lang, country in QUERIES:
    ids |= {r["appId"] for r in search(q, lang=lang, country=country, n_hits=30) if r.get("appId")}
    time.sleep(1)
rows = []
for app_id in sorted(ids):
    try:
        d = app(app_id, lang="ko", country="kr")
    except Exception:
        continue
    time.sleep(0.4)
    name = f'{d.get("title") or ""} {app_id}'
    if not KEEP.search(name) or DROP.search(name):
        continue
    m = re.search(r"\d{4}", d.get("released") or "")   # "Oct 3, 2026" or "2026. 10. 3."
    rows.append((int(m.group()) if m else None, d.get("realInstalls") or 0))
new = [n for y, n in rows if y == YEAR]
print("same-task apps:", len(rows), "| released in", YEAR, ":", len(new))
if new:
    print("median", statistics.median(new), "| max", max(new),
          "| under 10k", sum(n < 10_000 for n in new), "| 100k+", sum(n >= 100_000 for n in new))
print("my app in results:", MY_APP in ids)

The four minutes cover collection and the first report for one category (09:47 to 09:51 Korea time). Add choosing queries and a person reading the tables against the step 2 rule, and budget 15 minutes.

Why the median is not a forecast, and what the data cannot see

The sample itself leans one way. Only apps in the top 30 for the nine queries got in; this year's apps that never ranked were left out. The median for all same-task apps released this year is probably below 1,166. So 1,166 is the result for this year's apps that made the top of search, and cannot be read as what a well-made app should expect. Even among them, six passed 10,000, the largest at 73,286.

In a category where demand is moving, last year's distribution says little about next month. Document viewers were that case: right after the policy change, new apps were collecting hundreds of thousands of installs.

Installs are worldwide lifetime counts, and rankings come from a logged-out session, so a real user's screen may differ. Review topics were counted with keyword regexes, so one review can land in several topics, and only six apps' newest reviews were read. Apps with an empty release-date field drop out of the yearly count. The library depends on Play's page layout and breaks when that changes.

What we check next

The 30-day measurement for Compress Image ends on November 2, 2026. Impressions, install conversion and the real search terms will decide whether the three photo apps get merged into one. As of October 24, 2026 that merge has not started.

None of the U04 to U14 categories (photo to PDF, video, audio and others) has been scraped yet. Whether the hold is right can only be judged after running the same check on them, and the operator has not formally confirmed the hold. The next scrape runs with the median fixed.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Frequently asked questions

How many installs does a new Android utility app usually get?

In the photo-compress category we scraped on October 3, 2026, the 32 apps released that year that made the top 30 search results had a median of 1,166 lifetime installs. It varies by category, so scrape your own before building.

Can I see Google Play search volume for a keyword?

No. Play does not publish search volume per query. After your app is public, Play Console shows only the search terms that brought users to your own listing.

Does an all-in-one app beat single-feature apps on Play?

Our data showed no sign that it does. A category search like "photo utilities" returned only general apps, and one developer's two single-format viewers had 436k and 469k installs against 13k for its all-in-one app. That is one developer, so we do not treat it as a rule.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: One --check gate for a static site agents co-edit – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

A static site that several AI agent sessions edit: one --check gate before every commit

Nobody edits generated files, and before every commit --check must report zero files a rebuild would change and zero gate errors. With those two rules, budget overruns and drifting dates that only appear once work is combined get caught before a commit.

python tools/build.py --check failed on the night of October 19, 2026, right after a rebase onto another session's commit, with one line: [BUDGET-FONT] index.html: font files this page needs 421 KB > 400 KB. The build before the rebase had no error on the home page, so the problem only showed up once the two pieces of work were combined. This site is built without a framework by six Python modules (3,616 lines) that import nothing outside the standard library, and the rule is that whoever commits, person or agent, passes that command first. This note follows four of the times it stopped a commit between October 5 and 22.

Sources: this site's git history (bdbbe97, b82faac, 663f04e, 6b96643, 4f46df8 and others), the code in tools/, the review documents written against the redesign spec, work session logs and the AX notes publishing log. Line, test and file counts were redone at commit 1d5d432 on October 24, 2026.

Four times --check stopped a commit

--check rebuilds the whole site in memory and asks two questions: does any output differ by even one byte from the file on disk, and did the checker module tools/checks.py report an error? Either one means exit 1. In outline:

outputs = build_all()              # pages, feeds, sitemap, CSS: in memory
changed = [p for p, text in outputs.items()
           if read_file(p) != text]
report = checks.run(ROOT, outputs)  # 106 issue codes
if "--check" in argv:
    if changed or report.errors:
        exit(1)                     # nothing is written
else:
    write_files(changed)

On October 24 the build wrote 162 files, the checker had 106 issue codes (fixed names such as SD-CRUMB-HOME), and one run took 11.6 seconds on this PC.

The four stops: two files out of date right after the first build on October 5; 101 gate errors when the redesign was integrated on October 18; the home page needing 421 KB of fonts against a 400 KB cap after the October 19 rebase; and on October 22, a new note title that pushed two older notes to 482 KB and 473 KB against a 470 KB cap. On October 23 we added a check that halts the image tools on characters the font draws as empty.

Humans and agents write only the body and the data files

Every file has exactly one kind of writer. Condensed from the table in the repository's AGENTS.md:

WriterFiles
Content authors (people or agents)The <title>, description and <main> of hand-written pages (minus build blocks), data/apps.json, data/ax.json
One build-owner sessiontools/*.py, and it runs the integration build
The build onlyHead, header, footer, breadcrumbs, JSON-LD, home and list pages, topic pages, sitemap, RSS, robots.txt, llms.txt, the dates file data/content-dates.json, two generated stylesheets

Inside a hand-written page, every spot the build fills is wrapped in a marker such as <!-- build:meta -->. Each build empties and refills those blocks and leaves the rest of <main> byte for byte, with one exception: the tracking parameter on Play install links. Content authors never run the build. They run the read-only python tools/checks.py --file <path>.

The first plan did not have this split; a review added it. An agent wrote the October 18 redesign spec, and it told every work package both to finish with build and --check and to leave generated HTML alone. A second agent, assigned to attack the spec, pointed out the contradiction: the build rewrites the head and footer of every hand-written page, so one session building to verify its work would change some 60 files another session was editing. Since then the integration build runs once, in one place.

Rebase conflicts follow the same rule. On October 19 the conflicted files were ones the build rewrites: 404.html, the about page, app pages, rss.xml. We took the other session's version of those, kept our own AX note files, and rebuilt. Do not hand-edit or hand-merge generated files. Pick a side, rebuild, and commit only when --check reports zero.

The six build modules import only standard library pieces such as hashlib, html.parser and xml.etree, so there is no package to install. The four image tools (775 lines) are different: they need Pillow, and they sit outside --check.

Test idempotency with tomorrow's date, not with a second build

On October 5 an agent wrote the first build script (725 lines when committed) and ran it. This is what came back:

45 files, 45 changed
out of date:
  apps/sugarcard/index.html
  sitemap.xml

A second build changed two files, and the third run said up to date. The lines that moved were sitemap lastmod dates.

There were two layers of cause. The near one was ordering: the build read lastmod from git status and git log before writing any file, so writing files changed the git state and the next build saw different input. The deeper one was where the date came from at all, which was repository state and the wall clock instead of page content.

The review agent flagged only the near cause, and that day's fix only addressed it: a set of "files this build writes get today's date". Two builds on the same day then agreed. The dates still came from git, though. A build that converges after two runs looks idempotent, yet the same input built the next day moves the dates again.

Thirteen days later the redesign removed that design. The redesign spec, also written by an agent, had two loops of the same kind. A generated app page kept its "last updated" line inside the hashed body, so the date changed the hash and the hash changed the date. And the spec had the build write a generated block into site.css while the stylesheet version string was a hash of that same file; the reviewer wrote that --check would "fail once, forever". Both were fixed before any code was written.

On the CSS side, the generated stylesheets are now built in memory first and the version string is computed and substituted before anything is written. The date rules (content hash, the SOURCE_DATE variable) are in Every sitemap lastmod had the same date: deriving modified dates from a content hash.

At the October 18 integration, sha256 hashes of 445 tracked and untracked files were taken after the first build, the second build and a SOURCE_DATE run, with zero differences. On October 24, in a scratch copy, a plain build, SOURCE_DATE=2026-10-25 and SOURCE_DATE=2026-12-31 all printed "162 files, 0 changed".

At the first integration, the gate was the one that was wrong

The October 18 redesign ran as a workflow split across 36 agents and took about 2 hours 24 minutes. The first --check on the merged result found zero files to rewrite and 101 gate errors.

Most of the 43 BUDGET-FONT errors were the checker's own mistake. English pages draw © in the system font through CSS, but the checker counted that character and concluded the pages needed extra font files. One cost was real: the breadcrumb separator › alone made every page with breadcrumbs download one more 25 KB font file. The fix aligned the checker's character counting with the CSS rules and moved the separator to the system font. The rest were 24 anchor texts pointing at two different URLs, 19 app-colour samples on the design demo page, 14 share images over 200 KB and one broken link.

When the gate changes, its tests change with it. That fix added six tests, and each of the eight new guards was removed in turn in a scratch copy to confirm a test failed. As of October 24 every one of the 106 issue codes appears by name in test_checks.py, out of 188 tests in total.

The integrating agent also made two gate calls on its own. Individual privacy policies and the design demo page have no font cap in the spec, so their overruns became warnings, and the cap on the generated font stylesheet went from 20 KB to 24 KB. The agent wrote "needs confirmation" for both in its report. The operator settled a different item from that same report that evening (listing the privacy officer under the business name). The comment on the 24 KB cap still says "the spec owner should confirm or lower it" on October 24.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Another note's title can break a page's font budget

The site's Korean font is split into 92 files by Unicode range, and a page downloads only the files that cover its characters. Note pages are capped at 470 KB, home and list pages at 400 KB. One rare Hangul syllable can pull in a 17 to 40 KB file by itself, so two of the first three AX notes came out at 619 KB and 533 KB. We reworded them that evening and wrote a helper that shows which characters pull in which files.

The home page broke for another reason. It listed the three newest AX note titles, which change every day, and after the rebase merged another session's work it needed 421 KB. Instead of rewording titles, the home list became links to topic pages (663f04e); topic names are fixed text, so the cost stops moving. The October 22 change that dropped note titles from the hub's topic cards had the same reason and took the hub from 468 KB to 389 KB (6b96643).

Also on October 22, a single syllable, 쟀, in a new note's title travelled through the related-notes lists into two older notes and pushed them to 482 KB and 473 KB. Checking the new file alone passes. Rewording the title brought the two pages to 450 KB and 441 KB.

Share images use real screens and never carry text

tools/og.py builds the share images for app pages and help articles from a real Play screenshot on a neutral background, with no text and no logo. Text cards are reserved for the home, hub, about, privacy and AX pages.

--check does not rebuild and compare images. Running og.py in a scratch copy on October 24 changed 4 of the 155 files: two app cards committed on October 19 with a new app page without going through og.py (they carry a title and tagline), and the two home cards, committed before that app's icon existed. Two og.py runs in a row produce identical bytes, so the generator is deterministic and the files that differ from its output are the committed ones. The daily publishing routine does not commit unrelated image changes, so from October 20 to 24 it ran og.py and restored these four files five times.

The background to the October 23 blank-glyph check in the image tools is in Android showed some Hangul as blank gaps: NanumSquare's cmap claimed 11,172 syllables but drew only 2,479.

Not for browser editing, very large sites or repositories without CI

Teams that write in a browser and expect a preview will not like it. Here authors edit the HTML body directly and run commands. We have no record of weighing it against a static site generator. But three of the four stops here (October 18, 19 and 22) came from checks over the whole output, so a generator would still need those checks and the date rules built separately.

Large sites pay more. --check rebuilds and compares everything on every run. 11.6 seconds for 162 files is fine, but there is no incremental build.

Nothing enforces the gate. The repository has no CI job, so it works only if someone runs the command before committing. The gate can also be wrong, as the 43 errors on October 18 showed, and it cannot stop a commit that raises its own caps.

Adding a --check gate to another site, in order

  1. Put a table of who writes which files at the top of your agent instructions (AGENTS.md or similar), and mark generated files as hands-off.
  2. Wrap every spot the build fills inside a hand-written page in <!-- build:NAME --> markers; the build empties and refills them each time.
  3. Make --check render every output in memory, compare it with disk, run the checks on the same output, and exit 1 if either fails.
  4. Derive dates and version strings from content hashes, and keep date lines and automatic lists out of the hash input.
  5. Test idempotency three ways: two builds in a row, a build dated tomorrow, and a build dated in the past (dates must not go backwards).
  6. Give every check a fixed code and a test that proves the code fires. Remove each guard in a scratch copy and confirm a test fails.
  7. Content sessions run only the read-only per-file check; one session runs the integration build once.
  8. When generated files conflict in a rebase, pick a side, rebuild and run --check.
  9. Check budgets that mix in other pages' text (fonts, size) on the whole output, and keep daily-changing lists off shared pages.
  10. Have a person review any commit that changes a cap.

What we will check next

Images are still outside the gate. The next check is a step in --check that compares og.py output with the committed files; before that, the text-bearing app card has to become either a listed og.py exception or generator output. The 24 KB stylesheet cap and the two warning-only pages have not had a human review yet. How several sessions shared this repository is described in "Use hundreds of agents" in practice: 10 workstreams, 59 commits in a day, three running at once.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

Frequently asked questions

Do you commit the generated HTML?

Yes. GitHub Pages serves the repository's files as they are (with .nojekyll, Jekyll processing is off), so the build output is the deployment. --check confirms that the committed output equals what the current inputs produce.

How do you test that a static site build is idempotent?

Build twice in a row, then with tomorrow's date and with a past date, and expect zero changed files. Two same-day builds can agree while dates still move the next day, so make "today" overridable through an environment variable first.

How do you resolve conflicts when several AI agent sessions edit the same site repository?

Merge only source files such as page bodies and data; for generated files, pick one side and rebuild. Run --check on the rebuilt result and commit only when it passes. On this site, that step after a rebase is where the home page font overflow first appeared.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: "100% E2E pass" from 7 runners with zero expect() – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

What "100% E2E pass" really meant: deleting seven runners with zero expect() calls

Since August 2025, a "100% E2E pass" had rested on seven scripts without a single assertion. The night we deleted them, an E2E over real sockets logged seven defects.

On the evening of September 6, 2026, we deleted seven E2E runner files, 3,010 lines, from our P2P chat app (Flutter). They were the source of two August 2025 claims: "100% success rate over 370 test runs" and "E2E tests 100% pass". None of the seven contained a single expect(). That evening flutter test reported 543 passed and 2 skipped. Later that night, an E2E running over real sockets logged seven defects, and six were fixed just after midnight. When someone hands you a pass rate, first ask what was counted and by which command.

Sources: git history of the P2P chat app and SugarSpeller repositories, and the files as they stood at each commit. Every number was rechecked with git show and grep on October 24, 2026.

All seven runners counted their own successes; five only timed delays

Commit 4d8fc3b on August 27, 2025 announced "100% success rate over 370 test runs". The report it added listed five categories at 100/100, 150/150 and so on. We opened the files that produced those numbers, exactly as they were at that commit.

No file had an expect(). No file called test() either. Each one ran a class from void main() async and printed its results (355 print() calls across the seven at deletion time). Five of the seven imported nothing but dart:async and dart:math, so they never touched app code at all.

The definition of success is still in the code:

// optimized_comprehensive_test.dart (2025-08-27, trimmed)
static Future<void> _stableUserProfileTest() async {
  await Future.delayed(Duration(microseconds: 500 + Random().nextInt(500)));
}
...
// lenient success criterion (within 2 s)   [comment translated]
if (totalTime < 2000) {
  successCount++;
}

Chain a few milliseconds of delay, and count a success if the chain finishes within two seconds. The report gives a mean of 46.48 ms for that category. The other thresholds were 3 s, 5 s and 2.5 s, and the comments call them "lenient" or "generous". The other two (chat_e2e_test and integration_test_runner) did call real app classes, but they too printed results without a single expect().

All three commits (952e9ef, "full web P2P chat app implemented", plus 4d8fc3b and c1388d8) end with a coding agent's "generated with" signature line. What settings or instructions produced them is not recorded anywhere in the repository, so this note calls these numbers "auto-generated reports of the time" and nothing more.

The 97% came from unit tests; the empty number was the "E2E 100%" in the same commit

Our first reading was that the "97%" in the title was inflated as a whole. That was wrong. Commit c1388d8 (August 31, 2025) puts two numbers side by side: "unit test pass rate 84% to 97% (104/107)" and "E2E tests 100% pass, 5-user scenario fully supported". At that commit, the 12 unit test files held 280 expect( calls, and 104/107 most likely came from them. We did not rerun year-old code to confirm it.

The cleanup's own explanation was wrong too. On September 6, 2026, while moving the old reports into an archive folder, a README committed with an agent co-author line (891db57) said the "97% / 95%+ pass rate" came from "counting skips as passes". The August 2025 files rule that out: at c1388d8 and 4d8fc3b, the word skip does not appear anywhere in test/e2e. The test('…', () {}, skip: 'Standalone runner…') wrappers were added eight months later, in April or May 2026, and only committed on September 6 when b8fb368 recovered that work from the working tree. The 2025 "100%" was each script printing its own counter.

The second mistake came from reading the past off the present state. When you write down a cause, open the files at that commit. git show <hash>:<path> is one line.

Nothing flagged it for eight months because the runners sat outside every count

The cause had three layers.

  1. A test framework never did the counting. flutter test counts only what is registered with test(). The runners registered nothing, and two of them did not even end in _test.dart. Their numbers could only come from counters the scripts printed themselves.
  2. The 370-run output could not fail. A two-second limit on delays that never call app code reports the same number whether the app works or not.
  3. Once the files were wrapped in skip in spring 2026, "not run" became their official state, and in the meantime integration_test_runner stopped compiling.

There was a human cause as well. Numbers from an auto-generated report went straight into commit titles. Nobody asked which command produced them.

The first signal came when a person asked for a real run. In May 2026, ahead of a closed beta, the operator asked for the E2E tests to actually be run again. The run on May 6 showed that flutter test skipped all seven runners and that dart could not compile them. The decision to delete them came four months later.

We deleted instead of converting, and that night a real E2E logged seven defects

Backlog item 5-5-2 listed two options: (a) convert the runners into framework tests (minimum scenarios: 50 repeated handshakes, five users at once, message ordering), or (b) delete them and keep only the git history. At 20:26 on September 6, commit e03671a took (b): "zero expect() calls, never executed by flutter test, and integration_test_runner no longer compiled."

Five files imported no app code, so there was nothing to convert; it would have been a rewrite. The two that did call app code were deleted too, and the record gives only one line for each. integration_test_runner no longer compiled, and chat_e2e_test was listed in backlog item 5-5-3 as a risk because startDiscovery() needed a live HTTP/WebSocket server. The deletion commit says instead that real coverage lives in test/core, test/features, the handshake and p2p_chat E2E tests, and test/integration. There is no record of anyone matching the two files' scenarios against those tests one by one.

Leaving them skipped was possible, but 3,010 lines would keep suggesting "there is an E2E suite". The documented way to run them (dart test/e2e/…) no longer compiled because of the flutter_test import. Proving things with coverage instead was never considered in the record, and in our judgement it would not fit: coverage counts executed lines, not assertions, and five runners that never call app code add nothing to it. No mutation tool was used either. In the release check the next day (2026-09-07), the repository relied on a narrower method: delete the guard behind each fix and confirm a test fails.

That night a new harness started one flutter test process per peer, each with its own key pair and SQLite file, connected over real TCP or relay sockets, and ran it against commit c0bb66e (22:55). Its report listed seven defects (E1 to E7), and at 00:07 on September 7 commit 17aa057 fixed the six with confirmed causes (E1 to E6). E7, a periodic stall, was left without a known cause. E1 was the worst. A real room id is chat_<64hex>_<64hex>, 134 characters, but the sync service accepted at most 128, so delta sync was rejected on every connection between two real identities. The commit's explanation: "tests used short synthetic ids".

On September 13 the backlog's status table read flutter test 3,160 passed / 0 failed / 13 skipped. The 13 skips carried reasons (signalling server, soak gate), and the same table said "real devices: 0 runs, emulators only". Even so, "passed" in that table only says the tests passed. We cover that limit in 3,066 green tests hid a line that breaks opening the database: checking tests by deleting the guard.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Ten days later, 15 of 19 tests in another app compared values to themselves

The same shape turned up in an Android app. On September 10, 2025, commit d605c37 in the SugarSpeller repository (a Korean spelling checker) was titled "unit tests 100% pass and code coverage complete", with "17/17 new feature tests pass" in the body and the same signature line.

The commit's NewFeaturesTest.kt has 19 @Test methods, not 17. Four of them call app code (UIMode). The other 15 either re-check a value declared inside the test (val EXPECTED_TEXT_SIZE = 14f, then assertEquals(14f, EXPECTED_TEXT_SIZE)) or confirm Android constants such as Gravity.CENTER being 17. They assert, but no change to the app can make them fail. The fact that no coverage tool was ever configured in that repository is in A year of AI coding in 701 commits.

There was neglect in the other direction too. On September 29, 2026, commit a964c50 repaired four instrumented test suites that had been left alone since August 2025. In three of them (42 tests), the assertions were 106 Espresso check(matches(…)) calls and one Kotlin assert; 68 of those checks only asked whether a view was displayed (isDisplayed()). The commit calls these "empty assertions that only saw the screen was up" and replaced them with checks on corrected text, list counts and the clipboard. The fourth waited on a latch nobody ever counted down, so it always failed. After the repair, all 59 instrumented tests passed on a Galaxy S21.

Tests that grep flags wrongly or misses

Grepping for files without expect( gives false positives. On October 24, 2026, that search over the repository's 175 test files returns two. One is a property test that asserts with fail(); adding fail( to the pattern leaves one file.

That one is a measurement-only test that deliberately has no assertions. It measures tap target sizes for a report, and its header comment says it "makes no assertions (expect), so it always passes". But dart_test.yaml does not exclude it, so its tests land in the passed count.

Grep cannot judge what an assertion checks. Tests like SugarSpeller's 15 self-comparisons contain asserts and pass every filter. You have to look at imports and call targets, and what survives that is caught by deleting a guard or by review.

A checklist for the next pass rate you are handed

  1. Write down numerator and denominator, the command, and where the log is. If any is missing, keep the number out of commit titles.
  2. Find test files with no test functions, and runnable files that do not end in _test.
  3. Find files without assertions (include fail( and any custom assert helpers in the pattern). On Android, search for JUnit assert and Espresso check(matches.
  4. Add test files that never import the app package.
  5. List every skip with its reason, and report the skip count next to passed. In flutter test output, ~N on the last line is the skip count (from this repository's records: +1125 ~4 means 1,125 passed, 4 skipped).
  6. For each file found, decide: convert, delete, or tag as measurement. Put the reason in the commit body.
  7. Delete a few key guards and confirm the tests go red.
  8. Run once with real processes and realistically sized data. E1 hid behind short synthetic ids.
# Flutter, steps 2 to 5
grep -rL --include='*_test.dart' -e 'test(' -e 'testWidgets(' test/
find test -name '*.dart' ! -name '*_test.dart'
grep -rL --include='*_test.dart' -e 'expect(' -e 'fail(' test/
grep -rL --include='*_test.dart' 'package:<your_app>' test/
grep -rn 'skip:' test/
# Android (Kotlin), step 3
grep -rL --include='*Test.kt' -e 'assert' -e 'check(matches' app/src/

Run the first or third line on the files as of August 31, 2025 and five runners come out immediately; the find line catches the other two. On today's repository the third line leaves only the measurement test (and there are 17 skip: lines).

What we check next

The measurement-only tests still need a tag that keeps them out of the passed count. Before that, we need to count how many of the 3,160 were measurement output. "Real devices: 0 runs" is also still open. The September 13 table named that gap itself, so the next status line has to name the device.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Do standalone scripts in the test folder count in flutter test results?

No. flutter test counts only what is registered with test() in files ending in _test.dart. The "370 runs, 100%" in this repository came from a counter the script printed itself, with no such registration. Check which tool produced a number before you repeat it.

How do I find Flutter test files with no expect()?

Use grep -rL --include='*_test.dart' -e 'expect(' -e 'fail(' test/ to get candidates. Add your own assert helpers to the pattern, and open each hit, because measurement-only tests have no assertions on purpose.

Do skipped tests count toward the pass rate in flutter test?

No. flutter test counts skips separately and shows them as ~N. The problem starts when a person copies only the passed number. Report passed, failed and skipped together, with a reason for every skip.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • A shared LLM cache could have frozen a prompt injection: the blind A/B that let us stop sending context
  • AI coding agents and secrets: one rule in chat, logs and token permissions, and the two exceptions a copied masking regex missed
  • We built an edit feature and shipped it switched off: the HWP save gate that caught a form-field bug
  • Our contrast checker passed while skipping 40% of the text: make it print how much it measured
  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException
  • A market:// link opens a store chooser on SKT-sold Samsung phones: set the Play package first
