item.title: Finding fake tests by deleting their guards – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

3,066 green tests hid a line that breaks opening the database: checking tests by deleting the guard

A pass count proves nothing on its own. We only count a test once we have deleted the code it protects and watched it fail.

3,066 tests were passing when the review found a blocker. The fourth adversarial review of our P2P chat app (Flutter) flagged one new SQLite setting that, traced through the plugin source, stops the database from opening on a device; the fix landed on September 11, 2026. The test SQLite hid the failure completely: reverting the fix left all 13 storage tests green. The app already had a rule that a test must fail when its guard is deleted, and the same review still caught two fixes that broke it. Our HWP viewer SugarDoc keeps that check as 12 Python scripts with 970 mutation rows and runs them at release.

Sources: the chat app's commit 8f5a0a5 and the verification notes in that commit, plus SugarDoc's scripts/qa scripts and its 1.2.0 and 1.3.0 release records. All counts were taken again from git on October 20, 2026.

A row-returning PRAGMA sent through execute

The blocker was a single line, PRAGMA secure_delete = ON. It was added that round so deleted messages get overwritten with zeros, and the code sent it through db.execute(), which expects no result rows. This pragma returns one. We reran all five pragmas from that function on October 20, 2026 with Python's sqlite3 module (SQLite 3.45.1, in-memory database):

pragmarows returnedcall before the fix
secure_delete = ON[(1,)]execute (wrong)
foreign_keys = ON[]execute
synchronous = NORMAL[]execute
journal_mode = WAL[('memory',)]rawQuery
wal_autocheckpoint = 0[(0,)]rawQuery

In the same function, the two other pragmas that return rows already used rawQuery; only the new line did not. That setup code runs on every database open, before the version check. The review traced the iOS path through the plugin source: the execute path treats SQLITE_ROW as an error, so openDatabase itself fails and the whole storage layer goes with it. The Android side rests on the API contract of SQLiteDatabase.execSQL, which rejects statements that return rows. Neither platform has actually thrown the exception on a device yet.

The fix was one word:

- await db.execute('PRAGMA secure_delete = ON');
+ await db.rawQuery('PRAGMA secure_delete = ON');

The test SQLite could not see the failure

Unit tests run on sqflite_common_ffi, a desktop backend, not on the phone's SQLite. Its execute runs a statement without arguments and silently drops whatever rows come back. No exception, so the 3,066 tests could never have said anything about this bug. The commit message records that with the fix reverted, only the new guard fails.

Because no behavioural test can catch it, the guard reads source instead. pragma_execute_guard_test.dart pulls every string literal passed to .execute( under lib/, and runs each one that starts with PRAGMA through rawQuery on a real SQLite to see whether rows come back. The ffi backend returns rows normally from rawQuery, so the check tells the truth even inside the test environment. At the time lib/ had 14 such calls: 3 pragmas and 11 table or index statements.

The scanner also checks itself. If it finds fewer than 5 execute literals, it assumes its regex broke and fails, so an empty scan cannot pass for free. (The pragma list is not hard-coded either; the guard asks SQLite.)

Two fixes reported as verified had guards that guarded nothing

The same review ran revert checks: undo each fix and see whether the test said to protect it turns red. Two fixes that the AI coding agent had reported as verified in the previous round failed this check.

  • Removing the localisation wiring from the app (the part that makes screen readers speak the framework's labels in Korean) left its test green. The test launched the test harness's own MaterialApp, not the real app. It now drives the actual app widget and checks the localisations resolved beneath it.
  • Every message-eviction guard sat behind an environment variable that CI never sets. With eviction disabled, all 659 tests that run without that variable stayed green. They now run by default, and every revert in that area goes red.

The review logged 26 findings, and 24 of them had been introduced by that round's own fixes. Its notes say the pattern of the previous fix creating new defects had now repeated four times. What the agent got wrong was the report more than the code. It really had added tests, and they really passed; nobody had checked what they measured.

The reviewer was an agent too. It changed no code, and it restored the tree after every revert experiment. Its brief carried this rule: if a test still passes after you revert the fix, the test is wrong. After the fixes the suite stood at 3,099 passed, 13 skipped, 0 failed.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The rule had been written down two days earlier

When an agent says it added a test, delete the code that test is meant to protect and run it again. If it stays green, it does not count. The chat app's instruction file ties "done" to three conditions: zero analyzer errors, code reachable from main.dart, and code protected by a test. The release-readiness notes from September 9 already said every fix in that round was pinned by a test that fails when its guard is removed; two days later a second agent actually reverted the fixes and caught two that did not.

The order of checks we run before a release is in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app.

The guard-removal harness: plain Python, one guard per row

SugarDoc has shipped a guard-removal script beside each feature since its first commit on October 8, 2026. As of October 18 there are 12 scripts, 970 mutation rows and 1,919 lines. Each row is a promise: change this string in this file, and this test class must fail. Below is a real row from the 1.2.0 PDF export script, followed by the core of the harness, trimmed.

# (id, file, [(original, replacement)], module, test class that must fail)
("ctl.logOnlySaved", P + "ReaderController.kt",
 [("if (result == PdfWriteResult.SAVED) log(...)", "log(...)")],
 "sugardoc", "ReaderControllerTest"),
for mid, rel, edits, kind, target in MUT:
    path, orig = mutate(rel, edits)          # only ever in the copy
    try:
        ok, fails, out = run_row(kind, target)  # gradlew --no-daemon --tests *.target
        if "e: file://" in out:
            verdict = "COMPILE-ERROR"
        else:
            verdict = "FAILS-AS-EXPECTED" if ok else "STILL-PASSES"
    finally:
        open(path, "w", encoding="utf-8").write(orig)

(The log(...) is shortened here; the real row spells out the analytics event.) Five decisions carry the design:

  • The working tree is never touched. The repository is copied to a separate folder without .git, build outputs or signing keys, and every mutation happens there. Another agent session may be working in the same tree.
  • Each original string must match exactly once. Anything other than one match marks the row BAD-PATTERN, meaning the source moved and the row needs updating.
  • A catch needs two signals: Gradle exits with failure and the JUnit XML contains a failed test case. Compile errors are reported separately as COMPILE-ERROR. Going by exit code alone would count a typo in the mutation as a catch.
  • One Gradle run at a time, no daemon, only the named test class, with a lock file holding the process ID so two runs never share a copy.
  • The mutated file is always restored in finally.

Two rows that stayed green in 1.3.0

The SugarDoc 1.3.0 release record from October 18 holds real catches. After confirming that all 147 rows of the editing script still matched once, the 37 rows added or changed that day were run. Two came back STILL-PASSES on the first run.

RowMutationCauseFix
retry.partialFailsdrop partial || from the retry-save conditionweak testtest now loses only the second edit during replay
retry.cancelStopsdelete the cancel checkthe same defence existed in two placesremoved the duplicate and aimed the row at the guard that remained

The rerun after the fixes came back 4 of 4 failing, as it should. The PDF export script went 32 of 32 FAILS-AS-EXPECTED the same day. STILL-PASSES does not always mean a weak test. If the code defends the same thing twice, deleting one copy changes nothing, and the fix belongs in the code. (An agent wrote the tests for both features, too.)

What is still open

The Android failure in the chat app has not been measured. The verification notes list it as open: build an APK from the commit before the fix, install it on an emulator and read logcat at the first database open. iOS needs a macOS machine we do not have. On the SugarDoc side, 1.3.0 reran only the 37 changed rows of the editing script; the 110 untouched rows were not rerun. Whether those older rows still go red will show at the next full run.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

How do you find a fake test?

Delete or invert the code the test claims to protect, then run only that test. If it stays green, it does not protect that code. We write each such check down as a mutation row and rerun the rows at release.

Can I trust tests an AI agent wrote?

Not by the pass count. In the chat app 3,066 passing tests sat on top of a blocker, and two fixes reported as verified kept their tests green after the fix was deleted. We only count a test once we have seen it fail with its guard removed.

Why a hand-written script instead of a mutation testing tool?

The question we needed answered was whether this test guards this line. Each row pairs one guard with the one test class that should catch it, and runs only that class. We have not compared it with off-the-shelf tools for speed or catch rate.

Does STILL-PASSES always mean the test is weak?

No. Of the two rows that stayed green in SugarDoc 1.3.0, one had a weak test and the other guarded code that was defended twice. In the second case we removed the duplicate defence and pointed the row at the guard that remained.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Play Console DEX optimization and an R8 keep rule – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Play Console said our DEX was 39% optimized. The culprit was a keep rule for an SDK we never used

A leftover Kakao SDK ProGuard file kept every public member of every class out of R8; deleting it moved the bundle's r8.json numbers from 39% to 85%.

Play Console still rated the latest bundle of SugarSpeller, our Korean spelling checker, as "intermediate" on September 25, 2026: optimization 36%, obfuscation 39%, shrinking 39%. Five days earlier we had removed the -dontoptimize line that kept R8 from optimizing at all. The rest of the gap came from one seven-line ProGuard file for the Kakao SDK, which the app does not use. With it gone the same day, the unshrunk share in the bundle's r8.json fell from 61.47% to 15.18% (85% once subtracted from 100), and the AAB went from 18.4 MB to 11.6 MB.

Numbers come from SugarMount's app repository (sugarspeller): commits a597223 (2026-09-20) and e05f8e3 (2026-09-25), the changelog entries for 1.6.020 and 1.6.023, the post-release watch log, and an r8.json read again from a local release AAB while writing this note. Checked on October 20, 2026.

The Play Console figure is r8.json turned upside down

Those percentages line up with a file the Android Gradle Plugin (AGP) already puts in every R8-processed release bundle: BUNDLE-METADATA/com.android.tools/r8.json. Its stats block records the share of code that was not shrunk, obfuscated or optimized.

unzip -p app-release.aab BUNDLE-METADATA/com.android.tools/r8.json
"stats":{"noObfuscationPercentage":61.48,
         "noOptimizationPercentage":64.27,
         "noShrinkingPercentage":61.47}

Subtract each value from 100 and you get what Play shows: 61.47 became 39% shrunk, 64.27 became 36% optimized. We matched that from our own before-and-after numbers, not from a Google spec, but it held for the two Play readings we have (0% before, 36/39/39% after the first fix). That lets you read the metric locally before uploading anything.

The build used AGP 9.4.0 with R8 full mode, resource shrinking and the stock proguard-android-optimize.txt. Our repository notes say Play wants this metric addressed by February 2027; we could not re-check the wording on the Play screen for this note.

Dropping -dontoptimize took optimization from 0% to 36%

Commit a597223 on September 20 removed -dontoptimize from proguard-common.pro. It had been added on purpose, out of fear that optimization would break the Gson reflection that parses spelling results, and it pinned Play's optimization figure at 0%. The comparison baseline was the previous HEAD (1.6.019) built in the same environment.

Unoptimized code went from 100% to 64.25%, and uncompressed DEX from 16.31 MB to 14.84 MB. The AAB dropped from 29.95 MB to 18.33 MB, but most of that was a greeting-card editor and roughly 11 MB of its assets leaving in the same release. Optimization's own share sits inside the 1.5 MB of DEX.

Unobfuscated code rose from 54.16% to 61.46%. The commit put that down to "app code shrank, so the SDK keep rules weigh more" and moved on. Version 1.6.020 shipped on September 22. Three days later came the 36/39/39% reading from the top of this note.

The merged configuration.txt had a rule on class *

Every rule R8 actually applied ends up in one file, app/build/outputs/mapping/release/configuration.txt: the defaults, the app's six .pro files, and the consumer rules each library AAR brings along. The merged file from the October 9, 2026 release build is 1,369 lines, short enough to read end to end. Reading through it on September 25 turned up this block.

# proguard-kakao.pro (in the repo since the first commit, 2020-12-16)
-keep class com.kakao.** { *; }
-keepattributes Signature
-keepclassmembers class * {
  public static <fields>;
  public *;
}
-dontwarn android.support.v4.**,org.slf4j.**,com.google.android.gms.**

In the third rule, class * has no condition, so it matches every class in the app and in every library. Their public fields and methods can then not be removed, renamed or inlined. And the Kakao SDK (the SDK for KakaoTalk login and sharing) was not a dependency at all; even its Maven repository line in the root build script was commented out.

Commit e05f8e3 deleted the file and both build references to it, release and debug. It also deleted proguard-retrofit2.pro, which no build had ever referenced.

Do not ship an unconditional keep rule on class * in an Android app. Libraries that need rules already ship them as consumer rules inside their AAR.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Before and after: r8.json and sizes for both changes

Each pair of columns comes from a different day and a different commit, so compare within a pair. Even the same configuration drifts in the second decimal: 64.25% on September 20, 64.27% on September 25.

Metric1.6.019 baseline-dontoptimize removed (Sep 20)Before kakao file removal (Sep 25)After (Sep 25)
Not optimized100%64.25%64.27%15.68%
Not obfuscated54.16%61.46%61.48%15.14%
Not shrunknot recordednot recorded61.47%15.18%
As Play shows it (opt/obf/shrink)optimization 0% (Play screen)36/39/- (derived from r8.json)36/39/39% (Play screen)84/85/85 (derived from r8.json, not yet seen on Play)
DEX16.31 MB (uncompressed)14.84 MB15.6 MB (total)8.2 MB
AAB29.95 MB18.33 MB (asset removal included)18.4 MB11.6 MB

Measured by DEX size, deleting one rule did about five times what removing -dontoptimize did. DEX shrank by 1.5 MB on September 20 and by 7.4 MB (47%) on September 25, and the AAB lost another 6.8 MB.

Before release, a release APK signed with the debug key ran on an API 34 emulator. A spelling check against Naver (Korea's largest web portal) came back with the two corrections the server reported, and the post-check quiz bubble, the quiz screen and Remote Config content injection all worked. The five JSON key strings Gson reads were still present verbatim in the release DEX. (A headless emulator returns black screenshots, so we read screen text with uiautomator dump instead.)

From September 22 to October 3 the post-release watch log recorded zero crashes for 1.6.020, for 1.6.024 (the first release without the kakao rule) and for 1.6.025, and closed the item as "no regression".

The clue the agent explained away

An AI coding agent (Claude) wrote both commits. On September 20 it declared in the commit message that the -dontoptimize line was the cause. It also recorded, accurately, that unobfuscated code had gone up by more than 7 points. It did not check which rule was holding that code; it filled the gap with a guess that the keep rules had not changed and the SDKs simply weighed more.

On the afternoon of September 25 the operator pasted a Play Console screenshot, noted that the bundle still looked unoptimized, and asked for a deeper analysis. Only then did the agent open the merged configuration, and the seven-line file from 2020 surfaced. Opening configuration.txt first instead of guessing would have saved five days.

Two lines went into the repository's agent instructions afterwards: never add a keep rule on class *, and check the merged result in configuration.txt. The checks we run to catch release-only R8 failures before shipping are in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app.

Still open

  • Confirming the Play screen. The repository holds only the 85% derived from r8.json; nothing records the Play Console figure after release. We will capture it on the next upload.
  • The ratio creeping back. A new Firebase dependency in 1.6.025 pulled the build down about 5 points, to roughly 80%. The release AAB left on disk from October 9, 2026 reads 20.23% unoptimized with 9.30 MB of DEX (9,302,488 bytes). Next step: diff configuration.txt to see which consumer rule arrived.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Does the Play Console DEX optimization warning block uploads?

It did not in September 2026: bundles at 0% and at 36% optimization both shipped normally. Our repository notes say Play expects it fixed by February 2027, so it is not something to leave for later.

Can I see the optimization percentage before uploading to Play?

Yes. Extract BUNDLE-METADATA/com.android.tools/r8.json from the release AAB and subtract the three stats values from 100. For this app, 61.47 matched Play's 39%. That mapping is our inference from repository records, and nothing yet records whether Play showed the 85% that 15.18 implies.

How do I find the keep rule that is holding the metric down?

Search the merged configuration.txt for -keep or -keepclassmembers rules on wide patterns such as class * or ** with no condition attached. Here it was a single -keepclassmembers class * { public *; } block in a file for an SDK the app did not use.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

item.title: Accurate sitemap lastmod from a content hash – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Short note

Every sitemap lastmod had the same date: deriving modified dates from a content hash

Don't type lastmod by hand or copy it from git commit dates. Compute it from a hash of the page body, and keep the date itself out of what you hash.

Pull sitemap.xml out of commit 12ed443 and count its lastmod values: every one of the 51 URLs says <lastmod>2026-10-18</lastmod>. One commit earlier there were five different dates. Today a page's modified date only moves when its body hash changes. A commit on October 19 touched 99 HTML files and moved the date on just 6 existing pages.

Sources: this site's git history, tools/dates.py and tools/indexnow.py, checked on October 20, 2026.

Commit dates made every page look new

The old build set each URL's lastmod to the date of the last git commit that touched the file. That helper, git_date, arrived on October 5 in bdbbe97, a commit that carries an AI coding agent's co-author line. The agent's code measured when a file changed.

It broke on 12ed443, a site-wide pass. Fifty-two HTML files went into one commit, each gaining an RSS <link> in its head, and all 51 sitemap URLs ended up on that day. Re-running today's hash rule (the inside of <main>) over those 52 files, only 2 had real body changes: the SugarDoc app page in Korean and English. 42 had identical bodies. The other 8 differed by a single added line, a "last updated" date. (Counting structured data in the head as well, 11 pages changed their FAQ or feature list.)

Google's sitemap documentation says it uses lastmod only if the value is "consistently and verifiably" accurate, and gives a copyright date update as an example of a change that isn't significant.

The date moves only when the body hash changes

The October 18 restructure, b82faac, moved all page dates into one file, data/content-dates.json. The agent co-wrote that commit too. The new tools/dates.py opens by citing a written spec section for dates (IA spec 4.1). For a hand-written page it hashes the inside of <main> with breadcrumbs and build-generated blocks removed:

def hand_input(page_html):
    inner = main_html(page_html)       # inside <main> only
    inner = _CRUMBS_RE.sub("", inner)  # drop breadcrumbs
    inner = strip_build_blocks(inner)  # drop <!-- build:* --> blocks
    return _WS_RE.sub(" ", inner).strip()
# same hash: keep dates; new hash: modified = today
# new page: published = modified = today

The easy thing to miss is the date itself. In 12ed443 the "last updated" line sat inside <main> as plain HTML. Hash that line and every date change looks like a content change, so the next day's build moves the date again, forever. On hand-written pages the line now lives in a build:meta block. Those 8 app pages became generated pages built from data/apps.json, so their hash covers the input data, not the HTML. A unit test (test_every_marker_block_is_removed) asserts the phrase never reaches the hash input, and test_idempotent_next_day checks that a rerun the next day leaves the dates alone.

Never derive lastmod from commit dates or build dates. Don't let people edit it either: the repository's AGENTS.md says "never edit dates by hand" (how we write that file is in How to write AGENTS.md).

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

99 files touched, 6 dates moved

Commit b79f2d1 on October 19 touched 99 HTML files, mostly to bump a ?v= cache-busting value on the stylesheet links. Apart from 14 new pages, the modified date moved on 6 existing ones: the home page, the apps hub and the privacy policy list, in Korean and English, each of which now lists the new pages.

IndexNow pings follow the same dates. tools/indexnow.py picks only pages whose modified date is today, and it is a dry run unless you pass --send.

What we check next

The related-notes list (build:extra) is excluded from the hash. Google counts link changes as significant, yet when a new note joins that list, older notes keep their dates. We will decide after reading Search Console's crawl data in November 2026.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Does Google actually use sitemap lastmod?

Yes, but only when the values are consistently and verifiably accurate, for example when they match the page's real last change. The same page (updated 2026-07-08) says Google ignores priority and changefreq.

Do you send every URL to IndexNow on each deploy?

No. Only pages modified today go out. The full list (--all) is meant to be sent once, right after registering the site with Naver Search Advisor, the webmaster console of the Korean search engine Naver.

item.title: CarDrawer (차서랍) – Android app for used-car dealers in Korea | SugarMount
item.description:
CarDrawer 차서랍

Android app for used-car dealers in Korea

Recruiting 5 pilot shopsClosed testing on Google Play soon

One drawer
per car.

AI files every receipt and flags what's missing.

Snap a receipt, invoice or inspection report, or share a PDF. CarDrawer pulls out the vendor, amount, date and plate as suggestions and files them in that car's drawer. Every morning it shows what is due today, which papers are missing, which costs need approval and which cars have started losing money.

Apply for the pilot How it works

Free cost sheet template (CSV) · A per-car cost sheet that opens in Excel: 18 cost items with total-cost and difference formulas. No sign-up or email needed.

  • AI only suggests. A person confirms.
  • We never ask for your HeyDealer, Encar or other platform passwords.
  • Your costs are visible only to you and the people you allow.
The problem

Costs leak car by car, and papers scatter across chat rooms

Receipts in drawers and chats

Transport, polish, body work, dealer fees, listing ads: one car collects close to ten cost items. Matching each receipt to the right car falls on the office manager.

Deadlines in someone's head

Ownership transfer, inspection-report validity and platform claim windows differ for every car. Missing one means fines or disputes.

Profit known only after the sale

Financing interest and late invoices can turn a car you thought was profitable into a loss, and it is hard to see where each car stands today.

A car bought for ₩30.01M: about ₩630,000 left if sold in 3 months · cut the price in month 7 and it becomes a ₩970,000 loss

A dealer's public cost sheet (9 cost items; re-listing, interest and re-inspection added in month 7). Source: Clien post, 23 Aug 2025 (Korean), checked Oct 2026. One case, not a general figure.
What it does

Snap it, it sticks. Missing pieces come first.

  • Snap and it sticks

    “Snap the receipt. We attach it to the right car.”

    Upload from the camera, gallery or share menu in three taps. AI suggests the vendor, amount, date and plate; only values checked against the original reach your costs.

  • Today's deadlines, cars losing money

    “Do you know how much this car still makes?”

    The first screen gathers overdue tasks, today's deadlines, pending approvals and at-risk cars, with legal, platform and in-house deadlines labelled separately.

  • One shop, your costs stay yours

    “You decide who sees what.”

    Owner, buyers and office staff share the same car cards. Purchase prices, costs and counterparties are visible only with permission, and access ends the moment someone leaves.

  • Works next to your apps

    “Keep your apps. We fill the gaps.”

    Cars from any channel on one board. Platform screenshots are stored, never scraped. Export costs as CSV for your existing system or accountant.

Screens

Today · Review · Costs · Sales prep

Screen examples. All cars, plates, people and shop names are made up; the app is in development and may look different.

How it works

Upload → suggest → confirm → organise

  1. Upload on the lot. Buyers photograph receipts, invoices and inspection reports or share them. The app asks you to mask resident registration and similar ID numbers yourself with its masking tool before upload, and photo location data is removed on the device.
  2. AI suggests values. It sorts document types and copies vendor, amount, date and plate exactly as written. Fixed formulas, not AI, clean up and check the numbers.
  3. A person confirms against the original. Amounts, the car a document belongs to, odometer, accident or replacement marks and seizure or mortgage status always need human approval. The office can review in one batch later.
  4. Costs, deadlines and sales prep update. Confirmed values fill per-car costs and break-even, paperwork checklists, required ad items and draft descriptions.

“No information” is not “no problem”

Blank never means “none”. Every value carries a state, and anything not confirmed stays out of outgoing material.

  • Confirmed
  • AI suggestion
  • Needs review
  • Conflict
  • Unreadable
  • Not checked
  • Not entered
  • Confirmed absent
Open formulas

How costs and deadlines are calculated

Operating contribution

Sale income − purchase − direct costs − financing cost

Expected sale income₩22,300,000
Purchase− ₩20,000,000
Direct costs (body work, dealer fee, polish, ads, transport)− ₩1,330,000
Financing (₩20M · 12%/yr · 30 days, simple)− ₩197,260
Operating contribution₩772,740

Financing runs from the day funds were actually drawn, not the bid date. Overheads and tax are not included, so we never call it “net profit”. Demo figures.

Default deadline rules (reference)

TaskDefault reminder
Ownership transfer filing15 days by law; counting rules vary, so we remind at purchase date + 14 days
Inspection reportRe-inspection task after 120 days from the inspection date
Keeping report copies1 year from issue
Inspection warranty30 days or 2,000 km after delivery
Aged stockCaution at 60 days, warning at 90 (adjustable)

Reference settings based on Korean law and platform policies as checked in October 2026. Each rule is versioned and marked “dealer to confirm”; check before relying on it.

What it does not do

Things the app never does for you

  • Post listings, send messages, transfer money, bid or file documents. It prepares files and text and hands them to the share menu.
  • Connect to or scrape other platforms. Platform screenshots and auction diagnoses are stored only, never sent to AI.
  • Declare a car “accident-free” or write “warranty” or “lowest price” without evidence.
  • Perform statutory disclosure, inspections or ownership transfer. Those duties stay with the dealer.
  • Recommend purchase prices. The purchase-limit calculator only uses the assumptions you enter.
  • Give tax advice or file returns. It tags receipts and exports them.
Data and privacy

Customer data belongs to the dealership

  • For owner and buyer details in uploaded records, the dealership is the controller and we process them only as instructed. They are never used for marketing or AI training.
  • Data is stored in Google Cloud's Seoul region. Document reading uses Google Vertex AI (Gemini, paid tier), which may process outside Korea.
  • No advertising SDK or advertising ID. No payments inside the app.
  • Export everything as CSV and an original-file ZIP at any time, and for 30 days after you cancel.

Details: Privacy policy · Terms of service · Processors and sub-processors · Delete your account

We're looking for 5 pilot dealerships

For shops of 2 to 10 people that buy and resell their own stock. We visit Suwon and Gangseo (Seoul) dealer complexes first. Use it free for 4 weeks while we measure the time it saves together; if it saves none, you don't pay.

Apply for the pilot Pricing

Questions

Does it work on iPhone or a PC?

Android comes first. If pilot shops need review and cost screens on an office PC, we will add a web version based on the pilot results.

Does it sync with HeyDealer or Encar?

No. We don't take platform credentials or scrape anything. Screenshots or diagnosis files you upload are stored in the car's drawer and never sent to AI.

What if AI reads an amount wrong?

AI values stay marked “AI suggestion” until a person approves them against the original. Amounts and the car a document belongs to always need approval. Use “Report a problem” on any wrong result.

Can staff see each other's costs?

Purchase prices, costs, profit and counterparties are visible only with permission. Independent dealers sharing a shop name decide who sees their costs.

What happens to my data if I stop?

You can view and export (CSV, original-file ZIP) for 30 days after cancelling; then it is deleted. Cancel in the app or with one email.

How much does it cost?

The 14-day trial needs no card and never converts to paid automatically. See pricing.

Contact

For demos, onboarding or bug reports, email us with your shop name and how to reach you. We reply as soon as we can.

Email: sugarmount21@gmail.com

Package name
com.sugarmount.cardrawer
Developer

item.title: Block puzzle difficulty tuned with simulation bots – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · How-to

Block puzzle difficulty: how simulation bots caught a game you could never lose

If every tray of three pieces is guaranteed to fit, a player who finds each tray's solution never loses. Block Turn now keeps that guarantee for the first 10 trays only.

As first specified, the classic mode of Block Turn had no game over. We found out from bots: on October 3, 2026, under the supply rule written in the spec (v1), a bot that plans the whole tray played 80 games, and all 80 hit the 3,000-move cap. The shipped rule, v7, ends a planner's game after a median of 122 moves and a greedy bot's after 47.

Numbers come from the sugar-game repository: the supply experiment log (docs/block/lab.md, measured 2026-10-03), the spec review, and the engine code and tests. Checked on October 19, 2026.

One friendly promise removed the game over

Block Turn is an 8×8 block puzzle in the Block Blast mold: you get three pieces, place them, full rows and columns clear, and then you get three more. The spec we started from (v2.0) promised this in section 7.1: "When a new set of three pieces is dealt, there is at least one order in which all three fit on the current board." It was meant to answer players who feel the piece supply is rigged. The spec even added that a player can still get stuck by placing badly.

That caveat only covers weak play. For a player who finds the solution, the promise turns into a loop:

  1. When a tray arrives, some order places all three pieces.
  2. Play that order and the tray is empty.
  3. The next tray gets the same guarantee. Back to step 1.

The run never ends. Nothing in that argument depends on piece weights, so dealing more awkward pieces cannot break it. The bots confirmed that too (v3 and v4 below).

A greedy bot and a planning bot on the same seeds

The engine stores the board as a single 64-bit integer, so scoring a position takes a handful of bit operations.

  • Greedy bot: it scores every legal move right now with the formula below and plays the best one. A cleared line is worth 10, so it usually picks the move that clears the most lines.
  • Planning bot: it searches every order and placement of the pieces left in the tray, plays the first move of the best plan, and searches again on the next move.

Both use the same board score:

score = lines cleared × 10 − 3 × holes − 0.3 × filled cells + 2 × room
holes = empty cells boxed in on all four sides
room  = is there space for a 3×3 square, a 1×4 bar, a 4×1 bar (0–3)

In the final comparison each supply version got 160 greedy games and 80 planner games, and every version used the same seeds. A game stops at 3,000 moves. The bots are not models of people. We assume a person lands somewhere between them, and we use the bot numbers only to rank supply rules against each other.

The four numbers that decided it

  • Planner games that hit the 3,000-move cap. Anything above zero rejects the version, because it means the game cannot be lost.
  • Planner median divided by greedy median. In a high-score mode, "play better, last longer" is most of the fun, so we wanted skill to show up as run length.
  • Greedy run length, so a careless player doesn't wash out in a few trays.
  • Tray generation time at p95, to see whether supply cost matters on a phone.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

Supply rules v1 to v7, side by side

The awkward pieces are the 3×3 square, the 2×3 rectangle in both orientations and the four-cell bar in both orientations. "Pressure" means that every N moves those pieces gain one more multiple of their base weight, up to a cap.

VersionSupply ruleGreedy medianPlanner medianPlanner games at capOutcome
v1The spec: every tray fully placeable56 moves3,000 moves80/80Rejected
v2v1, plus 3× weight for pieces of 3 cells or fewer when fewer than 28 cells are emptyNot in the results tableDropped (made the game easier)
v3v1 plus pressure every 30 moves, up to 5×Not in the results table60/60Rejected
v4v1 plus pressure every 20 moves, up to 8×Not in the results table60/60Rejected
v5v7 plus pressure every 30 moves, up to 5×44 moves80 moves0A/B candidate
v6v7 plus pressure every 20 moves, up to 8×44 moves82 moves0Not used
v7Full guarantee for the first 10 trays, then only "at least one piece fits"47 moves122 moves0Default

Under v1 the planner's median game lasted 1,001 trays and scored 26,772 points. Under v7 it was 41 trays and 998 points. In the four versions with full numbers (v1, v5, v6, v7), the greedy bot never reached the cap.

We picked v7 for the skill gap: 122 moves against 47 is 2.6×. Adding pressure (v5, v6) cut that gap to 1.8 to 1.9×, mostly by cutting the strong player's runs short. Shorter runs mean more game-over screens, but they also mean a good player gets less for being good. So v7 shipped as the default, and v5 is parked as an A/B candidate.

Supply cost turned out to be a non-issue. Tray generation stayed at or under 0.2 ms at p95 for every version with timings in the table, and the spec's last-resort fallback (deal three single cells) never fired in 2,710 trays of the earlier Python simulation.

If a game spec says the player can "always" do something, run a bot that exploits that promise to the end before you build on it. Reading the sentence will not show you the problem.

The AI's first review pushed the other way

Earlier the same day, the spec review written by our AI coding agent had already simulated the supply rule in Python. It ran a random bot and a one-move greedy bot for 150 games each, with medians of 17 and 26 moves. It also tried a bot that reads the whole tray, then gave up on it: searching a single tray on an empty board took more than ten minutes in Python.

From those short runs, the review concluded that a solvable tray does not guarantee a long game, and recommended "relief" supply: deal smaller pieces when the board gets crowded. That is v2 in the table.

A promise that only matters to the strongest player had been tested with the weakest bots. Once the Kotlin engine existed, the planning bot ran in reasonable time and every v1 planner game hit the cap. v2 was dropped, and spec v2.1 rewrote the supply promise as v7. The engine, the experiment tool and the tests landed together in commit cd62087 (October 4, 2026, Korea time).

(The Python greedy bot used a different board score with no "room" term, so its 26 moves and the Kotlin greedy bot's 56 under v1 are not a like-for-like comparison.)

The v1 finding is pinned by a unit test, a planner cannot be stopped under the full guarantee: on 20 seeds, playing each tray's solution must pass 300 moves.

What we still have to check

  • We don't know how long a human run is yet. The target is a median of 60 to 150 moves (roughly 4 to 10 minutes), and if real runs fall outside it we switch to v5. The end-of-run event that carries the move count, post_score, had fired only twice in total as of our October 17 GA4 review. The same review noted that the first-run flow never showed classic mode, so commit d1f6de1 (1.1.2) added a button into classic mode after the last tutorial.
  • Since 1.1.4 (b2d305d, October 17) a classic run allows two revives. The supply experiment ran without revives, so run length with revives needs measuring again.
  • The default supply rule itself is pinned by a test (default supply guarantees the first ten trays fully and never deals a dead tray after), so switching the default back to v1 would fail it. What no test checks is that a planner actually loses before the cap under the default supply. Today only a fresh supply experiment run shows that.

How the earlier apps came out of the same agent-driven workflow is in How we shipped four Android apps in 20 days with an AI coding agent.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

What should the game over condition be in a block puzzle?

The game ends when none of the remaining pieces fits anywhere. If the supply only ever deals trays that fully fit, a strong player never meets that condition. Block Turn guarantees full trays for the first 10 and, after that, only that at least one piece fits.

Can't you fix it by dealing more hard pieces?

No. Even with awkward pieces weighted up to 8× (v4), every planner game reached the 3,000-move cap. While the full guarantee stands, weights only change which solvable tray you get.

How many games does a balance simulation need?

In the final comparison we ran 160 greedy and 80 planner games per version, on the same seeds for every version (the earlier v3 and v4 runs used 60 planner games). That was enough to separate results like 80/80 games at the cap versus 0/80.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • A reverse-construction generator and the gate behind 1,100 arrow-puzzle levels
  • Testers said the time was "too long, so it's easy": checking that with a simulation before cutting puzzle par times by 30%
  • Puzzle game day-one churn: per-device event timelines, exact board math and four walls in chapter one
  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException
  • A market:// link opens a store chooser on SKT-sold Samsung phones: set the Play package first
  • A splash that never moved on: addOnCompleteListener(this) and onStop

All notes on Game development · All AX notes

item.title: VIBRATE crash and the fresh-install monkey test – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Incident

The agent said it was tested. The game crashed on the first tutorial tap: a missing VIBRATE permission and the fresh-install monkey test

Scripted device tests missed a crash caused by one missing permission line. Running adb monkey on a freshly cleared app reproduced it at the 15th of 800 events.

At 22:58 on October 1, 2026 (Korea time), our AI coding agent installed a pre-release build of the puzzle game Arrow Knots on a Galaxy S24 and reported "launched in 857 ms, no crash". Four minutes later the operator reported that it errored out in the tutorial: the app closed on the first arrow tap. The code called Vibrator.vibrate, the manifest did not declare android.permission.VIBRATE, and the call threw a SecurityException. The fix, commit 65dcf41, landed 5 minutes 29 seconds after the crash report, and a fresh-install monkey script (f7beb3d) followed 15 seconds later.

Sources: the game repository's git history, the agent's session log from that night, and the agent's memory files. Times are Korea Standard Time (UTC+9). Checked on October 19, 2026.

Four minutes from "installed" to "it crashes"

TimeWhat happened
22:47Commit 3eb21df adds the tutorial and switches haptics to VibrationEffect composition primitives
22:58Agent reports the S24 install as "no crash". The S24 then drops off adb, so no screenshot. Asked "So is it tested?", it says the S24 was only installed and launched, and the S21 had "automated tests complete"
23:02Operator: it errors out in the tutorial. On the S21, with progress cleared, monkey seed 7 crashes the app at event 15 of 800
23:07Fix committed as 65dcf41; tools/monkey_check.sh follows 15 seconds later as f7beb3d

The agent's mistake was in what "no crash" rested on: am start -W returning Status: ok and a 857 ms launch time. Nothing on screen was ever tapped. (The logcat it read did contain a FATAL EXCEPTION, from a Samsung system app on September 30. The agent correctly ignored it.)

Cause: Vibrator.vibrate without the VIBRATE permission

Ten minutes before the install, commit 3eb21df replaced View.performHapticFeedback with Vibrator.vibrate(VibrationEffect.startComposition()…). The code comment gives the reason: on Samsung devices CONTEXT_CLICK is barely felt.

The two APIs have different rules. View haptics need no permission. Vibrator.vibrate needs android.permission.VIBRATE, and the manifest did not declare it. The game buzzes every time an arrow leaves the board, so the very first tutorial tap was the crash.

E AndroidRuntime: FATAL EXCEPTION: main
E AndroidRuntime: Process: (pre-release package name), PID: 12034
E AndroidRuntime: java.lang.SecurityException: vibrate: Neither user 10322 nor current process has android.permission.VIBRATE.

The fix touched two files, six lines added and one removed: declare the permission, and fall back to view haptics if the vibrator call fails for any reason.

<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.VIBRATE" />
runCatching { v.vibrate(VibrationEffect.startComposition().addPrimitive(primitive, scale).compose()) }
    .onFailure { view.performHapticFeedback(fallback) }

VIBRATE is a normal permission, granted at install with no dialog. Leave it out and the debug build still compiles.

Why the scripted tests missed it

Two device scripts were running on the S21 at the time. tutorial_check.py taps the three tutorial lessons in a fixed order. device_check.py writes a progress file to jump to a given level, then solves the board. Neither had a real pass condition. The tutorial script stops only if it cannot find the "Next" button, and the level script prints how many taps it sent. Neither looked for a crash in logcat or checked that the process was still alive.

The agent's own explanation was that the scripts only tap a fixed path. That is half right. The bigger hole was a check that never looked at crashes. (The tutorial script did run to the end on the S21 at about 22:45. Whether that build already had the vibration change was not checked that night, and the log does not say.)

device_check.py also writes tutorialDone=true when it jumps to a level, so it skips the first screens a new player sees by design. The new-player path only exists when the app has no data.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

The fresh-install monkey script

tools/monkey_check.sh loops over three fixed seeds (7, 21, 99). For each one it wipes the app's data, launches it, sends 800 random events, and counts FATAL EXCEPTION lines in logcat. Any non-zero count fails the run. Below is the core of the current version, without device selection, output cleanup and the exit code. The script defaults to the debug package; here it uses the release package published on Play.

PKG=com.sugarmount.arrows
adb shell setprop debug.firebase.analytics.app $PKG
for seed in 7 21 99; do
  adb shell am force-stop $PKG
  adb shell pm clear $PKG
  adb logcat -c
  adb shell am start -W -n $PKG/sugar.arrows.MainActivity
  sleep 2
  adb shell monkey -p $PKG --pct-touch 90 --pct-motion 10 --pct-nav 0 --pct-majornav 0 \
    --pct-syskeys 0 --pct-appswitch 0 --throttle 120 -s $seed 800
  n=$(adb logcat -d | grep -c "FATAL EXCEPTION")
  echo "seed=$seed fatal=$n"
done
  • -p keeps events inside this package.
  • --pct-touch 90 --pct-motion 10: 90% taps, 10% drags. Navigation, system keys and app switching are set to 0 so the run stays in the game.
  • --throttle 120 waits 120 ms between events. The last argument, 800, is the event count, so a run takes at least 96 seconds.
  • -s fixes the seed, which replays the same event sequence. Before the fix, seed 7 printed System appears to have crashed at event 15 of 800 using seed 7. After it, the same seed injected all 800.

"Fresh install" here means no app data at all. The first version deleted a single progress file through run-as, which only works on debuggable builds. When release signing went in on October 3 (commit f421333), it became pm clear, with the comment "works on release (non-debuggable) builds too". If you suspect the install itself, run adb uninstall and install again. The script does not reinstall per seed; it clears data.

The pass condition changed too. The first version counted every FATAL EXCEPTION on the device, which also counts other apps' crashes, like the Samsung one on the S24. On October 4 the block puzzle game's block_monkey.sh (commit 575aaa1) began counting only Process: <package>, lines plus am_anr entries from the events buffer. Its comment notes that uiautomator and the monkey tool can die on their own. On October 18 (dca02f2) both scripts gained a setprop debug.firebase.analytics.app call before the loop. That makes test runs visible in Firebase DebugView, but it does not keep them out of the GA4 reports; that takes a separate developer traffic data filter on the GA4 property (corrected 2026-10-26).

(During the post-fix check, the S21 briefly disconnected in the middle of seed 21. Any run that printed - waiting for device - was thrown out and repeated.)

The rule: no "done" without a fresh-install monkey run

After that night the agent's memory gained one rule. Before calling an Android build tested, run monkey_check.sh on the connected device, on top of the fixed-path scripts, and name every device it ran on. Always run it when the manifest, a permission or a system-service call changes. The rule also includes the line "installing is not verifying".

Commit messages changed after that. As of October 19, 2026, 19 of the 144 commits since f7beb3d mention monkey in the message, and 16 of those report a result, in lines like "release (R8, test ads) monkey 3x1500 0 fatals" and "Android 7 launch and monkey pass on API 24". The other three are a tool list or a "still to run". Reported event counts range from 600 to 4,000.

When an agent says "done", ask which device and what ran on it. Without a monkey result from clean app data, we do not accept it as done. The wider pre-release routine is in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app, and how we pin rules like this one for the agent is in How to write AGENTS.md for an AI coding agent.

The next day (October 2) a new stress suite crashed the game 28 times on its first pass through 300 levels: a blocked arrow springing back from far away overshot and read points[-1], an IndexOutOfBoundsException fixed in 69781a7. A fresh-install monkey run starts at the tutorial and the first level, so deep levels need their own runs.

What is still open

Arrow Knots' monkey_check.sh still counts every FATAL EXCEPTION on the device and ignores ANRs. It should match the block game's script and count only its own process's crashes plus ANRs. Several agent sessions share the same phones, so another app's crash failing our run is the first thing to fix.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Do I need to ask the user for the VIBRATE permission?

No. VIBRATE is a normal permission, granted at install once it is declared in AndroidManifest.xml. View.performHapticFeedback works without it, but calling Vibrator.vibrate without the declaration throws a SecurityException and kills the app.

How many seeds and events should an adb monkey run use?

Our default is three seeds (7, 21, 99) at 800 events each, and five commits record release builds with test ads run at 1,500 events per seed. Fixing the seed is what lets you replay the exact sequence that failed.

Can I run monkey on a build with live ads?

We never do. Random taps on real ads are invalid clicks and put the AdMob account at risk, so monkey and other automated taps only run on builds using Google's test ad IDs.

If unit tests pass, can I skip the monkey run?

Not if you want to catch this kind of crash. All 31 engine unit tests passed that night. Permission checks happen in the device's system service, so a JVM unit test never sees them.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • AI coding agents and secrets: one rule in chat, logs and token permissions, and the two exceptions a copied masking regex missed
  • What "100% E2E pass" really meant: deleting seven runners with zero expect() calls
  • We built an edit feature and shipped it switched off: the HWP save gate that caught a form-field bug

item.title: Building an Android HWP viewer with rhwp: measured – SugarMount
item.description:
AX notes · Measurement

Building an Android HWP viewer: rhwp in a WebView, measured on 222 documents

Running the open-source rhwp engine inside an Android WebView, 221 of 222 Korean HWP and HWPX files opened on a Galaxy S21, with a median of 1.2 to 1.5 seconds from tap to first page.

221 of 222 Korean word-processor files opened. Before writing HWP Viewer SugarDoc, we wanted to know whether the engine could carry an app at all, so on October 3, 2026 we opened every file from a cold start on a Galaxy S21 (Android 15, WebView 153). The engine passed, with two catches. Drawing every page of a 384-page file pushed the WebView renderer to 2.8 GB, and the set the first report called "24 government documents" held only 17 real government attachments.

Numbers come from the engine spike report in SugarMount's app repository (sugar-utils; measured 2026-10-03, commit 7b0e567), the follow-up verification report (2026-10-05), and a recount from the raw result JSON done while writing this note. Checked on October 19, 2026.

HWP, HWPX and why a viewer is hard

HWP is the file format of Hancom Office Hangul, the word processor that Korean government offices, schools and many employers still use. HWP 5 is a binary compound file; HWPX is the newer ZIP-and-XML version; very old files are HWP 3.0. On a phone they usually arrive as attachments in KakaoTalk (Korea's main messenger) or email.

Layout is the hard part. Government press releases lean on dense tables, logos and fixed line breaks, and exam papers add equations and two-column pages.

Setup: one phone, 222 files, a cold start each time

rhwp is an open-source HWP/HWPX parser written in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly. It renders each page as SVG and is MIT-licensed. We used the npm package @rhwp/core 0.8.6, and the shipped app is still pinned to that version.

The test app was a single WebView with rhwp and the font stylesheet rhwp ships (153 font rules). For every file the app was force-stopped and relaunched; the first three pages went into the DOM and the rest were only timed.

  • Attachments from Korea's government policy portal, korea.kr: 17 files downloaded on 2026-10-02 (14 press releases; 13 HWPX, 4 HWP).
  • 198 samples from the rhwp repository, each with a reference PDF printed from Hancom Office 2020 or 2022, so page counts and first-page images can be compared. Many are hard cases: exam papers, equations, converted HWP 3.0 files.
  • Seven more files, explained in the section on what the AI got wrong.

We had no low-end phone.

Results: 221 of 222 opened

"Tap to first page" is app launch time plus first-page render time, so it includes the cold start. p90 is the value where the slowest 10% begin. Renderer memory is the PSS (proportional set size: private memory plus a fair share of shared pages) of the WebView renderer process.

Metrickorea.kr, 17 filesFirst report's "24 government documents"rhwp samples, 198
Opened17/1724/24197/198
Tap to first page, median1.4 s1.5 s1.2 s
Tap to first page, p901.6 s2.1 s1.9 s
Tap to first page, max1.8 s3.0 s3.3 s
Render per page, median-10 ms6 ms
Renderer memory (PSS), max286 MB391 MB422 MB

The one failure, issue2063_huge_cellbreak_table.hwp, is a stress test built around a giant table split across pages; it ran past the 120-second limit. The spike report made a fallback path a condition for adopting the engine, and the app now lets you keep waiting or hand the file to another app after 10 seconds.

Fidelity held up. Against the reference PDFs, page counts matched for 195 of 197 samples (the other two were one page off), and the median first-page image similarity was 0.997. We also put seven files (two press releases, five samples) side by side with Hancom's output. The press-release tables, logos and bold text and the exam paper's equations and two columns looked nearly the same. The one visible miss was the first question number, "문1)", dropped from one exam paper.

Running into the same problem? Email us what you are seeing and we will reply. Email us

A 384-page file only works if you draw the visible pages

One rhwp sample is a 384-page government administration handbook (10.7 MB). With every page's SVG in the DOM, the WebView renderer process grew to 2.8 GB. Drawing only the visible pages, the same file sat at 255 MB in one run and 366 MB in another run the same afternoon.

If you build an HWP viewer on a WebView, put virtual scrolling (only the visible pages and their neighbours in the DOM) in from day one.

The shipped viewer gives every page an empty slot of the right size and keeps SVG only for the visible pages plus two on each side, or one on each side on low-memory devices. Rendered SVG strings live in a byte-capped LRU (least recently used) cache, so the pages viewed longest ago are dropped first.

Fonts went from 144 MB to 9.2 MB

The font folder that comes with rhwp is 87 files and 144,327,972 bytes. The spike report called it "138 MB", which is the same number counted in mebibytes. The 222 documents actually used 17 of those files, about 37 MB.

The app ships 10 files, 9,207,952 bytes, about 6% of the original. Two rules decided what went in: a clear license and a close look. Hancom's own Hamchorom fonts were left out because Hancom's license page does not spell out whether they may be bundled in an app; Hamchorom Batang is drawn with Noto Serif KR and Hamchorom Dotum with NanumGothic, both under the SIL Open Font License. rhwp's NanumGothic was a subset that kept the reserved font name, so we swapped in the original TTF from google/fonts.

On 2026-10-05 we measured the cost on the same S21: how much first-page ink overlap (F1) against the reference drops with the substitute fonts. The pass mark, fixed in advance, was a median drop of 0.02 or less; the median came out at 0.0071. One file went over at 0.0336, a college entrance exam (Suneung) paper whose title is in Chinese characters (hanja). The difference sat in the hanja title and the circled numbers ① to ⑤, which the bundled fonts lack, so the system font draws them.

What the AI got wrong, and what verification changed

An AI coding agent (Claude) session ran the engine spike and wrote its report. Two days later, the follow-up experiments split the work: one agent measured, a separate verifier agent reopened the evidence files and recomputed every number, and only corrected values went into the docs. The first report's statistics were recounted at that point.

First reportAfter verification
24 real government documents17 korea.kr files (14 press releases) plus 7 others: 4 byte-identical to samples, 3 rhwp test fixtures
Samples: 177 HWP, 21 HWPX180 HWP, 18 HWPX (9 of them HWP 3.0)
Number recall around 0.9A bug in the comparison script: text runs were joined with no separator, so 11:00 and 10. 2. became 11:0010. 2.. Fixed, all 17 korea.kr files score 1.0 (a lenient upper bound)
Bundled fonts 9,700 KB (the follow-up's measuring agent)KiB written as KB; 9,933,636 bytes is 9.93 MB (later cut to 9,207,952 bytes)

"24 of 24 government documents" reads well, and 7 of the 24 were not government documents. Counted alone, the 17 real files were faster (1.4 s median) and lighter (286 MB max). The engine decision did not change, but without the verifier we would have published a number with the wrong provenance.

Writing this note, we recomputed the medians once more from the raw s21b.json. The report's 1.5, 2.1 and 3.0 seconds came out exactly; the 366 MB run of the 384-page file turned up then. (The verification report also flagged that another script had overwritten one raw file, which must be regenerated before anyone quotes it.)

Still open

  • Low-end phones. According to the development plan, the Firebase Test Lab low-end run has not happened yet, so we do not know how a 400 MB renderer behaves on a 3 to 4 GB phone.
  • Hanja-heavy documents. The 0.0336 is only recorded, from a sample of two.
  • Upgrading rhwp. It is pre-1.0, so the app pins 0.8.6 and every build checks that the engine files match the pinned copy. An upgrade will be re-measured on the same 222 files. The other pre-release checks are in What to check before shipping an AI-built Android app.

Questions or ideas?

Send us where you got stuck applying this, a question about the numbers, or a topic you would like covered.

Email us sugarmount21@gmail.com

FAQ

Can rhwp be used in a commercial Android app?

Yes. rhwp is MIT-licensed, but the Rust crates compiled into its WASM (Apache-2.0, BSD and others) need their notices too. The fonts it ships carry their own licenses and need checking file by file. HWP Viewer SugarDoc bundles 10 font files with confirmed licenses, OFL and others, and leaves out Hamchorom.

Why does a WebView HWP viewer use so much memory?

Every rendered page stays in the DOM as SVG. A 384-page file took the renderer to 2.8 GB with all pages drawn and 255 MB with only the visible ones.

Does one engine open both HWP and HWPX?

Yes. rhwp 0.8.6 opens both, and 221 of the 222 mixed files here opened. The difference between the two formats is explained in HWP vs HWPX: what differs and how to open both. If an HWPX file from a chat app will not open on your phone, see How to open an HWPX or HWP file on Android.

This note is written from values SugarMount measured itself; an AI coding agent was used to draft it.

More AX notes

  • Pre-gzipping Android assets, measured: zero APK savings, and .pack.gz became .pack with a FileNotFoundException
  • A market:// link opens a store chooser on SKT-sold Samsung phones: set the Play package first
  • A splash that never moved on: addOnCompleteListener(this) and onStop
  • "6.7" < "6.11" is false: comparing Remote Config versions as strings froze content updates
  • A reverse-construction generator and the gate behind 1,100 arrow-puzzle levels
  • Daily users rose after the redesign while organic D1 retention fell from 15.2% to 11.2%
